title: .KPI Green gets LOI for 76.6-MW wind, solar hybrid project in Gujarat
content:
Indian integrated renewables company KPI Green Energy Ltd (BOM:542323) has received a letter of intent (LOI) for a 76.6-MWdc wind-solar hybrid power project in Gujarat under a group captive arrangement, it said in a stock exchange filing on Tuesday.
The project will install 33.6 MW of wind capacity and 33.6 MWac/43 MWdc of solar capacity, KPI Green said.
The company will establish a special purpose vehicle to develop, own and operate the project for a domestic private corporate customer, which has not been named. The project is expected to be completed within 14 months of Stage-2 connectivity and no later than December 31, 2027.
The energy supply agreement will have a 25-year term from its commencement date, according to the filing.
KPI Green said the order strengthens its presence in the commercial and industrial and group captive renewable energy segments and adds to its order book. It also aligns with its strategy to expand its renewable energy business through independent power producer, group captive and engineering, procurement and construction opportunities.

title: Aligned Climate Capital targets USD 500m for solar, storage fund
content:
US asset manager Aligned Climate Capital has held the first close of a fund targeting USD 500 million (EUR 431.3m) to acquire and finance construction-ready distributed solar and energy storage projects across the United States, the firm said on Tuesday.
The Aligned Solar Partners 7 (ASP7) infrastructure fund will source projects from development partners, finance their construction and manage the assets through operations. The first close includes commitments from existing investors in Aligned's strategy, including the Bush Foundation, a Minnesota-based charitable organisation.
The fund is Aligned's seventh infrastructure fund under its Aligned Solar Partners strategy, which the company has operated since 2018. It expects to make its first investments through ASP7 in the coming months.
Aligned said it has identified more than 500 MW of potential projects for the fund, providing a pipeline for deployment as fundraising continues.
The firm had acquired 56 projects across ten US states through its previous Aligned Solar Partners funds as of June 30, 2026. Its operating portfolio has generated more than 218 GWh of clean electricity, it said.
Recent activity includes construction financing for
two community solar projects
in Delaware and
the acquisition of a community solar project
in Illinois.
Aligned said rising US electricity demand, driven by data centre expansion, industrial reshoring and transport electrification, was increasing demand for new generation, while long delivery times for natural gas turbines were creating an opportunity for solar and storage.
“Distributed solar and energy storage are now among the fastest ways to add reliable capacity to the grid, and the middle market is where much of that build-out actually happens,” said Aligned Climate Capital’s CEO Peter Davidson.
Aligned Climate Capital invests in projects and companies in the clean energy transition space. Its investment strategies include the Aligned Climate Fund, which backs venture-stage clean energy companies, and Aligned Solar Partners, which owns and operates distributed solar, energy storage and other clean energy projects.
(USD 1.0 = EUR 0.863)

title: California sues Trump administration for Golden State Wind deal
content:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Energy Commission (CEC) have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration and Golden State Wind LLC over their agreement to terminate the developer’s 2-GW floating offshore wind project.
The deal
with the US Department of Interior (DOI) concerns the buyout of Golden State Wind’s lease in the Morro Bay Wind Energy Area off the Central California Coast in exchange for a refund of USD 120 million (EUR 106m) in lease fees and a commitment for an equal investment in fossil fuel assets along the Gulf Coast. According to California, the buyout violates federal laws, including the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act and the Judgment Fund Act, puts at stake thousands of jobs and threatens the general development of the offshore wind industry in the US.
Calling the deal “blatantly unlawful,” the state of California has requested the agreement to be revoked as the lease termination will harm the state’s clean energy and climate goals. It further argues that this “fabricated” arrangement risks over USD 100 million in investment commitments for port and transmission projects supporting offshore wind generation.
“The Trump Administration’s backroom buyout with Golden State Wind to stop offshore wind development in favour of gas and oil drilling is, unfortunately, a classic playbook for them to line the pockets of their Big Oil donors,” said Attorney General Bonta.
The court filing follows a
Notice of Intent to Sue
following an administrative investigative subpoena that the CEC served to Golden State Wind seeking information related to its agreement with DOI.
Golden State Wind is a joint venture of Ocean Winds and Reventus Power. Its deal with DOI is similar to arrangements made with Bluepoint Wind LLC,
Invenergy
and
TotalEnergies
to cancel leases for offshore wind projects in New York, New Jersey and New England in favour of oil and gas investments.

title: Cloudberry closes buy of Nordic renewables platform of Orron Energy
content:
Norway’s Cloudberry Clean Energy ASA (OSE:CLOUD) has wrapped up the acquisition of the Nordic renewable energy platform and organisation of Orron Energy AB (STO:ORRON) as part of its efforts to become a leading renewable independent power producer (IPP) in the region.
The deal
agreed in June
, will provide Cloudberry with 758 GWh of additional annual proportionate power generation, lifting its overall production to roughly 2.1 TWh, the Norwegian group said on Monday.
Orron Energy has transferred its Nordic development business to Cloudberry by selling 100% of its stock in Orron Energy Sweden AB, Metsalamminkangas Wind Oy, Orron Energy Greenfield Finland Holding Oy and their underlying assets and subsidiaries. The transaction entitles Orron Energy to receive 124.4 million new shares in the enlarged Cloudberry business, making it the largest shareholder with a 27.01% stake. The Swedish firm will also get EUR 4.2 million in cash compensations.
The acquisition is seen to strengthen Cloudberry’s operations in the Nordics, where it owns wind, hydro, solar and battery storage assets, and make it an active player in all Nordic price areas. “With increased scale, greater diversification and identified operational synergies, Cloudberry is well positioned to capitalise on opportunities created by the energy transition and deliver long-term shareholder value,” the Norwegian company said.
Orron Energy’s 86-MW Karskruv wind farm in Sweden and its 12-GW project development business in Europe spanning data centres, solar power and batteries in the UK, Germany and France, are not part of the deal.

title: France to launch 250-MW second round of clean hydrogen auction
content:
France's Directorate General for Energy and Climate (DGEC) announced that it will soon open the second round of the country's low-carbon hydrogen support scheme, targeting around 250 MW of electrolyser capacity.
The announcement from the DGEC follows the selection of
the scheme's first three winners
in July, which together secured EUR 778 million (USD 901.9m) in funding over 15 years for a combined 161.4 MW of electrolysis capacity.
Under the mechanism, run by the DGEC and operated by the French Agency for Ecological Transition (ADEME), eligible candidates for the second round will be selected in early September and will have until the end of 2026 to submit their bids.
The scheme, which supports hydrogen production by water electrolysis for direct industrial use over 15-year contracts, aims to bring around 1 GW of electrolyser capacity online through three tender rounds.
Details of the second auction are expected to be published on ADEME's website in the coming days, the DGEC said.
France is targeting 4.5 GW of electrolyser capacity by 2030 and 8 GW by 2035.

title: Italy's ERG starts up 22.5-MW repowered wind farm in France
content:
Italian renewable power producer ERG SpA (BIT:ERG) has commissioned a 22.5-MW wind farm in eastern France, following a repowering project that more than doubled its installed capacity.
The Montbeliard wind farm in the Doubs department now consists of five Vestas V136 turbines rated at 4.5 MW each, with a total height of 180 metres, ERG said on Tuesday.
The revamped facility is expected to generate about 62 GWh of electricity annually, almost three times the estimated output of the previous configuration. ERG said the project maintains the same land use while making use of existing infrastructure.
Montbeliard is covered by a 20-year contract for difference (CfD), providing long-term revenue stability and predictability, the company said.
The electricity generated is enough to meet the annual needs of about 44,000 households and is expected to avoid around 18,000 tonnes of CO2 emissions each year.
Montbeliard was ERG’s first wind farm repowering project in France. Its energisation and commissioning has taken ERG's total installed wind and solar capacity in the country to 755 MW, the company added.

title: Japanese consortium works on port-located floating data centre concept
content:
A consortium of Japanese companies and a bank has come up with a concept for a port-located offshore floating data centre.
The consortium includes NTT Facilities Inc, a subsidiary of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp (TYO:9432), Nippon Yusen Kabushiki Kaisha, Eurus Energy Holdings Co Ltd and Mitsubishi UFJ Bank Ltd.
The partners have considered a variety of concepts for offshore data centres that seek to deal with challenges such as shortages of construction land and power, as well as prolonged construction lead times. Eventually, they have formulated a concept where floating data centres are moored alongside quays in port areas. Such facilities can make use of various locations, ensure connectivity with existing infrastructure and utilise coastal resources, they explain.
The consortium said it will proceed with the further development of the concept.

title: Obama Foundation to anchor Reactivate's community solar in Illinois
content:
The Obama Foundation has agreed to act as an anchor tenant for a number of community solar projects in Illinois developed by Chicago-based Reactivate, the parties said on Tuesday.
The non-profit, founded by former US President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama, struck a multi-year partnership with the renewables developer to secure predictable, lower-cost electricity through subscriptions to community solar, helping to offset energy costs associated with the Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.
The arrangement is intended to improve the financial viability of Reactivate's solar portfolios and allow low- and moderate-income households and small businesses to subscribe to remaining capacity through the Illinois Solar For All programme or other regional community solar programmes.
Eligible subscribers can achieve energy cost savings of up to 50% on their utility bills and benefit from shared solar projects without installing panels on their own properties, Reactivate and the Foundation said.
The partnership will provide a model for commercial, industrial and non-profit organisations to support community solar while helping lower energy costs for local customers, the statement said.
"By stepping forward as an anchor tenant, The Obama Foundation helps power the Presidential Center with clean energy while actively lowering the barrier to entry for local families and small businesses to cut their energy costs," said Reactivate CEO Utopia Hill.
"We believe that taking care of the one planet we have starts with the choices we make right in our own backyard. That is why the Obama Presidential Center not only is sourcing 100 percent of our electricity from renewable energy, but we are also partnering with a company that will expand access to solar energy to our neighbors," added Valerie Jarrett, CEO of the Obama Foundation.
Reactivate,
a community solar joint venture
founded by Chicago-based power company Invenergy and investment platform Lafayette Square in 2022, will develop, own and operate the projects covered by the agreement.

title: Odyssey raises USD 74m for emerging-market renewables financing
content:
US distributed renewable energy promoter Odyssey Energy Solutions has raised USD 74 million (EUR 63.8m) in new financing to expand its platform connecting project developers with capital and equipment suppliers across emerging markets.
The financing, which Odyssey announced on Tuesday, consists of a USD-27-million equity round and USD 47 million of debt. New equity investors include Broadscale Group, FMO and Al Mada Ventures, while existing backers including Union Square Ventures, Equal Ventures, Abstract Ventures, Twelve Below, FJ Labs, MCJ and Transition Ventures also participated.
Debt financiers include British International Investment, BIO, the Facility for Energy Inclusion, represented by Cygnum Capital, and the Energy Entrepreneurs Growth Fund, represented by TripleJump.
Odyssey's platform connects more than 6,000 solar installers and engineering, procurement and construction companies with financiers and equipment suppliers in more than 50 countries across Africa, Asia and Latin America. It has facilitated access to USD 3.6 billion in capital for distributed energy projects and unlocked 1.5 GW of projects to date, according to Odyssey.
The company said the new funding would support expansion of its procurement platform, launched in 2024, which aggregates equipment orders from smaller buyers to secure volume pricing and provides embedded supply-chain credit.
Odyssey said smaller installers often have order books exceeding their ability to deliver projects because of working-capital constraints. Its procurement and financing services are designed to enable them to buy equipment and build more projects concurrently.
Demand for distributed solar and storage is growing in Odyssey's core markets as falling technology costs and higher fossil-fuel prices improve project economics, the company said.
The latest financing follows Odyssey's
USD-15-million Series A
announced in May 2023, taking its total capital raised to USD 94 million.

title: PowerX, Smart Energy team up for BESS co-location in Japan
content:
Japanese battery systems manufacturer PowerX Inc (TYO:485A) will work together with domestic provider of operation and maintenance (O&M) services Smart Energy Co Ltd to explore the co-location of Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) with power plants.
Under a memorandum of understanding (MOU), the duo will combine their respective strengths, working on co-located BESS projects from their inception, deployment and operation, PowerX announced today.
Specifically, Smart Energy will identify and evaluate candidate projects and provide operation and maintenance (O&M) services after deployment. PowerX will supply BESS developed and manufactured in Japan.
They plan to develop one project by December 2026, three projects by December 2027, and ten projects by December 2028.
The partners will "pursue aggregation, with a view to participating in the supply-demand balancing and wholesale electricity markets," PowerX noted.

title: Saipem gets pre-FEED job for Synhelion project at RWE site in Germany
content:
Italian oilfield services provider Saipem SpA (BIT:SPM) will support Swiss-based cleantech company Synhelion in the development of a commercial-scale renewable synthetic fuel plant in Germany.
Synhelion said it has hired Saipem to carry out pre-FEED (pre-Front-End Engineering Design) activities for a project to produce 30,000 tonnes of renewable synthetic fuels per year, the primary focus of which will be sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), together with synthetic diesel and gasoline for shipping and road transportation. A site for the development has been reserved at RWE’s Knapsacker Huegel in the town of Huerth, North Rhine-Westphalia.
Saipem will closely collaborate with Synhelion on advancing project engineering and refining the facility’s technical configuration, including the process integration of Synhelion’s proprietary technology with the downstream fuel synthesis and upgrading processes.
Synhelion explained that pre-FEED engineering is needed for consolidating the technical and economic basis of the project ahead of the subsequent FEED phase and final investment decision.

title: TEAL launches Spanish renewables development platform
content:
Renewable energy developer TEAL has established Teal Renovables, a new company focused on the early-stage development of renewable energy projects in Spain, as part of its strategy to expand its international footprint.
Teal Renovables will develop projects aimed at supporting Spain’s decarbonisation, industry electrification and energy independence, drawing on TEAL’s global expertise and a dedicated local team.
Spain has been selected as a key market due to its policy framework, growing demand for clean energy and ambitions to advance renewable power deployment and industrial electrification.
The new platform will focus on working with local partners and stakeholders to advance renewable energy assets, with TEAL saying the move supports its broader strategy to invest in markets with strong long-term fundamentals.
TEAL designs, builds and optimises solar, wind and energy storage systems. The company was founded in 2025 and has a 10.5-GW pipeline across four core markets, including 2.8 GW in early development, according to its website.

title: Turkey expects USD 200bn in energy transition spending by 2035
content:
Turkey intends to invest USD 200 billion (EUR 172.5bn) in its clean energy transition by 2035, with USD 80 billion dedicated to power transmission, according to an energy sector report released by the Investment and Finance Office of the Presidency of the Republic of Türkiye.
The document reaffirms the country’s 2035 target to reach an installed solar and wind capacity of 120 GW, with a 55% renewable generation share.
The
latest data
from the Energy and Natural Resources Ministry shows that the country’s installed solar and wind capacity was 42,865 MW at the end of July, including 27.5 GW of solar and 15.3 GW of wind. This means that Turkey needs to be adding more than 8 GW a year to achieve its goal.
The report also reiterates the energy ministry’s plan to auction 2.4 GW of wind and solar under the YEKA programme.
As previously announced
, applications for both tenders will be submitted on October 13, 2026, between 1000 and 1200 local time.

title: US battery storage installations hit record 20.2 GWh in Q2
content:
The US energy storage industry deployed a record 20.2 GWh of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in the second quarter of 2026, a 108% increase from the previous three-month period.
The record quarterly deployment brought installations in the first half of 2026 to 30.8 GWh, says the US Energy Storage Market Outlook Q3 2026 (ESMO) released today by the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) and Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.
Utility-scale projects accounted for the vast majority of Q2 additions, amounting to 17.9 GWh, while commercial and industrial (C&I) systems added 1.8 GWh and residential storage contributed 657 MWh.
Utility-scale storage capacity in the US has nearly doubled over the first 18 months of the Trump administration, rising to 165 GWh from 88 GWh. More than 74% of the Q2 installations took place in states won by President Donald Trump in 2024, led largely by Arizona, Texas and Utah.
Arizona alone recorded the largest quarterly deployment by any state, adding more than 6.2 GWh of utility-scale storage. Texas and California followed with 3.8 GWh and 3.6 GWh, respectively.
The strong deployment has prompted SEIA and Benchmark to raise their forecast for cumulative US energy storage installations through 2030 by 11.5% to 683 GWh. Annual installations are expected to exceed 110 GWh.
The US also expanded its domestic battery manufacturing capacity during the quarter, with two new cell plants opening in Ohio and Tennessee and a 50-GWh battery module facility in Texas. Total domestic cell manufacturing capacity surpassed 50 GWh, while module manufacturing capacity exceeded 100 GWh.

title: Waaree to spend USD 37m on solar module factory upgrade in Arizona
content:
Indian solar module maker Waaree Energies Ltd (BOM:544277) will invest around USD 37 million (EUR 31.9m) to upgrade its module manufacturing plant in Arizona and thus raise the site's capacity to 1.6 GW from 1 GW.
The move, approved by the company’s board of directors, will increase the Indian group's overall US manufacturing capacity to 4.8 GW, it said in a stock exchange filing.
The revamp, to be carried out through wholly-owned subsidiary Waaree Solar Americas Inc, will replace existing module lines with high-efficiency production lines. Upon completion, Waaree's US footprint will comprise 3.2 GW at its Texas facility and 1.6 GW in Arizona.
The planned investment will be funded through a mix of debt and internal accruals.
Waaree Energies’ board also approved the consolidation of the company's Indian manufacturing base by relocating plant and machinery from its 1-GW Tumb and 1.11-GW Nandigram facilities to its existing site at Chikhli, Gujarat.

title: Wind installations surge 30% as Europe eyes record year - WindEurope
content:
Europe installed 8.8 GW of new wind capacity in the first half of 2026, a 30% jump from a year earlier, putting the continent on track for a record-high wind year, but industry body WindEurope warns that this momentum could stall unless governments tackle the persisting structural problems related to permitting, grid investment and electrification.
According to
WindEurope's Autumn Report
, the new capacity added in the reported period was fuelled by a strong summer construction season and is enough to power around 7 million European households and to displace fossil fuel imports equivalent to 25 LNG tanker shipments a year. The association now expects the continent to install 24 GW of new wind capacity by the end of 2026, part of what it describes as the start of a ramp-up toward annual installations of around 30 GW in the 2030s.
Onshore wind made up 74% of new installations for a total of 6.5 GW. The country that topped the chart was Germany, accounting for 3.4 GW of the total, followed by the UK with 789 MW and Spain with 612 MW. Denmark, Poland, Portugal and France also reported significant increases, while Ukraine alone added more than 400 MW despite the ongoing war.
Investment is keeping pace with construction as the capital raised for new wind projects stood at EUR 9 billion (USD 10.4bn) in H1 2026. This financed 5.2 GW of new capacity, which will be installed over the next few years, including 4.5 GW onshore and 0.6 GW offshore.
National governments awarded more than 17 GW of wind capacity through auctions in H1 2026 and plan to tender a further 26 GW in the second half -- what WindEurope called the largest volume of wind auctioned in Europe in a single year.
On the back of this, the association now projects that Europe will reach 436 GW of total installed wind capacity by 2030, with 342 GW of that in the EU, equivalent to 27% of EU electricity demand.
As for the structural problems, permitting remains the sector's central bottleneck, the report says.
Germany permitted more than 9 GW of new onshore wind in the first half of 2026 and is on track for another record year, which WindEurope attributed to its early and thorough implementation of EU permitting rules. However, permitting volumes fell over the same period in Spain, France, the UK, Italy and Ireland.
"2026 may well be a record wind year. But we can't take that momentum for granted," WindEurope CEO Tinne Van der Straeten said, adding that government decisions on permitting, auctions, grids and electrification in the coming months will make or break this momentum.
The association called on the EU and national governments to concentrate on five key fronts, such as finalising and implementing EU permitting rules, closing the EU grids package and clearing grid connection queues, directing ETS revenues toward industrial electrification through the Innovation Fund and Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. The other critical measures needed include setting a binding 2040 renewable energy target and standardising on two-sided Contracts for Difference (CfD) in auctions rather than continuing to experiment with auction design.

title: Ørsted wraps up construction of 920-MW Greater Changhua 2b and 4
content:
Ørsted A/S (CPH:ORSTED) has wrapped up major construction works on the 920-MW Greater Changhua 2b and 4 offshore wind farms in Taiwanese waters, the Danish energy group said as it marked the milestone in a ceremony at the Port of Taichung on Tuesday.
Once remaining commissioning activities are completed and customary contractual and regulatory requirements fulfilled, the wind farms can begin full commercial operation, which Ørsted expects to see happen in late third-quarter 2026.
“Delivering 920 MW of offshore wind capacity at this scale and complexity is a major achievement, and I’m proud of the teams and partners who’ve helped bring this project safely through construction and closer to full operation while also implementing cutting-edge technologies
like suction bucket jackets
,” said Ørsted’s chief construction officer Patrick Harnett.
The project is Ørsted's second gigawatt-scale offshore wind development in Taiwan and will take its total installed capacity in the Greater Changhua cluster to 1.82 GW.
Located about 35-60 kilometres off the coast of Changhua County, the 920-MW project consists of the 337-MW Greater Changua 2b and 583-MW Greater Changhua 4 wind farms. Greater Changhua 4 is
50%-owned by Ørsted
and 50% by Taiwan's Cathay Life Insurance.
The project was preceded by Greater Changhua 1 and 2a, with a combined capacity of 900 MW, which became operational in 2024. Once 2b and 4 are powered up, the four Greater Changhua offshore wind farms expected to generate enough electricity to power about 2 million Taiwanese households annually, Ørsted said.
The commissioning of 2b will also mark the closing of the transaction between Ørsted, Cathay Life Insurance and its energy-focused affiliate Cathay Power. Under the deal, the two Cathay companies will
acquire a 55% stake
in the combined Changhua 2 offshore wind farms.
The 2b and 4 wind farms will operate under
a 20-year fixed-price corporate power purchase agreement
with semiconductor manufacturer TSMC signed back in 2020.
Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai said at the ceremony: "We’re deeply grateful for Ørsted's long-standing commitment to Taiwan since 2016 and its continued efforts to drive our offshore wind development. By actively introducing innovative technologies, cultivating local talent, fostering industry-academia collaboration, and vitalising green finance, Ørsted and its partners have played a crucial role in realising our nation’s energy ambitions and policy goals.”

title: LG Energy Solution secures US lithium supply for ten years - electrive.com
content:
LG Energy Solution has signed a long-term supply agreement with Smackover Lithium. Starting in 2029, the battery manufacturer plans to source 8,000 tons of lithium carbonate from Arkansas annually as it scales US production of batteries for EVs and stationary storage.
LG Energy Solution secures long-term lithium carbonate from Arkansas.
Image: LG Energy Solution
The agreement covers a total of 80,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate over a ten-year period. Deliveries are set to coincide with the start of commercial production at the South West Arkansas (SWA) Project in 2029. According to LG, the agreement is a binding take-or-pay contract, with prices and other commercial terms remaining confidential.
Smackover Lithium is a joint venture founded in 2024 by Standard Lithium and Equinor. Standard Lithium holds 55 per cent and acts as the operator, while Equinor owns 45 per cent. Together, the partners are developing multiple projects involving direct lithium extraction from brine in Arkansas and Texas. The South West Arkansas Project could achieve an annual production capacity of 22,500 tonnes of lithium carbonate in its first phase. With the agreed 8,000 tonnes per year, LG Energy Solution would take more than a third of the planned production.
LGES is already the second major customer for the project. In March, Smackover Lithium signed another
ten-year contract for 8,000 tonnes per year with commodity trader Trafigura
. Overall, the joint venture aims to secure long-term buyers for around 80 per cent of its planned production capacity. According to Smackover Lithium, the two existing contracts already cover around 90 per cent of this targeted offtake volume. Another, smaller contract is still to follow.
US lithium to strengthen local supply chain
The offtake agreements also play a key role in financing the project. According to Smackover Lithium, three export credit agencies have expressed interest in providing debt financing totalling more than one billion dollars. However, a final investment decision is still pending and is expected to be made later this year. Construction is then set to begin ahead of commercial production in 2029.
The lithium is to be extracted from brine using Direct Lithium Extraction (DLE) and then processed into battery-grade lithium carbonate. This method involves separating the lithium directly from the brine, rather than using large evaporation ponds. In its announcement, LGES highlights the sustainability benefits of the process, though the company does not quantify how these compare to other extraction methods.
For LG Energy Solution, the contract is key to localising its North American supply chain. The lithium carbonate produced in Arkansas is intended to meet the requirements for raw materials that do not originate from a so-called ‘prohibited foreign entity’. The Korean battery manufacturer now has an
extensive production network in the USA
. In its announcement, LGES particularly points to the strong growth of the North American market for stationary energy storage. The company is currently significantly expanding its US business with LFP cells for such applications. By the end of 2026, more than 50 GWh of production capacity for LFP cells for stationary storage is set to be established across three of its own sites and two partner-operated locations in North America.
In its new
plant in Lansing, Michigan
, LGES has recently started battery production. The facility produces LFP cells for stationary storage,
including for Tesla
. In the future, NMC cells for Toyota’s electric vehicles will also be manufactured in Lansing.

title: $33.4M autonomous launcher uses swappable pods for flexible firepower
content: The U.S. Army has started prototype development of a new autonomous launcher that could give commanders more flexible firepower across the battlefield. The service awarded a $33.4 million Other Transaction Agreement to the Georgia Tech Research Institute (GTRI), which will integrate the system’s major components.The effort centers on the Common Autonomous Multi-Domain Launcher (CAML), part of the Army’s broader Fires modernization push. GTRI will spend roughly 36 months developing and integrating the prototype before the Army begins Increment Zero demonstrations.Modular launcher takes shapeCAML will use a modular architecture instead of relying on one complete launcher design. The Army plans to pair an autonomous mobility platform with interchangeable munitions pallets, allowing engineers to test different combinations.That separation could make the launcher easier to adapt as the Army evaluates new technologies. Engineers can develop mobility and weapons components independently, then connect them through common interfaces during the integration process.The approach also allows multiple technical partners to contribute specialized systems. The Army can therefore evaluate individual technologies without requiring one contractor to develop every part of the launcher.GTRI will serve as the link between those independently developed components. Its responsibilities include systems engineering, interface integration, modeling and simulation, along with integrated testing of the prototype.GTRI integration roleGetting separate components to operate as one system will become a central engineering challenge for CAML. GTRI will need to verify that the launcher’s mobility, mission systems and munitions interfaces work together under realistic operating conditions.The institute will also develop the integrated acceptance test plan and lead physical testing. Those tests should reveal how well the modular architecture performs once individual components operate as part of a complete launcher.The Army expects another major award to follow, covering the Autonomous Mobility Platform. Additional prototype awards could support other CAML components as the competitive development effort continues.That structure gives the Army several opportunities to compare competing technologies during development. It also creates the possibility of replacing individual components without forcing engineers to redesign the entire launcher.Soldiers to test prototypesThe Army plans to use several forms of experimentation before deciding whether CAML should move beyond the prototype stage. Live-fire demonstrations, virtual simulations and direct Soldier testing will generate data for future decisions.Those results could influence the launcher’s requirements, software integration and eventual production configuration. Soldier feedback will also give engineers a clearer picture of how the system performs outside laboratory and simulation environments.Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, the Army’s Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Fires, said CAML will help the service experiment with different launcher concepts. He described the effort as a way to learn quickly while pursuing more adaptable and survivable Fires capabilities.CAML does not represent a production decision at this stage. The Army instead wants to use the prototype effort to determine which autonomous and modular technologies can deliver useful capabilities on the multi-domain battlefield.

title: Army air defenses get $40M boost with actuators and rugged computers
content: Curtiss-Wright has won roughly $40 million in contracts to supply critical hardware for the U.S. Army’s Indirect Fire Protection Capability Increment 2 (IFPC Inc 2).Leidos awarded the contracts for the ground-based air-defense system. Curtiss-Wright will provide electromechanical actuators and compact mission computers for mobile defense platforms.IFPC Inc 2 will help the Army counter cruise missiles, rockets, and unmanned aircraft systems. The system can acquire, track, and engage threats from ground-based positions.Precision control for launchersCurtiss-Wright’s electromechanical actuators will provide precise movement and positioning for the system. The company adapted commercial roller screw and motor technologies for military applications.Roller screws convert rotary motion into controlled linear movement. That makes them useful when equipment needs accurate positioning while handling substantial forces.The actuators can operate across different force, speed, and positioning requirements. Curtiss-Wright also modified the technology to meet the Army’s environmental and performance standards.Electromechanical actuation can offer advantages over hydraulic systems in certain defense applications. It eliminates hydraulic fluid while providing direct electrical control over mechanical movement.That can matter on mobile platforms where engineers must manage space, weight, and power consumption. Defense equipment also needs to maintain reliable performance under demanding operating conditions.Lynn M. Bamford, Curtiss-Wright’s chair and CEO, said the contracts expand the company’s support for Leidos and the Army’s IFPC program.She highlighted the military’s demand for more efficient systems with lower size and weight requirements. Higher power efficiency also remains important as mobile platforms add more onboard technology.Rugged computers handle missionsCurtiss-Wright will also supply its DuraCOR 8044 mission computer for IFPC applications. The rugged system targets platforms with strict size, weight and power requirements.The DuraCOR 8044 uses Intel’s 11th-generation Xeon W processor, known as Tiger Lake-H. Curtiss-Wright designed the computer for demanding mobile and embedded applications.Its intended applications include ground and airborne platforms, sensors, and manned or unmanned vehicles. That makes rugged computing an important component of modern defense systems.Mission computers process information from sensors and other onboard equipment. In an air-defense system, that processing supports the flow of information needed to identify and track potential threats.The physical design also matters in military environments. Computers mounted on vehicles can face vibration, temperature changes, and limited space.The DuraCOR 8044 addresses those constraints while providing computing capability for systems that cannot depend on conventional computing infrastructure.Guam defense adds strategic roleIFPC Inc 2 has a broader role in the Army’s plans for defending against evolving aerial threats. The system is expected to support operations in the Indo-Pacific, including the Defense of Guam.Guam holds strategic importance for U.S. forces in the region. Its location also makes layered air defenses important as potential threats become more diverse.IFPC is designed to address several threat categories from a ground-based platform. Its ability to detect, track, and engage those targets depends on multiple technologies working together.Curtiss-Wright’s actuators will contribute to the system’s mechanical control. Its mission computers will provide computing hardware for the mobile defense architecture.Curtiss-Wright will perform the work through its Aerospace & Industrial and Defense Electronics segments. The $40 million award adds specialized hardware to an Army program focused on countering increasingly complex aerial threats.

title: China targets deeper copper-gold reserves with planned 1.8-mile scientific drill
content: East China could gain a major local source of copper and gold after an exploration campaign mapped a large ore body at the Chating deposit in Xuancheng, Anhui Province. The findings could support a production base serving nearby smelters, cable manufacturers and new-energy industries, according to CCTV News. China’s Ministry of Natural Resources announced the findings on Tuesday, following more than 70 drilling operations completed in four months this year. The campaign established the scale of the Shangchang village ore body within the Chating mining area and pointed to further resources beneath and around the deposit. Drilling reveals extensive mineralization The main ore body identified so far measures approximately 1.2 kilometers (0.75 miles) long and 1.1 kilometers (0.68 miles) wide. Mineralization encountered in a single drill hole exceeded 1,370 meters in thickness, while one exploration hole extended beyond 2,000 meters. Chating is currently the largest identified porphyry copper-gold deposit in the middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River, according to the report. The ministry described its copper resources as equivalent to several large copper mines and its gold resources as exceeding those of 10 large gold mines. The figures cited for comparison were 500,000 tons of copper and 20 tons of gold per large mine. Local supply for industrial demand Lin Bin, the exploration site’s technical lead and a deputy laboratory director at the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences, said the campaign had clarified the deposit’s deeper and surrounding resource potential. “Discovering a copper-gold deposit of this scale in the heartland of the Yangtze River Delta gives it particularly strong geographical and infrastructure advantages,” Lin said. The delta hosts major copper smelting, cable manufacturing and new-energy industries, but has relatively limited locally sourced copper and gold. Much of its copper concentrate arrives from western China or overseas, adding transportation costs and exposing supply chains to international market and geopolitical disruptions. Developing Chating could bring raw materials closer to those users. Lin said the exploration work aims to help mining enterprises increase reserves and production, strengthening the region’s ability to supply its own mineral needs. The deposit also contains silver and sulfur, which could be recovered alongside copper and gold to improve resource use. Lin said its relatively high gold grades add to its development potential. A deeper search beneath volcanic basins Beyond the resource findings, the campaign could broaden exploration in eastern China’s volcanic basins. According to the report, the discovery challenges the traditional geological view that extensive volcanic basins are unlikely to contain large porphyry copper-gold deposits. It also highlights mineral potential associated with the Yanshanian Orogeny along the middle and lower Yangtze. The team plans a 3,000-meter scientific drilling project to examine the mineralization system and deeper resources beneath the continental volcanic basin. “We believe that many volcanic basins along the Yangtze River metallogenic belt could contain similar porphyry copper deposits, indicating enormous potential for further mineral exploration,” Lin said . The findings suggest that volcanic basins around Xuancheng and Nanling in Anhui, and Lishui and Liyang in Jiangsu, could warrant further investigation.

title: Continuous-fiber 3D printing embeds power pathways in military drones
content: Continuous Composites has secured a U.S. Navy Phase II SBIR contract for a new approach to UAV manufacturing. The company will develop composite aircraft components that can carry electrical power through conductors embedded inside their structures.The work could reduce the wiring and connectors currently needed across unmanned aircraft. It also aims to turn structural components into active parts of the aircraft’s electrical system.Continuous Composites will use its CF3D process for the project. The manufacturing technology deposits continuous reinforcement during 3D printing.That approach gives engineers greater control over how materials sit within a finished composite component. It also creates opportunities to incorporate electrical functions during the manufacturing process.Conductors become structural elementsThe Navy-funded work builds on demonstrations completed during Phase I. Engineers produced fiberglass-reinforced panels with conductive elements printed directly into the composite.Those tests included copper wiring and fiber-optic components. Mechanical testing examined whether the added materials weakened the resulting structures.The results showed minimal effects on structural performance. Electrical testing also helped validate the basic concept for multifunctional composite parts.Phase II will push the idea toward higher-capacity electrical pathways. Engineers will study how those pathways can fit within components that must withstand operational loads.Material placement will become especially important at this stage. Conductors need electrical isolation without creating weak points inside the composite.The team will test the manufacturing process at the coupon and sub-scale structure level. Those experiments should reveal how much electrical functionality engineers can integrate into load-bearing parts.Simpler UAV architectureThe potential payoff extends beyond eliminating a few wires. Aircraft designers could gain more freedom when arranging electrical systems inside compact UAV structures.Traditional wiring requires dedicated routing, connectors, and attachment points. Those components can add complexity and create additional areas that require maintenance.An integrated approach could combine structural and electrical functions within the same component. That could help simplify the internal architecture of future unmanned aircraft.Field maintenance could also benefit. Damaged components could potentially be swapped without disturbing separate wiring assemblies running through the airframe.That matters for military UAVs operating in environments where repair time and reliability can directly affect mission availability. Fewer exposed connections could also reduce the chances of electrical damage during maintenance.Continuous Composites CEO Steve Starner said the project moves the company beyond printing structural components alone. The focus now includes placing useful functions directly into those structures.Full demonstration aheadThe Phase II program will run for 30 months. Engineers will focus on materials, manufacturing validation, and embedded conductor integration during that period. A one-year option follows the research phase. It could support a system-level demonstration using a functional component.Such a demonstration would provide an important test of whether the manufacturing concept can move beyond laboratory-scale structures. The long-term objective is to bring the technology closer to operational UAV applications.The Navy effort fits into a wider Pentagon push to reduce complexity across military platforms. Multifunctional composites could offer one way to achieve that goal without treating every aircraft function as a separate subsystem.

title: DOE selects Lightbridge for program aimed at accelerating advanced nuclear fuel
content: Lightbridge Corporation has been selected for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Nuclear Energy Launch Pad INL program, giving the advanced nuclear fuel developer an accelerated pathway to establish a manufacturing facility at Idaho National Laboratory (INL). The move could be an important step for Lightbridge’s proprietary metallic nuclear fuel, which is being developed to eventually operate inside commercial nuclear reactors. The company says the facility would manufacture Lead Test Assemblies (LTAs), full-scale fuel assemblies that can be placed into operating commercial reactors for testing. In nuclear fuel development, LTAs represent a critical bridge between laboratory experiments and eventual commercial deployment. From laboratory samples to a commercial reactor Lightbridge is developing a metallic fuel intended to improve the performance of existing and future nuclear reactors. According to the c ompany’s announcement , its selection by the DOE’s National Reactor Innovation Center provides a pathway toward DOE authorization to design, build, and operate a dedicated manufacturing facility at INL. The company calls the planned facility the Special High-assay low-enriched uranium Extrusion Demonstration (SHED) facility. Lightbridge says SHED would allow it to manufacture its first LTAs at production scale and test them in commercial reactors. The facility would also allow the company to validate its manufacturing equipment, processes and quality-control systems before moving toward a much larger commercial manufacturing operation. Developing a new nuclear fuel isn’t simply a matter of proving that the material works in a laboratory. The fuel must also be manufactured consistently, meet stringent quality requirements and demonstrate its performance under the demanding conditions inside a reactor. Why metallic fuel could matter Lightbridge Fuel is a proprietary metallic nuclear fuel designed around the company’s goal of increasing the power reactors can generate. The company says the fuel could increase the power output of an existing reactor by up to 10% without modifying its steam generators . Plants equipped with higher-capacity steam generators could potentially see increases of up to 20%, while new reactors designed around the technology could achieve roughly a one-third increase, according to Lightbridge. Those figures are company projections, however, and the technology still needs to progress through testing and qualification before such benefits could be demonstrated commercially. The attraction is straightforward: increasing the output of existing nuclear plants could add electricity without requiring an entirely new reactor. That could become increasingly relevant as electricity demand rises from data centers, artificial intelligence and broader electrification. SHED is a stepping stone, not the final factory Lightbridge is already testing fuel material at INL’s Advanced Test Reactor. The company said an initial batch of irradiated samples was discharged in May 2026, with post-irradiation examination expected to begin later this year. SHED would represent the next stage, producing full-scale LTAs for commercial-reactor testing. In parallel, Lightbridge is working with an engineering, procurement and construction firm on its proposed Lightbridge Expandable Fuel Facility (LEFF). That facility is envisioned as a commercial-scale manufacturing plant capable of initially producing a few reactor reload batches per year and expanding over time. The sequence is therefore deliberate: test the material, demonstrate production at a larger scale, put the fuel into commercial reactors , and then develop the infrastructure needed for broader manufacturing. Lightbridge expects SHED construction to potentially begin as early as next year, although detailed costs and timelines are still being developed. A faster route toward nuclear fuel commercialization The DOE’s Launch Pad program is intended to give nuclear technology developers a more streamlined route for demonstrating technologies at INL. For Lightbridge, the significance is less about having a new nuclear fuel design on paper and more about gaining a pathway to actually manufacture and test it at reactor scale. The company still faces substantial technical and regulatory milestones before its fuel could become a commercial product. Its upcoming irradiation results, SHED development, and eventual LTA testing will provide some of the most important evidence of whether the technology can move beyond the laboratory.

title: Kratos to build military hardware to help US troops operate in field
content: Kratos Defense & Security Solutions has secured an approximately $35 million production award to manufacture military-grade hardware and related systems for a national security program, the company announced on August 31.The equipment is expected to support warfighters operating directly in the field. Kratos will produce the hardware at a secure facility but has withheld details about the customer, equipment, location, and program for national security and other reasons.Hardware designed for large-scale productionKratos develops and manufactures hardware for the United States and allied national security programs, with its current production work spanning hypersonic systems, counter-unmanned aerial systems, air defense, missiles, radars, and high-powered directed-energy technologies.The latest award falls under the company’s C5ISR business, which produces military-standard hardware and weapon-system components intended to meet demanding operational requirements. Kratos says its approach involves working with customers during the initial engineering and design stages so that systems can subsequently move into production without significant changes.“Kratos is a recognized industry leader in the engineering and large-scale production of military-grade hardware in support of certain of the United States’ and its allies’ most important National Security programs and initiatives,” said Tom Mills, President of Kratos C5ISR. “If a customer wants its product or system engineered correctly up front, for successful, on-schedule, on-budget production, we believe that we are the preferred, go-to partner,” he continued. Recent missile and air-defense awardsThe unidentified program adds to several national security contracts Kratos has announced over the past year. In July, the company received an approximately $36 million sole-source contract for a new air-defense missile system, with work also assigned to a secure manufacturing facility.Kratos separately secured a $7 million production order in March for a counter-UAS system designed to detect, track, and classify low-profile drones, cruise missiles, and other airborne threats.In August, the U.S. Army’s DEVCOM C5ISR Center selected the company to develop, build, and test an enhanced infrared seeker for the Javelin Close Combat Missile System. That project is intended to replace obsolete elements within the missile’s existing guidance section and produce a seeker ready for future manufacturing.None of these previously announced projects has been publicly connected to the new $35 million award.Production capacity for national security systemsKratos has been expanding its domestic manufacturing infrastructure as demand grows for missile, counter-drone, radar, hypersonic, and air-defense equipment. In July, it opened a 167,000-square-foot facility in Pennsylvania to manufacture and test military hardware, including equipment for directed-energy weapons, missile transporters, mobile launchers, hypersonic systems, and strategic radar platforms.“Kratos’ C5ISR Business is a crown jewel of Kratos and a national asset for our country,” said Eric DeMarco, President and CEO of the company. “Kratos has the workforce, infrastructure, technical capability and past performance qualifications to complete the mission and engineer and build mil-spec hardware and weapon systems correctly the first time for our partners and customers,” he added. Kratos said it would not release additional information about the latest program because of customer and national security restrictions.

title: New MH-139 helicopter boosts US nuclear security by 50% more speed
content: The U.S. Air Force has started using the MH-139A Grey Wolf for its nuclear security mission, announcing the helicopter’s initial operational capability (IOC) on August 10. This marks the beginning of replacing the Vietnam-era UH-1N Huey, which has guarded the country’s intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) fields for over 50 years.The new helicopter offers more speed, range, troop space, and better defenses for a mission where security teams must respond quickly across wide, remote areas. This change comes as the Air Force also gets ready to replace its Minuteman III ICBMs with the new LGM-35A Sentinel system.A faster aircraft for missile securityThe MH-139A Grey Wolf is almost 50 percent faster than the UH-1N Huey and can carry twice as many troops. Its longer range and better defenses help security teams reach missile sites and respond to threats faster.“For more than half a century, the UH-1N Huey has been a key element of our Inter-Continental Ballistic Missile (ICBM) security, and we owe a debt of gratitude to the crews who flew and maintained it over all these years,” said Gen. S.L. Davis, commander of Air Force Global Strike Command. “Securing these missiles demands our best efforts and the MH-139 will significantly improve our capabilities.”The Grey Wolf will support 20th Air Force to cover an area of about 33,600 square miles. The mission includes prairies, plains, and mountains, where helicopters need to fly over remote areas at any time of day.Testing paved the wayThe IOC announcement came after years of testing, training crews, and getting ready for operations, all led by the 582nd Helicopter Group.The 550th Helicopter Squadron finished the MH-139’s first test and evaluation flight in January 2025. One year later, the 40th Helicopter Squadron carried out the helicopter’s first operational Minuteman III convoy mission.In January 2026, an MH-139 escorted maintenance and armored security vehicles for over 100 miles during a six-hour trip. The helicopter finished the mission without needing to refuel, showing it can handle long operations across missile fields.Supporting the Sentinel transitionThe Grey Wolf will also help as the Air Force brings in the LGM-35A Sentinel and retires the Minuteman III facilities. Its longer range, faster speed, and modern controls are meant to help security teams protect nuclear assets during this change.“It has been a distinct privilege to watch the iconic Huey faithfully support our global operations throughout my entire career,” expressed Col. Bryant Bevan, commander of the 582nd Helicopter Group. “However, this transition represents a critical leap forward.”“The advanced capabilities of the MH-139A Grey Wolf will directly empower our airborne forces with the enhanced speed, range and survivability required to decisively defend and secure the Minuteman III weapons system,” Bevan added.Beyond the missile fieldsThe Grey Wolf’s role will extend beyond escorting convoys and responding to emergencies around ICBM sites. The helicopter will also support search and rescue missions, disaster response, and medical evacuations.With the IOC milestone now reached, the Air Force can begin a broader operational transition toward the MH-139A as the Huey gradually leaves the nuclear security mission. The change brings a modern helicopter into a mission that has relied on the UH-1N since the Cold War era.

title: New lithium isotope tech gets $7M to power advanced reactors
content: A New Mexico company has raised $7 million to scale a technology designed to produce enriched lithium-6 and lithium-7, two isotopes needed for next-generation nuclear energy systems.Molten Salt Solutions (MSS) said the oversubscribed seed round will help move its isotope-enrichment technology from laboratory validation to pilot-scale production. The company plans to use the funding to expand its technical and operations teams and fulfill active customer agreements.Lithium-6 is particularly important for fusion reactors because it can help produce the tritium needed to sustain fusion reactions. Lithium-7, meanwhile, is used in advanced fission concepts, including molten salt reactors.The US currently lacks commercial-scale production of either isotope, making domestic enrichment capacity an important part of the country’s effort to build a secure nuclear fuel supply chain.Enriched lithium powers reactorsThe financing was led by Dolby Family Ventures, with participation from Vanedge Capital Partners, Alumni Ventures, Gaingels, True Ventures and Future Ventures.MSS said its technology is designed for large-scale lithium enrichment and is intended to address a supply bottleneck that could become more important as fusion and advanced fission technologies move toward commercial deployment.“Fusion and small modular fission reactors are racing toward commercialization and are necessary to meet growing global power demands. Both depend on a secure domestic supply of enriched lithium. MSS meets this need,” said John Elling, CEO of Molten Salt Solutions.“This investment enables us to scale our technology and production capability to meet the demands of advanced reactors today and in the future.”The company describes its enrichment platform as 100 times more efficient than legacy enrichment approaches. That efficiency claim is central to its attempt to build production capacity without relying on existing isotope-enrichment infrastructure.The new funding will also support MSS as it expands beyond lithium. The company said it is developing a broader portfolio of enriched isotopes aimed at emerging technology markets.US rebuilds lithium isotope supplyMSS’s funding comes as the US seeks to strengthen domestic supply chains for materials needed by advanced energy systems. Enriched lithium is a particularly specialized part of that chain because the two isotopes serve different functions in nuclear technologies.For fusion, lithium-6 has a role in the fuel cycle because reactions involving the isotope can generate tritium, which is itself a key fusion fuel. Future fusion plants therefore need a reliable source of lithium capable of supporting fuel production.Lithium-7 has a different role. It is used in advanced fission molten salt reactor designs, where molten lithium-containing salts can serve as part of the reactor system.MSS said the $7 million round follows a previous $3 million pre-seed raise and more than $5 million in grants, including funding through New Mexico’s Advanced Energy Award. The latest round brings the company’s disclosed funding from these sources to more than $15 million.The company was founded by entrepreneurs and isotope-enrichment specialists from Los Alamos National Laboratory. Its immediate goal is to establish pilot-scale production while continuing to develop partnerships across the fusion and advanced nuclear industries.The timing is significant because both fusion and advanced fission developers face a common challenge beyond reactor design: building the specialized supply chains needed to operate these systems at scale.For MSS, producing enriched lithium domestically could therefore become an enabling technology for reactors that are still moving from experimental systems toward commercial power generation.

title: New soft robotic hand grips eggs gently and lifts a full water bottle
content: Robots can automate factories and speed down racetracks, but these machines are still imperfect in many ways. For instance, the simple human act of gripping an object with just the right amount of force remains one of automation’s toughest challenges. But experts are slowly solving this.Now, Korean researchers have developed a soft, 3D-printed robotic hand so delicate it can cradle a raw egg without cracking the shell, yet strong enough to hoist a full one-liter water bottle without losing its grip.The Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) used AI to discover an optimal material recipe that makes 3D-printed products as stretchable as rubber without clogging printers.Interestingly, this optimal chemical recipe for a 3D-printable material stretches to over six times its original length without tearing.“This research is significant as it shows that combining researchers’ experimental data with artificial intelligence can efficiently identify optimal material combinations that were previously difficult to find,” explained Professor Seungchul Lee. “We expect it to be used to more rapidly develop 3D-printing materials with the performance needed across a range of fields, including soft robots, wearable devices, and custom medical devices,” Lee added. AI-based material design framework proposed in this study and its application to soft robotics. Credit: KAISTOvercoming printing challengeDigital Light Processing (DLP) 3D printing operates by projecting light patterns onto a vat of liquid resin, instantly curing it into solid layers to form complex shapes. However, creating stretchable objects with DLP created a engineering impasse: the polymer chains required to give a material high elasticity and durability make the liquid resin thick and viscous, preventing it from flowing smoothly into thin layers during the printing cycle. On the other hand, diluting the resin with solvents or low-molecular-weight additives thins the liquid for easy printing, but it disrupts the polymer network, leaving the final product brittle and prone to tearing.Instead of relying on years of manual trial and error, a collaborative Korean research team (KAIST, KIST, and SEOULTECH) used machine learning to discover an ideal 3D-printing material. The AI was trained on a dataset of chemical formulations, including hard-to-print, high-viscosity failures. The model mapped out how minor chemical adjustments influenced flow rates and light-curing speeds. This allowed the AI to identify a balanced recipe that flows smoothly during the printing process while curing into a highly durable resin that stretches to over six times its original length without tearing.Soft actuator demonstrationTo test their creation, the team printed soft pneumatic actuators — small hollow structures that flex when filled with air. When pressurized, the material expanded like a balloon, curling into the natural shape of a human finger.Combining these actuators into a soft robotic hand produced remarkable results. The hand effortlessly adapted its grip to hold computer mice, egg cartons, slick glass bottles, and fragile eggs, demonstrating a level of adaptable soft-touch control that rigid robotics struggle to replicate.Apart from flexible robotic grippers, this AI-driven approach promises to accelerate production across multiple biomedical and industrial fields. This AI-driven framework eliminates years of manual testing by rapidly predicting optimal material formulations for specific manufacturing needs. As a result, it accelerates the creation of custom anatomical medical implants, tear-resistant wearable sensors for human joints, and gentle robotic tools designed to work safely alongside humans.The development proves that sometimes the best way to tackle a rigid engineering challenge is to soften it up.The findings were presented in the journal Nature Communications.

title: Old industrial robot transformed into a badminton partner for practice
content: A used industrial robot arm has been transformed into a badminton-playing machine that can serve shuttlecocks for practice.The project repurposes a Denso VS-050 robotic arm, turning it into a court-side training system that delivers repeatable shots without requiring another player. The unusual conversion was undertaken by badminton enthusiast Travis Mitchell, who spent about six months developing the system. The project demonstrates how industrial robotics can be adapted for recreational applications, combining a surplus robot arm with a custom-built launching mechanism to create an automated badminton partner.Industrial arm servesA used Denso VS-050 industrial robot arm has been transformed into an automated badminton training machine that can select, aim, and fire shuttlecocks across a court. Mitchell developed the system by repurposing a six-axis industrial arm with a custom launcher, shuttlecock magazine, pneumatic actuators, and high-speed spinning wheels. The project took about six months to develop, with much of the work focused on designing a reliable mechanism that could consistently grip and launch shuttlecocks without damaging or misdirecting them.At the heart of the machine is the Denso VS-050, a compact industrial robotic arm that provides the positioning and movement required to pick up shuttlecocks and place them into the launcher. Denso’s published 3D model of the arm allowed Mitchell to import accurate geometry into Fusion and design a custom wrist-mounted assembly around it. The resulting mechanism combines the robot’s movement capabilities with a dedicated shuttlecock-feeding system.The launcher uses two 400-watt AC servo motors to drive a pair of spinning wheels. When a shuttlecock is positioned between the wheels, friction between the rotating surfaces accelerates it and sends it over the net. Two pneumatic cylinders handle the feeding process: one grips and holds the shuttlecock, while the other pushes it toward the spinning wheels. The entire assembly is mounted to an aluminum frame attached directly to the robot’s wrist.Automated badminton coachBuilding the launcher required extensive experimentation with the materials used for the high-speed wheels. The wheels need to remain lightweight and precisely balanced while rotating at speeds of up to 6,000 rpm. They must also provide enough grip on the shuttlecock’s nylon skirt to generate consistent launches without deforming or expanding at high rotational speeds.Several materials were tested, including EVA foam, gum rubber, silicone sheets, and 3D-printed components coated with Flex Seal. These approaches either failed to provide sufficient grip or stretched excessively under rotation. The final design uses a 3D-printed plastic wheel hub with a narrow silicone strip serving as the contact surface. This combination provided a better balance between grip, weight, and high-speed stability.The system also includes an automated ammunition system. A motorized carousel holds six tubes, each capable of storing roughly 20 shuttlecocks, giving the machine a capacity of about 120 shots before reloading. A time-of-flight sensor checks whether a shuttlecock is correctly positioned in the active tube. If the tube is empty, the carousel advances to the next one; if it is loaded, the system waits for the robotic arm to retrieve the shuttlecock.The software stores different robot positions and launch configurations and can repeat them. Up to 127 programmed positions can be used, allowing the machine to vary where and how it serves shuttlecocks. The arm can therefore function as more than a simple launcher, providing repeatable shots from different positions and trajectories.The completed system is mounted on a height-adjustable base and transported on a wheeled cart carrying the compressor and electronics. The setup operates from a 240-volt supply and was first tested in the workshop before being moved onto a badminton court. After refining the pneumatic feeding mechanism and launcher wheels, the converted industrial robot could repeatedly serve shuttlecocks for training without requiring another player to feed them.

title: Quadruped robot learns to jump through tight gaps without human help
content: Researchers have developed a learning-based approach that enables four-legged robots to pass through narrow openings rapidly. The system is designed to help quadruped robots perform agile movements that are difficult to achieve using conventional control methods. Inspired by how dogs sprint toward obstacles and leap through tight spaces, the approach allows a robot to decide when to jump and adjust its movement accordingly. The researchers demonstrated the system on a quadrupedal robot, showing how learning-based control could help machines navigate confined spaces faster and more autonomously.Robot learns leapingThe new system allows a quadruped to assess an obstacle, select an appropriate movement, and dynamically leap through it without relying on a pre-programmed jumping sequence. The technology was demonstrated on a 48-pound (22 kilograms) Unitree Aliengo robot, which autonomously traversed gates comparable in size to its own body.At the core of the system, developed by researchers at the University of Hong Kong (HKU) and the Oxford Robotics Institute, is a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework called ConsJump. Rather than teaching the robot every movement from scratch, the researchers divided control into two levels.Legged robots require highly aggressive locomotion skills and perception when they jump through a narrow space that is comparable with their body size.The low-level controller gives the robot a library of agile movements. It was trained using imitation learning to reproduce animal-like motion patterns, including pacing, cantering, jumping, and steering. These movements were adapted to the robot’s physical structure using inverse kinematics, allowing the system to learn how to coordinate its joints while maintaining a natural movement style. Jumping motions were given greater emphasis during training to help the robot master the more demanding aerial maneuvers.The high-level controller acts more like a decision-maker. It receives information about the environment and determines which movement should be used and when the robot should transition between them. Instead of directly controlling individual joints, it generates forward velocity and turning commands that are passed to the low-level locomotion system. This allows the robot to combine different learned movements continuously rather than switching abruptly between fixed motion sequences.Quadruped learns agilityVision is another key part of the technology. The robot uses an onboard Intel D435i RGB-D camera to identify the gate and determine its size and position. The perception system processes both color and depth information to detect the rectangular opening, calculate its center, and estimate its geometry. That information is then fed into the high-level controller, which uses the robot’s own state and the gate’s position to determine how it should approach the obstacle.According to the team, it allows the robot to make decisions dynamically instead of following a fixed trajectory. As it approaches a gate, the robot can transition from a slower-paced gait to a high-speed running jump. During testing, it accelerated to as much as 2.5 meters per second before rapidly decelerating to prepare for landing. The system also coordinates the robot’s joints during flight, allowing its feet to avoid the edges of the opening. The airborne phase lasted about 0.44 seconds.The researchers trained the low-level controller in simulation using 5,480 agents running in parallel and then transferred the learned behavior to the physical robot. To improve the transfer from simulation to reality, the training varied factors such as motor strength, latency, offsets, and added mass. On the physical Aliengo, the controllers ran on an onboard computer, while the perception system processed camera data separately.The approach also allows the robot to cope with changing conditions. Tests showed that it could adapt to different gate positions and uneven terrain, including situations where its feet slipped before takeoff. Because the low-level movement policy remains fixed while the high-level controller selects how those skills are used, the researchers say the same architecture can be adapted to other demanding robotic tasks without retraining the entire locomotion system.The result is a quadruped that combines animal-inspired movement with machine vision and hierarchical AI, bringing robots closer to the rapid, coordinated agility that allows animals such as dogs to navigate challenging environments.

title: Tennessee grants first fusion license for 400MW stellarator plant
content: A 400-megawatt fusion power plant using a stellarator design is moving closer to construction in Tennessee after Type One Energy received the state’s first fusion-specific license.The license clears a key regulatory step for Project Infinity, which is planned for the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run Energy Complex in Clinton. Type One Energy plans to break ground on the project’s first phase this year and expects full startup by 2034.The company’s Infinity Two is designed to generate 400 megawatts of electricity using stellarator technology. The project is being developed with the Tennessee Valley Authority, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the University of Tennessee.Stellarators use complex, three-dimensional magnetic fields to confine the superhot plasma needed for fusion. Unlike the more widely known tokamak design, the magnetic coils in a stellarator are twisted around the plasma chamber, creating a configuration intended to keep the plasma confined without relying on a large electrical current running through it.Stellarator design reaches deploymentThe Tennessee license is significant because it is the first issued under a state regulatory framework specifically created for nuclear fusion machines. Tennessee developed the framework after the Nuclear Regulatory Commission delegated regulation of fusion energy production to the states.That gives Type One Energy a defined licensing route as it moves its stellarator technology from development toward a commercial power plant.The Bull Run project will be developed in phases. The site is also intended to become a fusion development campus involving Type One Energy, TVA, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and the University of Tennessee.“For the first time, a fusion power plant-specific licensing process has been developed and then used to grant a fusion-specific license to operate a fusion machine, consistent with a national regulatory framework for fusion energy,” said Christofer Mowry, CEO of Type One Energy. “The importance of this milestone cannot be overstated. Tennessee’s licensing process is now the international benchmark for how to ensure fusion power plant ‘safety by design’ in a manner that can unlock the compelling economics of this transformational power generation technology. We are grateful and honored to receive this initial fusion machine license for Project Infinity.”Fusion works by combining light atomic nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy in the process. The challenge for power developers is maintaining the extreme conditions required for the reaction while controlling the resulting plasma and extracting useful heat.Type One Energy’s approach is built around stellarator confinement. The company says its Infinity Two design is based on a deuterium-tritium fusion reaction and is designed to produce 800 megawatts of fusion power, with 400 megawatts delivered to the electrical grid.Tennessee builds fusion testbedThe project is also notable for where it is being developed. Bull Run is a former fossil-fuel power site, and the planned fusion campus would repurpose existing energy infrastructure while bringing together a commercial developer, a major utility and research institutions.The first phase of Project Infinity involves Infinity One, a prototype and workforce training facility that will help Type One and TVA test technologies intended for the larger power plant. Type One says Infinity One is scheduled for commissioning and startup in 2029.The new license therefore covers more than a paperwork milestone. It establishes a regulatory framework that Tennessee expects could be used as other fusion machines move toward commercial deployment.“As the global epicenter of nuclear energy, Tennessee is building the workforce, infrastructure and regulatory framework needed to lead the next generation of nuclear innovation,” said Gov. Lee. “By creating a clear path for emerging technologies like fusion, we’re advancing the reliable, abundant American energy we’ll need for generations to come.”If Project Infinity stays on schedule, Tennessee could become an early test case for whether stellarator technology can move from experimental fusion systems to a grid-scale power plant.
