title: China-built 240m battery-hybrid LNG ferries land major equipment deal
content: Two new 240-meter battery-hybrid LNG ferries being built in China for TT-Line will receive a major cargo-handling equipment package for their Baltic Sea operations.MacGregor has signed contracts with China Merchants Jinling Shipyard to supply comprehensive roll-on/roll-off equipment for the two vessels, marking one of its most extensive scopes for roll-on/roll-off passenger ferries to date.The vessels will carry freight and passengers on Baltic Sea routes connecting Sweden, Germany, Poland and Lithuania. Each will have 5,400 lane meters of cargo capacity and accommodation for up to 1,000 people.They are part of TT-Line’s Green Ship 2.0 program, which is designed to increase transport capacity while improving energy efficiency and reducing the environmental impact of ferry operations.The vessels will use LNG-hybrid propulsion supported by an onboard battery energy storage system with between 5.5 and 10 megawatt-hours of capacity, according to TT-Line. The system can be expanded in the future as the ships move toward greater electrification.The contracts cover several roll-on/roll-off equipment systems for each vessel. Roll-on/roll-off technology allows wheeled cargo such as trucks and trailers to be driven directly onto and off a ship, making efficient loading and unloading important for vessels handling both freight and passengers.More cargo, faster turnaroundsThe new ferries are designed to handle substantial freight volumes across the Baltic while also carrying passengers. Their large cargo decks will give TT-Line more room for wheeled freight on each sailing.The battery system adds another layer to the vessels’ design. TT-Line says it will enable silent and emission-free operation during port stays and maneuvering. Enhanced shore-power connections will also support high-capacity battery charging while the vessels are in port.The hybrid system combines battery storage with LNG propulsion and power-management technology. TT-Line says the arrangement is designed to optimise energy consumption, reduce peak loads and give the vessels greater operational flexibility. The ships are also designed for fully electric operation in the future.“Our Green Ship 2.0 program is a cornerstone of TT-Line’s commitment to sustainable, high-efficiency transport across the Baltic Sea,” says Bernhard Termühlen, Managing Director at TT-Line. “Equipping these vessels with high-performance, reliable cargo handling systems is essential for optimising our port turnarounds and delivering high service standards for our freight and passenger customers. We value MacGregor’s technical expertise and shared dedication to continuous improvement as we work together to set new environmental standards in ferry transport.”Engineering for faster portsThe first vessel is expected to enter service on the Baltic Sea before summer 2030, according to TT-Line.MacGregor says the order is one of its most extensive roll-on/roll-off passenger ferry scopes to date. The company will supply multiple roll-on/roll-off equipment items per vessel and support the vessels across their operational lifecycles.“We are proud to continue our partnership with China Merchants Jinling Shipyard and TT-Line on this ambitious Green Ship 2.0 program,” says Magnus Sjöberg, Executive Vice President, Merchant Solutions Division at MacGregor. “By combining technical refinements with a passion for continuous improvement, our cross-border teams across Sweden, China, Poland, Germany and Croatia have delivered an integrated cargo handling solution.”For TT-Line, the ships represent the next stage of its fleet renewal, while MacGregor’s equipment will handle a less visible but critical part of their operation: moving freight on and off the vessels efficiently.

title: Dual-molecule method pushes perovskite solar cells to 24.6% efficiency
content: Inverted perovskite solar cells can reach an energy conversion efficiency of 24.6 percent when treated with a new chemical process. The performance marks a clear step up from standard versions of the device. Untreated control cells managed an efficiency of 21.21 percent. Meanwhile, devices prepared using conventional single-chemical treatments reached 23.17 percent. The gains rely on a two-step method using two organic molecules of different sizes and shapes. The process targets structural defects at two distinct depths within the solar material.“The researchers first used the smaller PDAI molecule to fill microscopic voids remaining at grain boundaries and stabilize charge-transport pathways,” said a press release.Filling the internal voidsThe compound travels into the tiny gaps between individual crystal grains. These narrow spaces naturally trap charge carriers if left unsealed. By filling the internal voids, PDAI secures the pathways that electrical charges use to move through the crystal.Next, researchers deposit a second compound called 4TF over the outside of the thin film. In untreated films, bare lead atoms remain exposed on the outer boundary. These uncoordinated atoms create electrical traps that stall the flow of current. The 4TF molecules bind directly to the exposed lead atoms. “This chemically stabilized the surface and facilitated more efficient charge transport,” added the press release.“The researchers also experimentally demonstrated that sequentially applying the two molecules produces complementary effects in defect passivation and surface stabilization, resulting in better performance than using either molecule independently.”These chemical repairs address a fundamental issue in perovskite thin films. When manufacturers produce the films, microscopic flaws form across the surface and along grain boundaries. When sunlight strikes the cell, it generates positive and negative electrical charges. If charges run into these structural flaws, they recombine and cancel each other out. This recombination prevents the charges from reaching the electrodes, which wastes potential electrical power.Different molecular designsFixing these defects has proved difficult in the past. Standard engineering methods relied on just one type of molecular layer to cover the flaws. However, a single compound cannot easily squeeze into tight internal fissures while also binding to wide open surfaces. The two physical environments require different molecular designs.Overcoming this defect problem is an important goal for inverted perovskite devices. Engineers prefer the inverted cell layout because it requires lower processing temperatures during manufacturing. Lower temperatures keep production costs down and make the materials easier to fabricate on high-speed commercial lines. This will help engineers print solar cells on flexible, lightweight sheets instead of rigid glass panels.Suitable for various industriesThe research was carried out through a joint effort in South Korea. Dr. Sungjun Hong from the Korea Institute of Energy Research led the project alongside Professor Young Seok Park from UNIST and Professor Kyung-Koo Lee from Kunsan National University.“This technology provides a key fundamental platform for accelerating the commercialization of high-efficiency, flexible solar cells for applications such as building windows, automotive sunroofs, and portable devices,” concluded Dr. Hong. “We plan to expand its application to a broader range of high-performance next-generation solar cell products and strengthen technological competitiveness in the clean and renewable energy market.”

title: General Dynamics kit takes 155mm artillery past 31 miles in Army trial
content: General Dynamics says its new Long-Range Precision Guidance Kit (LR-PGK) has successfully guided 155mm artillery projectiles to ranges exceeding 50 kilometers, marking a significant milestone for extended-range precision fires.The demonstration took place at Yuma Proving Ground, where General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems (GDOTS) used the LR-PGK to guide XM1113 Rocket-Assisted Projectiles. The company says the test makes LR-PGK the first U.S. guidance kit to demonstrate accurate guidance of 155mm cannon artillery beyond 50 kilometers.New guidance kit pushes artillery range furtherAccording to General Dynamics, the test achieved accuracy that significantly exceeded requirements for legacy guidance kits and validated key performance objectives for the LR-PGK and XM1113 programs.The development aims to support the U.S. Army’s emerging requirement for long-range massed cannon fires, while also improving the capabilities of existing 155mm artillery systems.The LR-PGK is designed to be compatible with multiple 155mm projectiles, including the M1128 and next-generation rocket-assisted ammunition. That compatibility could allow the guidance technology to be used across both existing and future artillery platforms rather than requiring an entirely new weapon system.The significance of the demonstration lies in combining extended range with precision. Conventional artillery can cover substantial distances, but increasing range generally makes accurately placing a projectile more challenging. Rocket-assisted projectiles can extend that reach, while a guidance kit can correct the projectile’s flight and improve its accuracy.General Dynamics says the LR-PGK is intended to provide that capability while remaining compatible with a range of existing and emerging artillery systems. Designed for future battlefield conditionsThe company says the LR-PGK uses a modular architecture that can accommodate further upgrades as technology and military requirements evolve. Beyond range and accuracy, GDOTS is also testing the system against operationally relevant threats. The company says the guidance kit has demonstrated resilience in both laboratory and live-fire testing, with additional improvements still under development.The technology is being positioned for the Army’s emerging Mobile Tactical Cannon program, while also offering a potential upgrade path for the military’s existing 39-caliber cannon fleet. Extending the effective capability of existing artillery could offer an alternative to replacing entire fleets. A guidance kit that can work with different projectiles and platforms could allow established systems to benefit from newer precision and range technologies.The demonstration also comes as militaries are placing renewed emphasis on long-range fires. Artillery remains an important component of ground warfare, but the proliferation of precision weapons, drones, electronic warfare, and other battlefield technologies is increasing the pressure to engage targets from greater distances while improving accuracy.The successful test represents another step toward making extended-range precision guidance available for 155mm artillery. The company has not disclosed a production timeline or the number of LR-PGK systems expected to enter service. However, the demonstration suggests that the technology has progressed beyond laboratory development and is being tested against requirements for future Army artillery programs. If adopted, the LR-PGK could give both new and legacy 155mm systems greater reach and precision without requiring a completely new artillery platform.

title: Helogen is taking medical manufacturing to space with two new missions
content: Helogen is preparing two missions in October 2026 that it says will advance commercial manufacturing in orbit while beginning a regulatory pathway for biomaterials intended for medical applications.The company is developing autonomous factories in space and plans to use the upcoming missions to manufacture materials for artificial retinas and orthopedic applications. The flights will also generate data that Helogen intends to use as it works toward Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) compliance and eventual U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) review.Turning microgravity into a manufacturing advantageHelogen says its approach is based on the unusual manufacturing environment created by microgravity. On Earth, gravity can influence how cells, proteins, and other biological structures organize as they grow. With those forces greatly reduced in orbit, some materials may form in ways that are difficult to reproduce terrestrially.The company’s HEL-IOS platform is designed to automate this process. The orbital system combines cell and tissue cultivation, fluid and media management, environmental control, processing, separation, harvesting, and quality monitoring in a closed-loop system.Helogen also uses CELS, an autonomous analysis system that the company says won NASA’s 2025 TechLeap Prize. CELS uses imaging, spectroscopy, and sequencing to characterize biological production in real time, allowing the company to monitor the manufacturing process with limited human intervention.The October missions will put this architecture to work for commercial customers. One flight will manufacture material for LambdaVision, which is developing a protein-based artificial retina. The mission will be the first time Helogen takes this manufacturing work beyond the International Space Station, building on LambdaVision’s previous microgravity experiments.The second mission will produce Helogen’s proprietary biomaterials for orthopedic repair, including potential knee and shoulder applications. The company says the flights will generate mechanical, structural, and quality data that can be compared with terrestrial alternatives.First steps toward regulated space manufacturingPerhaps the more ambitious part of the October campaign is regulatory. Helogen says the missions will test whether its orbital manufacturing process can satisfy requirements associated with terrestrial GMP production, including bioburden control, material recovery, process consistency, traceability, and documented quality systems.At the same time, the company says it is beginning work toward FDA oversight of its own proprietary materials manufactured in orbit. Data from the missions are expected to help establish the testing and documentation needed for future regulatory submissions.That does not mean the resulting materials are already approved for human use. Rather, Helogen is attempting to establish the manufacturing and quality framework that could eventually allow space-produced biomaterials to enter regulated medical applications.The missions will fly as rideshare payloads, with Helogen working with D-Orbit on one of the launches. The company says the October flights are the first in a planned series of eight missions over the next year, with each intended to validate production, retire technical risks, and build manufacturing data.Helogen ultimately wants to move beyond individual experiments toward an autonomous manufacturing hub in orbit. Its longer-term plans include developing the high-power, thermal-management, and orbital infrastructure required to operate manufacturing systems at much larger scales. The company says it has raised $7.1 million to date and is now preparing for a Series A financing round as it increases its flight cadence.

title: Hydrogen-hybrid ship cuts fuel use 24% over 8,500 nautical miles
content: Newlight has completed an 8,500-nautical-mile commercial voyage using its hydrogen-hybrid system aboard a Lomar Shipping bulk carrier. The voyage produced a 24 percent reduction in fuel consumption, according to measurements released by the maritime energy company.The 199-meter vessel traveled from Singapore to Ghana with the retrofit system installed on its existing diesel engine. Newlight also reported a 28 percent reduction in CO₂ emissions and a 22 percent decrease in carbon monoxide emissions during the voyage.The results give the technology its first extended commercial test at sea. Newlight now says it has agreements covering 12 vessels across several shipping companies.Hydrogen joins existing enginesNewlight designed the system as an add-on for conventional marine diesel engines. It introduces a controlled amount of hydrogen into the combustion process.A real-time controller adjusts hydrogen delivery as engine conditions change. It accounts for factors such as load and engine speed during operation.That control system aims to extract more useful energy from each combustion cycle. Operators can also continue using diesel when hydrogen supplies are unavailable.The approach could matter for shipowners facing expensive fleet upgrades. Replacing large commercial vessels with alternative-fuel ships can require years of planning and significant capital.Newlight says its retrofit can go onto an operating vessel within one to two weeks. The installation does not require a drydock, according to the company.Commercial potentialThe reported fuel savings could translate into substantial operating benefits for large vessels. Newlight projects annual savings of roughly $500,000 for similar ships.The company also estimates a technology payback period below 18 months. Those figures could make efficiency retrofits attractive as marine fuel costs and emissions requirements rise.The voyage involved a 57,038-DWT bulk carrier, giving the system a test under real commercial operating conditions. That distinction separates the deployment from shorter demonstrations or controlled engine tests.Newlight’s commercial pipeline now includes 12 vessels. Broader fleet deployments are planned for next year. The company also received regulatory approval for its system from RINA. The classification society named Newlight the winner of its Hydrogen Innovation Award.Shipowners seek lower emissionsShipping remains heavily dependent on liquid fuels, creating a difficult transition for operators with existing fleets. The industry moves more than 80 percent of global trade by volume.Fuel can also represent roughly half of a vessel’s operating expenses. That makes even modest efficiency gains financially significant across long voyages.Newlight’s results suggest hydrogen could serve as an efficiency tool without replacing an entire propulsion system. The technology keeps the existing diesel engine at the center of the vessel’s operation.That could offer shipowners another route toward lower fuel use and emissions. It also avoids waiting for alternative-fuel infrastructure to reach every major shipping route.The company now faces a larger test as deployments expand beyond a single vessel. Sustaining the reported performance across different ships, engines, routes and operating conditions will determine how far the retrofit can scale.

title: IBM unveils fastest quantum processor with 25x improved computation speed
content: IBM has unveiled its fastest quantum processor yet, the Nighthawk r2, with over 25 times the number of circuits over its predecessor and containing more than 7,500 gates. With this, IBM has improved the speed of computation on its processor without impacting the scale or accuracy of the system, paving the way for future improvements along its Quantum Roadmap. Quantum computing is the next frontier of computing, promising us computations in seconds that even the fastest supercomputers of today would take years to complete. The dawn of the quantum computing age is expected to help us solve problems of climate change, drug discovery, new material research, clean energy and much more. Much like research universities and startups that are working to build quantum computers, commercial entities like Google and IBM too have set their eyes on building commercial-scale quantum computers. IBM has publicly unveiled its roadmap to build quantum computers with a billion circuits and over 2000 qubits by 2033. An important milestone in this path is a fault-tolerant computer with over 100 million gates running on 200 qubits. The arrival of the Nighthawk r2 with 7,500 gates in 2026 is also part of this roadmap. What is Nighthawk r2? In all the hype about how quick quantum computing is, there is a small bit of a delay in computations that is usually missed out. It lasts just a few microseconds but is a major bottleneck that isn’t spoken about much in the media coverage. This is the conditional reset where the qubits inside the quantum circuit must return to their ground state before the next round of computations can begin. For a full reset, a quantum system has to sit idle for hundreds of microseconds between executions. With the Nighthawk r2, IBM has replaced the conditional reset with a dissipative reset gadget where a high-dynamic-range coupler can draw a programmable qubit to its ground state on demand. This reduces the qubit’s T1, or how long it holds its energy, from 200 microseconds to about 25 nanoseconds. Since each qubit is individually connected to the coupler, each qubit can be individually reset without disturbing its neighboring qubits. This reduces the overall idle time between circuit runs to as little as one microsecond and increases computation speeds to 100,000 circuits per second, which is 25 times faster than its predecessor, the Heron. Faster and more usefulAs scientists have long noted about quantum computing, being fast is not enough. Faster computing also comes with the risk of introducing a large number of errors in the computation, which makes it futile. The higher speed reset in IBM’s new quantum processors has another advantage. It reduces initialization errors by 25x since the system is starting in the ground state every time. The processor also uses square-lattice architecture wherein most qubits are connected to four nearest qubits, an improvement over its predecessors. Nighthawk r2 can use the dissipative reset not hyst between circuits but also during its execution, bringing efficiency gains within the runtime, the company said in a press release. Better circuit throughput also means that Nighthawk can run more workloads within the same allocation, a major win for researchers. IBM also said that the Nighthawk r2 quantum processor is now available on its Quantum Platform.

title: New US factory opens to scale up hydrogen-powered drone production
content: Hydrogen-powered drone manufacturing is expanding across the United States as Heven AeroTech opens a 56,000-square-foot production facility in Winchester, Virginia, establishing its first East Coast site and launching a national manufacturing network.Announced on September 2, the opening builds on the company’s existing manufacturing operations in the Columbia River Gorge. The Virginia facility will support production of its Z1 hydrogen-powered drone while establishing the processes and supply chains needed to expand American-made unmanned aerial systems for defense partners.From boutique production to industrial scaleHeven says the new network is intended to move hydrogen-powered drones beyond small-scale manufacturing, creating a repeatable production model that can be deployed across multiple facilities.“U.S. national security demands a resilient, sovereign technology base capable of scaling beyond prototyping,” said Bentzion Levinson, Founder and CEO of Heven AeroTech. “The launch of Heven AeroTech’s coast-to-coast manufacturing network transitions hydrogen-powered UAS from boutique production to an industrialized, highly repeatable capability, aligning directly with the deployment mandates of our defense partners,” he added. The Winchester operation will serve as the blueprint for a phased expansion across the country. Each planned facility is expected to include hydrogen propulsion manufacturing capabilities. However, the company has not specified how many additional sites it intends to open or where they will be located.Virginia will serve as a production site and support the broader expansion.Virginia facility established within 90 daysThe company said it stood up its first East Coast facility within 90 days, with the opening intended to demonstrate how quickly domestic drone manufacturing capacity can be established.“By standing up our first East Coast facility within 90 days, we are proving that domestic UAS manufacturing can move at tactical speed to meet the immediate and emerging needs of those carrying out critical missions,” said Michael Buscher, President of Heven AeroTech USA.Production at the site will support the company’s flagship Z1 hydrogen-powered drone, which Heven identifies as a Defense Innovation Unit Blue UAS Select platform.Alongside aircraft production, the Virginia operation is establishing manufacturing processes, quality systems, supply chain infrastructure, and operational practices for sustained growth. These functions are central to the company’s stated goal of building a scalable domestic manufacturing network.Expansion plans include research and hiringHeven’s longer-term plans extend beyond aircraft assembly. Its vision for the network includes advanced hydrogen research and development laboratories, automated manufacturing infrastructure, and dedicated areas where technology providers could operate alongside its facilities.Those elements remain part of the company’s long-term vision, rather than capabilities confirmed as operational at the newly opened Virginia site.The company expects the expanding network to create hundreds of jobs nationwide over the coming years. Recruitment is underway as production ramps up, with future hiring focused on manufacturing technicians, aircraft assembly, quality, operations, and supply chain positions.Heven did not provide a production target for the Winchester facility or a detailed timetable for the remaining network rollout. The immediate focus is establishing the Virginia operation as a repeatable model for future sites while supporting its hydrogen-powered drone program.

title: New humanoid robot lets developers build skills for real-world tasks
content: Chinese firm Zeroth has launched Bridge, which it describes as the world’s first AI-native embodied robot, alongside OpenBridge, an open-source ecosystem for embodied intelligence.The Suzhou-based company said the platform is designed to support real-world robot development through an AI-native architecture, compact humanoid form, and open developer interfaces. The first batch of Bridge Geek Edition units is now available for purchase, giving developers access to the company’s latest embodied robotics platform. Zeroth has also introduced the Bridge Builder program, inviting developers worldwide to create and contribute new robot capabilities through the Openbridge ecosystem.Open-source platformFounded in 2024 and headquartered in Suzhou, China, Zeroth develops embodied AI systems, motion-control technologies, and robotic products for consumer and real-world applications. Bridge is the company’s latest effort to bring those technologies into a developer-focused platform.Bridge is a compact humanoid robot designed around an AI-native architecture, alongside OpenBridge, an open-source ecosystem aimed at letting developers build and share capabilities for embodied robots.Standing 34.65 inches (88 centimeters) tall and weighing about 28 pounds (13 kilograms), Bridge is designed as a lightweight, desktop-friendly humanoid. It has 12–16 inches (30–40 cm) arms, two-finger grippers, and a compact form factor intended to make physical AI development more accessible.Unlike conventional robots that rely heavily on fixed, pre-programmed motions, Bridge is designed around an AI-native software and hardware stack. Zeroth says its motion system and developer interfaces support physical interaction and adaptable behaviors rather than limiting the robot to predefined sequences.The robot includes bipedal walking, obstacle avoidance, and a library of human-like movements and choreography. “Engineered with fully proprietary, high-torque actuator modules, Bridge packs serious performance into a frame—capable of everything from dynamic locomotion and backflips to full-body teleoperation,” reads the description of a video the firm posted on YouTube. Developers can also access software development kits (SDKs), open motion-control APIs and motion-capture and virtual-reality integration tools. These interfaces are intended to allow developers to deploy their own algorithms, tune the robot for specific scenarios and create new physical skills.Advancing robot developmentOpenBridge forms the software and community layer around the robot. The open-source ecosystem provides unified development tools, shared training resources, and a public Skill Hub where developers can contribute and share capabilities.The approach is designed to make robot skills more reusable, allowing developers to build on capabilities created by others rather than developing every behavior from scratch.Zeroth is also using the Bridge Builder Program to expand participation in the platform. The first phase will shortlist 500 developers for a co-creation challenge. Of these, 200 will receive complimentary access to Bridge and participate in OpenBridge development. The remaining 300 developers will receive priority purchase access to the Bridge Geek Edition, SDK access, and eligibility for future program opportunities.According to the firm, the combination of an AI-native robot and an open development stack reflects a broader shift in robotics toward platforms where software, rather than hardware alone, determines what a robot can do. It says Bridge is intended to provide developers with an accessible physical platform for experimenting with embodied AI. In contrast, OpenBridge provides the tools and community infrastructure needed to develop, train, and distribute new robotic capabilities.The Bridge Geek Edition is now available for global booking, while Zeroth has also opened its Bridge Builder Program for developers to participate in testing and developing the platform.

title: New marine battery uses immersion cooling to prevent fire spread
content: Taiwanese battery maker XING Mobility has unveiled a marine battery system that uses liquid cooling to keep individual battery cells safer while delivering high power for electric vessels. The firm introduced its IMMERSIO CTP system at SMM Hamburg 2026, positioning it for ships that need compact, high-performance energy storage.The system uses an immersion-cooling design in which every battery cell is submerged in a dielectric coolant. The liquid does not conduct electricity while drawing heat directly away from the cells. This approach is designed to control heat buildup during demanding operation and reduce the risk of thermal runaway spreading from one cell to another.XING says the cell-to-pack architecture can deliver up to twice the energy density of conventional marine batteries. Higher energy density means more stored energy can fit into the same amount of space, potentially leaving more room on a vessel for passengers, cargo or additional range.The battery is also designed to provide continuous 3C power, supporting the high-rate discharge and rapid charging needed by fast-transit vessels. Its dimensions and capacity can be scaled for different hull sizes, which XING says could reduce the engineering work required to adapt battery systems to different electric ships.Liquid cooling tackles heatThermal management is a major engineering challenge for lithium-ion batteries, particularly when cells are repeatedly charged and discharged at high rates. Heat can affect performance and, in severe cases, trigger thermal runaway, a chain reaction in which a battery cell rapidly overheats and can ignite.With IMMERSIO CTP, the coolant surrounds each cell rather than relying on cooling components positioned around groups of cells. XING says this direct contact helps remove heat at the source while actively suppressing thermal runaway and preventing fire propagation between cells.The architecture also combines cooling, safety and packaging in a cell-to-pack configuration. By removing some intermediate structures found in conventional battery packs, cell-to-pack designs can increase the proportion of a pack occupied by active battery material.For marine applications, that packaging advantage can be significant. Battery systems compete for limited onboard space with propulsion equipment, fuel systems, passenger areas and cargo. A more compact battery can therefore provide practical benefits beyond simply increasing energy density.From prototypes to watersXING is not presenting the marine system as laboratory-only technology. Its immersion-cooled batteries are already being used in vessels, according to the company.The zero-emission Porrima P111, launched in Taiwan, uses an IMMERSIO battery system and has operated in open-ocean conditions. XING also says an IMMERSIO system has been integrated into a new vessel from Austrian electric-boat specialist Smart IQ, with commissioning and system-integration testing completed in April 2026.The company says the new marine-ready IMMERSIO CTP builds on technology it has developed for other demanding applications, including commercial vehicles, agricultural machinery and energy storage.XING began with battery development for Taiwan’s MISS R electric supercar and later expanded its immersion-cooling technology. In 2024, it established what it describes as the world’s first mass-production facility for immersion-cooled battery systems.The company is now targeting maritime electrification, where batteries must deliver high power in a confined space while meeting strict safety requirements. By combining direct liquid cooling with a compact cell-to-pack design, IMMERSIO CTP is aimed at making electric vessels more practical without sacrificing power or safety.

title: Salt-water battery uses bleach side reaction to rival lithium power
content: Researchers at the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) turned an “unwanted” side reaction into the primary driver for saltwater batteries. The team created a safer, cheaper, and higher-performing battery for large-scale grid storage after deciding to embrace a sodium hypochlorite (bleach) side reaction instead of suppressing it.The innovation promises to strengthen the U.S. electric grid by helping utilities manage peak demand, cut energy costs, and maintain reliable power during blackouts.Saltwater spark for grid resilienceA saltwater battery uses a liquid salt-water solution as its electrolyte to transfer sodium ions between electrodes and conduct electricity.These batteries hold the potential to replace lithium-ion components with a safe, abundant, and self-cooling liquid electrolyte that avoids critical material issues. However, relying on a slow oxygen reaction that requires shifting between liquid and gas states adds system complexity, depends on expensive catalysts, and ultimately restricts power output.While working to fix that oxygen process, ORNL postdoctoral researcher Wooseok Go noticed a side reaction occurring beforehand. It produced sodium hypochlorite — plain bleach.Usual battery chemistry treats these rogue side reactions as pests to be suppressed at all costs. Go saw an opportunity.“Why don’t we just make the side reaction the dominant reaction, because it shows higher voltage than the oxygen reaction?” Go asked.  Adding just 5 percent more bleach into the system completely transformed the outcome.The side reaction took center stage. As the entire chlorine-bleach cycle happens purely in liquid form, the phase-change challenge vanished. The need for pricey catalysts disappeared instantly as internal resistance dropped. It depends on a reversible hypochlorite/chloride redox reaction that continuously toggles between chloride and hypochlorite ions during charge and discharge cycles. Operating entirely within the liquid phase, this chlorine process delivers faster electrochemical kinetics and operates at a higher electrical potential than slow oxygen reactions.Moving to this liquid-only chlorine reaction eliminated gas conversion steps, cut internal resistance, removed catalyst requirements, and more than doubled the battery’s peak power to rival lithium-ion performance. This shift yields a highly efficient, stable energy source that delivers rapid power during outages and offers ideal, salt-water-compatible storage for nautical applications.Safer alternative to lithium-ionAlthough heavier and bulkier than lithium-ion cells, salt-water batteries are well-suited for stationary grid storage where physical size is not a limiting factor. These are impractical for smartphones or electric vehicles, but could excel in large-scale applications where low cost, safety, and long operational lifespans outweigh weight considerations.The discovery could reshape how power grids handle extreme demand spikes and blackouts. While giant banks of lithium-ion batteries require energy-intensive liquid cooling systems to prevent catastrophic fires, salt water provides built-in temperature regulation. According to lead researcher Ruhul Amin, accessing this new chemistry is like swapping a family sedan for a sports car. When the grid needs power instantly, the battery responds without flinching.Industry partner Coulomb Technology is already moving to bring the innovation to market. The Tennessee-based startup aims to deploy the technology to back up massive data centers and support utility grids over extended periods. The technology may even hit the high seas, powering ocean-bound cargo ships surrounded by the saltwater that makes the battery tick. Now, researchers are exploring alternative anode metals to streamline manufacturing and enhance safety. The goal is to refine the electrodes to suppress the original, inefficient oxygen reaction further.

title: Sentinel nuclear missile program advances to modernize US defenses
content: The U.S. Air Force is moving forward with its LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) program. Work is underway in digital engineering, missile manufacturing, launch-silo development, and booster integration. This program aims to replace the aging Minuteman III and modernize the land-based part of the U.S. nuclear triad.The program is progressing at several sites in Utah, where Northrop Grumman and Air Force teams are building and testing the infrastructure for the new missile system. The Sentinel is expected to serve the U.S. ICBM force into the 2070s.Digital tools drive Sentinel developmentAt Northrop Grumman’s Roy Innovation Center in Utah, engineers use computer-based engineering tools to speed up development and improve the design of new ICBM features.Digital engineering allows teams to work with detailed virtual models before moving on to building physical systems. This method is combined with manufacturing and integration work at the nearby Promontory site.The Promontory site supports several key parts of the program. These include building a standard launch-silo prototype, making missile cases, and providing facilities to integrate the Sentinel’s boosters.New infrastructure takes shapeModernizing the Sentinel involves more than just the missile. The Air Force is also getting ready to move from the current Minuteman III force and is developing equipment to support operations during the transition.Plans include a new Minuteman missile transporter erector and possibly using the Air Force Repair and Enhancement Program. These steps are meant to keep the current force ready while the new system is prepared for deployment.Air Force Global Strike Command’s Detachment 13 is also contributing operational knowledge. Missile operators and maintainers are giving feedback to help decide how Sentinel will be run and supported.Airmen prepare for the transitionGen. S.L. Davis, commander of Air Force Global Strike Command, said Sentinel would “significantly improve the effectiveness of America’s ICBM force,” helping the country deter any aggressor. “It was good to see the progress on Sentinel firsthand,” he said.“Sentinel is not simply an upgrade to our ICBM mission; it’s a necessary leap forward that improves our capabilities while also improving safety and security. The dedication of our Airmen and industry partners is what will make this critical modernization effort possible.”Chief Master Sgt. Shawn M. Aiello, Air Force Global Strike Command’s command chief, said personnel will be able to use their current skills with the new system. “Sentinel is an evolutionary step in our ICBM capabilities,” Aiello added.“Our maintainers, defenders, command post controllers, our weather Airmen, airfield operations … our Airmen are going to see a newer version of our ground-based strategic capability in Sentinel. It’s great to see the progress made in the last two years with our partnerships.”A decades-long defense effort“In the coming years, Airmen will start seeing pieces and parts of this that will make it very real,” Aiello added. The Air Force expects Sentinel to provide a more effective, safe and secure ICBM capability well into the 2070s.Davis described the project as a broader national-defense effort rather than simply a missile replacement. “What we’re building here is more than just a new missile; we are building the future of national defense. The work being done here in Utah is at the very heart of that effort.”Sentinel remains a central part of the Air Force’s long-term plan to modernize U.S. land-based nuclear forces. The program also supports the Department of War’s policy of delivering peace through strength.

title: Single mobile battery hub hits 1 GWh across 33,600 charging runs
content: A single Xos Hub has delivered more than one gigawatt-hour of electricity during field operations, according to Xos, Inc. The mobile charging unit reached 1,020,143.6 kilowatt-hours after entering heavy-duty service in early 2025. Xos says the result offers a long-term look at how its storage system performs under repeated charging demands. The milestone arrives as U.S. demand for energy storage continues to rise. The country added a record 18.9 GW of energy storage capacity in 2025, according to Wood Mackenzie and the American Clean Power Association.Grid access remains a major hurdle for new power projects. About 2,061 GW of generation and storage capacity currently sit in U.S. interconnection queues, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.One hub, 33,600 sessionsThe system averaged between 1,800 and 2,000 kWh of delivered energy each day. It reached that figure through more than 33,600 charging sessions.Those numbers point to sustained utilization rather than occasional demonstration runs. The Hub has operated near continuously during its heavy-duty deployment.That operating history gives engineers another metric beyond the unit’s rated specifications. Energy throughput can reveal how a storage system behaves after repeated use.Battery health also matters when equipment operates as an energy asset. Degradation can affect output, operating costs, and the useful life of a deployed system.Xos has used the Hub across different operating environments in the United States. Deployments have included cold Northeast winters and extreme Arizona summer conditions.The equipment has supported electric trucks, passenger vehicles, buses, and autonomous vehicles. Its applications have also included fleet operations and disaster-response scenarios.Mobile power skips delaysThe Hub’s grid-independent design addresses a practical problem facing U.S. electrification projects. New generation and storage projects can spend years waiting for grid interconnection.LBNL says a typical project now takes more than five years to reach commercial operation. Mobile storage can provide power without waiting for the same utility-scale infrastructure upgrades.That capability could prove useful for fleets that need charging capacity before permanent infrastructure arrives. It also creates a potential option for temporary power during emergency deployments.The 1 GWh milestone adds operating data to that proposition. A storage system must deliver energy repeatedly if customers expect it to support commercial operations.Xos has also expanded the platform beyond its original configuration. The company introduced its megawatt-scale Power Hub and has increased its utility deployments.Its connected Hub fleet has now delivered more than 5 GWh in the field. That broader figure provides performance data from multiple deployments and operating environments.Xos CEO Dakota Semler said the single-unit milestone provides multi-year operating data. He described that experience as a foundation for expanding into new products and markets.The company has also entered the defense market as it broadens the Hub’s potential applications. Utility projects add another path for mobile energy storage.Reaching 1 GWh does not establish every aspect of long-term battery performance. It does provide a substantial field dataset from equipment operating under real charging loads. The next test will be whether that performance holds across larger systems and new markets.

title: Solid-state battery hits 381 Wh/kg as Taiwan mass production begins
content: ProLogium Technology has started mass production of its Gen 3.5 Lithium Ceramic Battery in Taiwan, putting an all-solid-state battery design with high energy density into Giga-level manufacturing.A third-party test by TÜV found that ProLogium’s 185.4 Ah large-format cell reached 381 Wh/kg of gravimetric energy density and 903 Wh/L of volumetric energy density. In simple terms, the cell can store more energy for its weight and size, an advantage for electric vehicles and other applications where battery space is limited.The cell also passed a separate test by UL Solutions under China’s GB/T 43568-2026 methodology for all-solid-state batteries. After six hours under vacuum at 120 degrees Celsius, the cell recorded less than 0.05% weight loss, compared with the standard’s maximum threshold of 0.5%.That result allows the cell to be classified as all-solid-state under the Chinese standard. GB/T 43568-2026 has also been submitted to the International Electrotechnical Commission as a reference for international standardization.Battery numbers meet factory scaleThe bigger development is not just the cell’s performance figures but the manufacturing scale behind them. ProLogium says its Gen 3.5 battery is now in mass production at its Giga-level facility in Taiwan, moving the technology beyond laboratory and pilot-line production.The company’s Lithium Ceramic Battery platform has been developed since 2012. ProLogium began commercial production in 2013 and says it has since shipped more than 2.4 million cells for consumer, specialty and automotive applications.Its manufacturing process has also evolved in stages. A Sheet-by-Sheet production line began commercial operation in 2013, followed by a Roll-to-Roll line in 2017. The company’s third-generation Giga-level manufacturing platform entered operation in 2024.That progression is important because solid-state batteries have faced a difficult transition from promising laboratory cells to reliable, high-volume manufacturing. ProLogium’s approach is to carry manufacturing knowledge, equipment, and process improvements from one battery generation to the next instead of starting over at each stage.Same architecture, new chemistryAt the center of the platform is ProLogium’s Logithium cell architecture. It uses a ceramic separator and an edge-frame structure that extends around the electrode perimeter to help isolate potential burrs while providing sealing and insulation.The architecture has remained in place as ProLogium has changed electrolyte chemistry and active materials. The company says this allows new battery generations to use much of the existing manufacturing foundation.That strategy will be tested further with Gen 4, which uses a fully inorganic superfluidized electrolyte while retaining the same Logithium architecture and manufacturing process. ProLogium expects only about 10% of its existing Giga-level production line and related equipment to require modification for Gen 4 production.Gen 4 is also designed to add an Active Safety Mechanism intended to prevent thermal runaway by stabilizing electrode active materials at high temperatures. The company is targeting applications including electric vehicles, maritime systems, aerospace, unmanned systems and data centers.ProLogium is also building a manufacturing strategy beyond Taiwan, with France planned for scaled production and North America targeted for phased localization. The company says the model could use battery inlays produced at scale in France or Taiwan before downstream partners assemble them into cells, modules and packs closer to customers.For now, the Gen 3.5 production milestone puts ProLogium’s solid-state battery technology on a manufacturing line rather than leaving it at the prototype stage.

title: Thin-film tandem solar cells set new world record at 26.7% efficiency
content: Tandem solar cells are emerging as the leading next-generation photovoltaic solution. The technology could help future satellites and space data centers run on ultra-lightweight solar power. In this vein, researchers at the Korea Institute of Energy Research (KIER) have set a new world record for perovskite/CIGS tandem solar cell efficiency, advancing next-generation, high-efficiency thin-film solar technology.KIER achieved a laboratory-measured efficiency of 27.0 percent and an officially certified efficiency of 26.7 percent. Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems officially certified the result. It is now listed in the U.S. National Laboratory of the Rockies’ Best Research-Cell Efficiencies Chart.The tandem solar cell stacks a perovskite layer over a CIGS layer to capture different sunlight wavelengths simultaneously, creating a light, flexible, and efficient thin-film device.“This achievement is significant in that both cell efficiency and stability can be enhanced by minimizing potential interfacial and optical losses during the integration of perovskite and CIGS. The resulting efficiency was also officially certified by a world-renowned institute and recognized as a world-record performance, underscoring Korea’s technological competitiveness,” said Inyoung Jeong, a senior researcher at KIER, who led the research. Tandem architectureTo overcome the physical efficiency limits of silicon solar panels, scientists stack a top perovskite layer and a bottom copper indium gallium selenide (CIGS) layer to capture different wavelengths of light without adding extra weight. Perovskite and CIGS form an ideal scientific pairing for tandem solar cells because their complementary bandgaps allow them to divide and absorb the solar spectrum with minimal energy loss. The top perovskite layer absorbs high-energy blue and ultraviolet light while allowing longer wavelengths to pass through to the bottom CIGS layer, which efficiently captures the remaining low-energy near-infrared light.Although combining these delicate thin films usually causes damage and blocks light, special protection layers and modified electrodes overcome these assembly issues to maximize power output.The KIER team solved this by inventing an advanced interfacial protection layer and re-engineering the transparent top electrode. This reduced both electrical damage and unwanted light absorption simultaneously, pushing raw laboratory tests up to 27 percent.“The developed technology is expected to increase electricity generation per unit area and thereby expand the potential applications of photovoltaic power generation,” the researchers stated. Surpassing previous recordsThe development shows South Korea’s strong competitiveness in next-generation thin-film solar technology. By reaching 26.7 percent, KIER surpassed the previous record of 26.3 percent set just a year prior by a joint team from Seoul National University and KIST.Reportedly, this 26.7% record applies to small-area laboratory research cells (sub-1 cm²).Earlier, Germany’s Helmholtz-Zentrum Berlin (HZB) and Humboldt-Universität held the world-record efficiency at 25.5 percent for perovskite-CIGS tandem solar cells with an active area of over 1 cm². Formally verified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI), this benchmark shows the technical progress in scaling up high-efficiency thin-film architectures beyond sub-centimeter laboratory devices.Thanks to their flexible and lightweight thin-film design, these cells are ideally suited for integration into buildings and vehicles, as well as weight- and space-constrained space applications such as small satellites and orbital data centers.KIER is now working with industry partners to scale these tiny lab samples into large commercial modules.

title: This 3D-printed heatsink can cut cooling size and weight by over 50%
content: Engineers at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) are developing a new type of heatsink that could help electronics manage short bursts of intense heat while taking up significantly less space and weight.Called SPEAR, the system combines phase-change materials (PCMs) with additive manufacturing to create compact thermal-management systems for applications where size, weight, and available cooling options are tightly constrained.A heatsink that melts to absorb heatTraditional metallic heatsinks absorb heat and transfer it away from an electronic component. SPEAR takes a different approach by using a phase-change material that absorbs and stores heat as it transitions from a solid to a liquid.The principle is similar to ice melting in a drink. The ice absorbs heat as it changes state, helping limit how quickly the surrounding temperature rises. According to APL, this approach can provide substantially greater thermal storage capacity within the same volume. The researchers say a phase-change heatsink can reduce size and weight by more than 50 percent while maintaining the thermal capacity of a conventional design.That could be particularly useful for systems that generate large amounts of heat for relatively short periods but do not have continuous access to cooling. Potential applications include hypersonic vehicles, spacecraft, radio-frequency electronics, transmitters, and interceptors, according to APL mechanical engineer Yoni Ferneau.These systems can face a difficult thermal-management problem. They may need to handle intense heat during a brief operating period while having limited space for conventional cooling hardware.3D printing makes the heatsink in one piecePhase-change heatsinks are traditionally assembled from multiple machined components, but APL researchers realized that additive manufacturing could allow the structure to be produced as a single piece.The SPEAR team designed and 3D-printed its own heatsinks before filling and sealing them with the phase-change material. For testing, the researchers created two SPEAR heatsinks and compared them with a baseline aluminum heatsink. One SPEAR design occupied the same volume as the aluminum version, allowing the team to compare how much additional thermal storage could fit into the same space.The second was designed to provide the same thermal capacity as the aluminum heatsink, allowing the researchers to measure the potential reduction in size and weight. The prototypes were successfully filled, sealed, and tested without leaks. APL then built an integrated test unit that applies heat to multiple heatsinks simultaneously while monitoring their temperatures in real time.The team’s ability to design, manufacture, package, and test the components in-house also allows it to rapidly modify the designs and evaluate their performance.Compact cooling for demanding systemsSPEAR is still a development effort rather than a commercially deployed cooling technology, but its design highlights how additive manufacturing can enable thermal-management approaches that would be difficult to produce using conventional manufacturing.For systems where every gram and cubic centimeter matters, storing heat rather than immediately removing it can provide another way to manage short-duration thermal loads.APL says the technology could ultimately be adapted to different mission requirements, potentially giving engineers a compact alternative for managing heat in systems ranging from spacecraft to high-performance defense electronics.

title: US Army to procure 30-kW anti drone laser weapon systems
content: The U.S. Army is moving laser weapons toward large-scale deployment, awarding AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract to produce its LOCUST laser systems for counter-drone missions.The contract is for the Army’s Enduring-High Energy Laser (E-HEL) program and will see AeroVironment deliver dozens of LOCUST X3 systems over the next few years. The company describes the award as the first production contract for a directed-energy weapon in U.S. history, marking a shift from experimental laser systems toward an enduring battlefield capability.30-kW laser will target swarms of dronesThe LOCUST X3 is a 30-kilowatt, platform-agnostic laser weapon designed to counter Group 1–3 unmanned aircraft systems. AeroVironment says the system can be integrated onto platforms including the Army’s Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV), while palletized configurations are also being considered.The company is also evaluating integration with the Infantry Squad Vehicle (ISV). Unlike conventional missiles, a laser weapon does not need to carry an explosive warhead to destroy a target. Instead, it concentrates directed energy onto an object until sufficient damage is inflicted. This can potentially give operators a deep magazine, provided the system has access to electrical power and can maintain the laser on its target.That makes directed energy particularly attractive for countering drones, where forces can face large numbers of relatively inexpensive threats. Using a high-cost interceptor against every low-cost drone can quickly become unsustainable.The E-HEL program builds on the Army’s earlier Multi-Purpose High Energy Laser (AMP-HEL) prototypes. AeroVironment says LOCUST has also undergone counter-drone testing at White Sands Missile Range, demonstrating the system in U.S. airspace.From prototype to productionThe scale of the new award is significant because it moves the technology beyond the demonstration phase. Under the Other Transaction Agreement, AeroVironment will provide the Army with production systems, along with training and ongoing support. The company says the program is intended to provide a scalable and cost-effective layer of air defense against unmanned aircraft. AeroVironment is also preparing to expand its production capacity. The company announced a $30 million investment in its Albuquerque, New Mexico, facility earlier in 2026 to support the ramp-up.The Army’s move comes as drones have become increasingly important on modern battlefields, both as surveillance platforms and as weapons. Their low cost, availability, and ability to operate in large numbers have created demand for defensive systems that can engage multiple threats without exhausting expensive interceptors.Lasers offer one potential answer, although their effectiveness can be affected by factors such as weather, atmospheric conditions, line of sight, and the amount of time required to dwell on a target.AeroVironment’s new contract does not mean laser weapons are replacing conventional air-defense systems. Instead, E-HEL is intended to add another layer to the Army’s defenses, particularly against drone threats.The company says the multi-year award will establish a foundation for sustained production and fielding of directed-energy weapons. If the program delivers as planned, the Army’s transition from high-energy laser prototypes to dozens of operational systems could represent one of the clearest signs yet that laser weapons are moving from battlefield demonstrations toward routine military service.

title: US fusion reactor stops plasma instability 200 milliseconds in advance
content: Engineers have successfully run five live tests using an automated system to stabilize a fusion reactor in real time. The trials took place at the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego. The software platform is called PACMAN, which stands for Prediction And Control using MAchiNe learning. During the experiments, the platform handled several difficult control tasks without human intervention. In one test, the system predicted a destructive tearing mode instability 200 milliseconds before it could form. Standard controllers only spot these disturbances after they start. Standard controllers then attempt to suppress the issue, which often degrades reactor performance. PACMAN adjusted the reactor settings early enough to prevent the disturbance altogether. Solving an optimization problemThe software also solved an optimization problem that previously had no single working formula. It coordinated all six of the reactor’s gyrotrons, which are high-power microwave systems that heat the fuel. The program changed mirror angles and adjusted beam power outputs across all six units at the same time. In other trials, a reinforcement-learning model took full control of the heating systems. The platform also forecast sudden bursts of energy at the edge of the fuel.PACMAN divides its workload into four sequential stations. “The whole PACMAN framework typically runs in about 20 milliseconds, and it’s not running once,” explained Andy Rothstein, co-lead author of the paper published in Nuclear Fusion. “It’s running again and again and again. It can see small things happening in the plasma and adjust in a way that a human would never be able to do.”First, the software gathers raw diagnostic readings from the reactor, including temperature, density, and magnetic data. A screening routine then inspects these values, strips out measurement errors, and packages the clean data.Next, specialized machine learning algorithms pull the parameters they need from the package. These models predict what the fuel will do in the immediate future. Finally, downstream controllers convert those predictions into hardware commands, such as firing a heating beam. An output stage resolves any conflicts between separate commands, enforces strict equipment safety boundaries, and routes the signals directly to the reactor.Speeding up experimental workThis assembly line setup solves a major engineering limitation in fusion research. Traditional computer simulations model plasma physics with great precision, but they often take days or months to run. That makes them too slow for live experiments that last only a few minutes. Machine learning models, by contrast, make predictions in fractions of a second.The modular design also speeds up experimental work. Past machine learning projects in fusion were custom-built from scratch, making them difficult to link together. In PACMAN, each model operates as a standalone module. Researchers can modify or replace an algorithm in a matter of days without altering the surrounding software.The trials address a core challenge inside tokamak reactors. These devices use powerful magnetic fields to contain plasma, a superheated gas hotter than the core of the sun. The fuel can develop instabilities within thousandths of a second. Human operators need whole seconds to react, which is far too slow to keep the reaction stable.Human operators still supervise the process. Physicists define the experimental goals, tune the parameters between shots, and rely on hardcoded limits to prevent equipment damage. The creators say the framework can easily move to other tokamak facilities, offering an adaptable control standard for future commercial fusion designs.

title: Wind assisted propulsion could power large fleet of commercial shipping with new project
content: A new innovation project has been launched to accelerate the adoption of wind propulsion in commercial shipping. Called WINTEGRATE, the project has been launched by Kongsberg Maritime and a consortium of leading Norwegian maritime companies and research institutions.The project will develop technologies and methodologies that integrate Wind Assisted Propulsion Systems (WAPS), such as rotor sails and suction wings, with ship propulsion, power management, routing and control systems. The goal is to maximize fuel savings and emissions reductions while making wind propulsion easier to implement on both existing vessels and newbuilds.Important step toward making wind propulsion a scalable solution“WINTEGRATE represents an important step toward making wind propulsion a practical and scalable solution for commercial shipping,” said VP Technology, Erik Hjortland in Odfjell. “By integrating sail technologies with onboard systems, we can unlock significant emission reductions and strengthen the competitiveness of the Norwegian maritime industry.” While wind propulsion is increasingly recognized as a promising decarbonization technology, its full potential remains limited by insufficient integration with other onboard systems. WINTEGRATE aims to address this challenge through a holistic approach that combines digital technologies, operational optimization and full-scale testing, according to a press release.Wind-assisted shippingBy combining wind propulsion with advanced control, energy management and weather routing systems, the partners aim to significantly increase the emissions-reduction potential of wind-assisted shipping and support the industry’s transition toward low- and zero-emission operations, as per the release. It was also revealed that the project will use demonstration vessels from shipping companies Odfjell SE and Seatrans, providing operational data to validate technologies and support commercial deployment.The consortium includes Kongsberg Maritime (project owner), SINTEF Ocean, SINTEF Digital, Odfjell SE, Seatrans, DNV, StormGeo, OsloMet, Norsepower, bound4blue, Corvus, OMS and DIGICAT.WINTEGRATE is a three-year research and innovation project funded through Norway’s Green Platform initiative. The project focuses on developing integrated solutions for wind-assisted propulsion to accelerate the decarbonization of global shipping. The project has been awarded up to NOK 68 million through Norway’s Green Platform programme, according to Kongsberg Maritime. A modern commercial ship is effectively a complex energy-management platform. Its propulsion system, engines, navigation equipment, weather information, voyage planning and automation systems constantly interact. Wind conditions add another variable to this equation.A vessel equipped with wind-assisted propulsion needs to determine when wind energy is available, how much thrust it can provide, how that affects engine loading and how the vessel should alter its route or speed to make the best use of the available wind.Laboratory simulations can demonstrate what a technology should theoretically achieve. Commercial vessels operating on real routes provide a much harder—and more valuable—test. They can reveal how the technology performs over long voyages, how crews interact with the systems and how wind propulsion affects the broader economics and operation of a vessel.

title: First fully solvent-free perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell reaches 27.3% efficiency
content:
First fully solvent-free perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell reaches 27.3% efficiency
Researchers at the University of Freiburg's Early-Career Research Group on Optoelectronic Thin-Film Materials (INATECH) and the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE), together with Martin Luther University Halle, Universidad Pablo de Olavide, and the King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), have fabricated what is described as 'the world's first perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell manufactured entirely without solvents'.
The device reached a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 27.3%, stabilized at 27.0%, and retained 97.06% of its initial efficiency after 6,800 hours of dark storage in a nitrogen atmosphere.
Thermal evaporation offers a solvent-free, industry-compatible route to depositing perovskite films, but the mechanisms governing perovskite formation during sequential evaporation, particularly on the textured silicon substrates used in high-efficiency tandems, have remained poorly understood. Solution-processed single-junction perovskite cells have reached efficiencies as high as 28%, but their limited upscaling potential and reliance on toxic solvents have hindered industrial adoption. Co-evaporation, an alternative vapor-deposition approach, struggles with precise stoichiometric control because of material-flux fluctuations and crosstalk between organic and inorganic precursors inside the deposition chamber. Sequential deposition avoids that problem, since the perovskite precursors mix during or after deposition rather than requiring multiple evaporation rates to be aligned simultaneously, which the researchers say makes it faster and more favorable for industrial scale-up.
At the heart of the work is a wide-bandgap (Cs,FA)Pb(I,Br)
perovskite absorber built entirely by physical vapor deposition: four sequentially evaporated layers, lead bromide, lead iodide, formamidinium iodide, and cesium iodide, deposited onto a silicon heterojunction bottom cell, with the hole-transport layer also evaporated rather than solution-processed. An evaporated ethylenediammonium diiodide (EDAI) passivation layer followed the perovskite, then a 15 nm evaporated C60 electron-transport layer, 20 nm of tin oxide by atomic layer deposition, sputtered indium tin oxide, and silver and magnesium fluoride top contacts. The resulting two-terminal tandem reached an open-circuit voltage of almost 1,900 mV alongside its 27.3% champion efficiency.
To understand how the perovskite phase actually forms during this process, the team fitted in-situ X-ray diffraction directly to their evaporation chamber and combined it with electron microscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry, comparing planar silicon against industry-relevant micro-textured silicon with pyramid features above 1 µm. Textured silicon converted the lead halides into perovskite more completely than planar silicon: the initial lead-halide layers formed more porously on textured surfaces, compared with a compact, distinctly layered structure on planar substrates, letting formamidinium iodide penetrate deeper and react more fully even before annealing. Planar substrates showed greater bromine incorporation into the final perovskite lattice alongside a residual, unreacted layer of lead iodide, while textured substrates showed no detectable residual lead-halide phase.
Achieving high performance required both elevated annealing temperatures and an ambient atmosphere, a combination the researchers found narrows the usable choice of hole-transport layer: two of the four materials they tested, Spiro-TTB and TaTm, degraded under the annealing conditions needed for good device performance. The team's evaporated EDAI passivation layer separately improved surface electronic properties, producing a more uniform surface potential and shifting the work function toward the conduction band, with evidence that the EDAI penetrates below the perovskite surface rather than remaining confined to it.
Fraunhofer ISE and the University of Freiburg frame the result as a foundation for further optimization rather than an end point, noting that the in-situ diagnostic work now gives the team a detailed, mechanistic picture of how the perovskite film forms during deposition and annealing on textured silicon. The institutions describe identifying the right combination of solvent-free deposition methods as a necessary step for moving perovskite-silicon tandems from laboratory demonstrations toward reliable, large-scale, high-throughput industrial manufacturing.
