title: Range Rover Electric Combines Power and Luxury
content:
Automotive & Mobility
Design & Manufacturing
The all-electric SUV combines luxury refinement with advanced traction control that responds 100 times faster than combustion models.
September 3, 2026
5 Min Read
The Range Rover Electric proves its mettle on the off-road course.
Jaguar Land Rover
At a Glance
The electric drivetrain produces 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque for a 4.3-second 0-60 time.
Traction control responds in 50 milliseconds, enabling superior off-road performance on steep slopes.
The 118.5-kWh battery charges from 10% to 80% in 22 minutes and provides 333 miles of EPA range.
Jaguar Land Rover brand
Range Rover
continues to position itself among the most premium luxury brands with the introduction of the
Range Rover Electric
, a model that is the quietest, smoothest, and quickest Range Rover to date.
It accomplishes these things while improving on the brand’s legendary off-road capability with an electric drive system whose traction management system responds 100 times faster than that on the
combustion-powered model.
In numbers, that means a combined 542 horsepower and 627 lb.-ft. of torque from its front and rear electric drive units, propelling the Range Rover Electric to 60 mph in just 4.3 seconds. It does this with a serene silence that is impossible in the combustion-powered model, with a sound level reduction of 7 decibels. “That’s the sound level of a living room versus a library,” Range Rover managing director Martin Limpert told
Design News
during a sit-down at the press launch.
The electric drivetrain is the key driver of the sound reduction, but as with other EVs, reducing drivetrain noise only showcases other noise sources. So, the Range Rover engineering team attacked wind noise through vehicle aerodynamic design and acoustic glass in the windows.
Our low-speed test drive on the JLR test track in Gaydon, England, wasn’t fast enough to reveal any high-speed wind or road noise, but it did confirm the Range Rover Electric’s utterly placid cabin environment at around-town speeds.
It is one thing to create a design with flush glass that can be made to work in theory and another thing for it to work in production, every time. Scanners check the part’s alignment at multiple spots on the assembly line, then in addition to the conventional water leakage test at the end of the line, Range Rover also checks for wind noise, according to chief engineer Lynfel Owen.
“We have some adjustments on the door glass to make sure it's truly fixed in a in a flush condition,” he noted. The mirrors were complicated by the A-pillar’s rearward position. “It brings that A-pillar into play with the wing mirror,” Owen observed.
“We had to put the wing mirror on the door,” he said. “When you do that without a [window] frame, you need to put more material and more stability into that door structure to stop the mirror moving, he said. “It might be small movements, but that sense of vibration goes into the body structure, and it gives you that feeling of something vibrating. So it's more costly, and it puts more structure into place, but it gives you elevated levels of refinement when you do it.”
Forget about fears of electricity and water, the Range Rover Electric is rated to handle 18 inches of water. JAGUAR LAND ROVER
As an EV, the battery technology and electric drive units are critical to the vehicle’s success. Range Rover is bucking the current trend toward piling cylindrical cells directly into the pack or even to the car’s body shell, as the 118.5-kilowatt-hour, 800-volt battery pack comprises 344 prismatic cells that are organized into modules.
The break from convention is that the cell’s contacts are on the sides rather than on the top, reducing the height of the battery pack. Rather than building the silicon carbide control electronics into the pack, they reside in a separate housing outside the pack.
The Range Rover Electric mounts the silicon carbide power electronics atop the pack in a housing shaped to fit into a conventional transmission tunnel. JAGUAR LAND ROVER
Range Rover says that the battery can charge to 80% state of charge from 10% in 22 minutes on a 350-kW charger, and the pack can split into two 400-volt packs for charging without voltage conversion on the more plentiful 400-volt charging stations. The EPA rates the driving range at 333 miles, and the charging port on US-market vehicles is the Tesla-style North American Charging Standard type.
On the trail, the Range Rover Electric delivers everything drivers expect from a Range Rover. That’s because the suspension provides the same 18 inches of wheel articulation as the combustion-powered version. And a wading depth of 35 inches combines with the ability to ascend 45-degree slopes.
Driving on Range Rover’s test track, we found that the Electric can not only climb steep slopes, it can cope with a slippery surface and obstacles like rocks and roots along the way. The traction control system can respond in just 50 milliseconds, making Range Rover Electric’s ability to handle treacherous conditions seem almost magical.
The Range Rover Electric's minimalist aesthetic might have too few physical buttons and knobs for some drivers' liking. JAGUAR LAND ROVER
Unlike in a combustion vehicle, there is no drama. For drivers who really use their billy goat vehicles for access to remote cabins and ski chalets rather than for tackling the Rubicon Trail, this is preferable because it doesn’t stress the driver or the passengers.
The ticket for admission for US customers starts at $138,000.

title: Flex Pays $4.4B for EPC Power as AI Data Centers Push 800V DC
content:
Flex will acquire EPC Power for $4.4 billion, adding 800V DC, grid-forming, and other power-conversion technologies to its data center infrastructure business, the companies said Friday. The deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to regulatory approvals and other closing conditions. Flex said EPC Power will join its Cloud and Power Infrastructure segment, which Flex plans to spin off as an independent public company in the first quarter of 2027.
EPC Power develops power-conversion systems for data centers, utility-scale energy storage, and microgrids, including grid-forming technology, digital rectifiers, and DC-DC converters, with a roadmap for
solid-state transformers
. Flex said EPC Power’s platform is designed to connect 800V DC loads more directly to grid voltages and can consolidate functions traditionally provided by UPS systems and AC power distribution. EPC Power said its 800V architecture is designed for
next-generation AI data centers
Related:
SLB’s $4.1B Kelvion Deal Expands AI Data Center Push
800V DC: Raising Rack Power While Cutting Losses
For data center operators, 800V DC could change how power is delivered in high-density AI facilities. Higher voltage allows more power to move at lower current, reducing conductor requirements and electrical losses. It can also reduce some of the conversion equipment between the grid and the rack.
As rack power rises, the electrical systems serving those racks become a larger part of the facility design. EPC Power’s technology targets the power-conversion portion of those systems, rather than the computing equipment itself.
Power Conversion Becomes a Strategic Layer
Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group, said the $4.4 billion purchase signals that power conversion is becoming a more strategic part of AI infrastructure.
“The $4.4 billion price itself is a signal that power conversion is moving from a supporting component to a strategic control point in AI infrastructure,” Osnato said.
He said higher rack and campus power densities make the way electricity is converted between the grid,
on-site generation
, storage, and computing loads more important.
“AI infrastructure is becoming as much a power-systems problem as a compute problem,” Osnato said.
Power Electronics Change the Grid Interface
EPC Power’s technology also targets rapid changes in power demand associated with AI workloads. Its Agile Grid-Forming platform is designed to respond to changes in milliseconds. The company said its systems can integrate energy storage and on-site generation while supporting grid connections and
microgrid applications
Related:
Solid-State Transformers Power Next-Gen AI Data Centers
Osnato said those capabilities can give a facility greater control over how its electrical loads appear to the grid. Power electronics and storage can smooth rapid changes in demand, he said, while converters can help manage the electrical behavior seen at the grid interface. But he cautioned that the capabilities should not be treated as a substitute for addressing the underlying requirements of a large load.
“Load smoothing is not load elimination,” Osnato said.
For utilities evaluating large AI facilities, Osnato said the relevant information goes beyond a site’s stated maximum demand. Utilities should consider ramp characteristics,
power-electronic controls
, storage capability, on-site generation, ride-through behavior, grid-forming and grid-following modes, harmonics, and fault behavior. He added that utilities must verify claimed capabilities during interconnection. “Declared capability is not demonstrated capability,” Osnato said.
For example, if a developer says a large campus can smooth its load, ride through disturbances, or provide grid support, utilities need evidence showing what the capability is, under what conditions it works, how long it lasts, and what changes would require it to be revalidated, he noted.
Related:
Trump Targets Foreign Grid Equipment as Data Centers Expand
EPC Scales US Manufacturing to 27-40 GW
The acquisition follows EPC Power’s expansion of its US manufacturing footprint. In July, the company opened a 167,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Fountain Inn, South Carolina. EPC Power said the facility nearly tripled its production capacity, with 27 GW of annual capacity initially and the ability to scale to 40 GW. The facility produces M and MRACK series power inverters for grid, storage, and AI data center applications and is expected to create about 275 jobs.
EPC Power said its annual US manufacturing capacity is expected to exceed 30 GW in 2027.
Deal Sets Up Q1 2027 Spin-Off Plan
Flex said EPC Power is expected to generate about $800 million in revenue during calendar 2026. Flex also said it expects organic revenue growth of about 40% in 2027 and an EBITDA margin of approximately 30%. The acquisition will be financed through a combination of debt and equity.
Goldman Sachs Alternatives and Cleanhill Partners acquired a majority stake in EPC Power in 2022, following an initial investment in 2021.

title: Self-Improving AI Could Drive Innovation but Strain Data Centers
content:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes AI systems that can design, code, and deploy their successors with minimal human input. If achieved, improvements could compound rapidly as smarter models beget even smarter generations – potentially accelerating beyond human comprehension and, worryingly, control. For data center operators, RSI would reverberate across power, cooling, orchestration, governance, and certification.
What RSI Is and Where It’s Heading
Although RSI is loosely defined, much like artificial general intelligence (AGI), there are signs it’s edging closer to reality. Achieving RSI depends on fast advances in AI-assisted coding, which labs say are already underway. For example, frontier AI model creator Anthropic, in its report titled “
When AI Builds Itself
,” says its Claude model now authors a substantial proportion of
its own codebase
: “As of May 2026, more than 80% of the code we merge into Anthropic’s codebase was authored by Claude. Before Claude Code launched in research preview in February 2025, this number was in the low single digits.” If sustained, this kind of contribution is a step toward systems that can improve themselves.
Related:
The Corrosion Blind Spot in the AI Buildout
On the hardware side, breakthroughs such as
quantum computing
could catalyze step changes in RSI or AGI. “In the recursive AI world, it's basically an optimization problem. What is the best AI? What is the best AI model neural network going forward? Quantum can support this,” said Jay Guilmart, lead product manager at Q-CTRL. “There's an algorithm called [Grover’s algorithm], which is really good at searching large parameter spaces. It can support the recursive operation to help [the system] perform better and pick the best option faster.”
If AI can repeatedly build better versions of itself, the implications for physical infrastructure are immediate. What does that mean for IT hardware lifecycles, energy use, workload orchestration, and the way we design and operate data centers?
“The basic premise of ‘self-improving systems’ is not new in and of itself,” said John O’Brien, senior analyst at Uptime Institute. “What’s different now is that … advances in AI models and infrastructure
make it likely we are at the point where some of this blue-sky theorizing is becoming technically feasible – or soon will be.”
A practical lens on RSI separates systems that truly author and deploy new code (RSI) from those that self-optimize continuously without rewriting themselves. The latter is already emerging in data centers, often underpinned by reinforcement learning (RL). “Successful AI applications in the data center today often make use of reinforcement learning (RL), a well-proven machine learning technique that uses penalties and rewards based on feedback from the environment,” O’Brien said. “This can work well in closed-loop systems where parameters are defined, such as data center cooling, IT, and power.”
Related:
How AI Is Changing Construction from Blueprint to Build
Systems that can self-improve in situ are already emerging. “Startups Emerald AI and Phaidra are making breakthroughs in early pilots and demonstrators that show the potential of dynamic, self-improving systems,” O’Brien added.
Autonomous improvements, especially in
energy use
, are a goal of a new wave of data center management software platforms, agreed 451 Research senior analyst Zoe Roth. “Players like Phaidra, etalytics, and Vigilent are already proving that closed-loop AI can continuously optimize physical facility variables on the fly,” Roth said. “Current AI engines like Phaidra act as autonomous control layers over existing cooling (Building Management System) and power (Electric Power Management Systems) systems. They don't rewrite their own code, but they do retrain and update neural networks on real-time sensor telemetry.”
Operational Impacts for Data Centers
For operators, self-optimization promises tangible benefits in monitoring and maintenance. “Condition-based maintenance today needs a substantial historical dataset before it can identify fault risk with any confidence,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro. “A system that improves on its own operating experience could get there much faster and much more effectively, with real gains in uptime and performance.”
Related:
Meeting AI Demand: Alternate Power, Design, and Site Strategy
But that raises a thorny question: how do you certify software that keeps changing? “If a software suite, or an AI agent, were judged capable of performing data center management duties, I'm not sure how you certify something that keeps changing underneath you,” Cordovil said. “You can't certify a moving target.” In practice, this could require ongoing re-approval of models or continuous monitoring and rollback controls that keep humans in the loop, reducing some of the efficiency gains.
“You can't certify a moving target.” – Alex Cordovil, research director, Dell’Oro
Self-improving AI that shifts between training and inference could also exacerbate the wide power swings already challenging AI data centers. “Sustained synchronous training behaves nothing like inference: large fleets swing between near-idle and near-peak in lockstep, tens to hundreds of megawatts at fractions of a hertz,” Cordovil said. “A fleet that trains and serves at the same time would make that a permanent design requirement rather than a training-cluster problem.”
Strategic Outlook and Industry Effects
Beyond near-term design choices, RSI could alter industrial dynamics. A system that can code and design its successor would have huge ramifications for those designing, building, and manufacturing data center infrastructure,” O’Brien said. “Would they want to automate half of their workforce? What would that do to their business?”
For now, RSI remains a nascent concept. But if it’s ever achieved, the effects – good and bad – will extend well beyond the models themselves, reshaping the entire AI stack and rippling through society. One plausible scenario features AI not only coding more powerful successors but also designing and even prefabricating the data centers that will house them. Even then, self-optimizing, self-replicating AI data centers would face hurdles in regulation, certification, safety assurance, and
public acceptance
. Expansion already feels too fast for many communities; RSI could accelerate the pace further.

title: The Corrosion Blind Spot in the AI Buildout
content:
The global race to build artificial intelligence infrastructure represents one of the largest capital investment cycles in modern history. Technology companies are investing unprecedented sums in AI infrastructure and new data centers as demand for advanced computing capacity continues to accelerate. Every hyperscale campus represents an enormous investment in computing hardware, electrical infrastructure, cooling systems, and supporting utilities.
Despite this unprecedented growth, one important aspect of asset reliability often receives little attention during project planning: corrosion.
Much of the industry's attention has understandably focused on power availability,
liquid cooling
, rack density, and deployment speed. These are critical challenges, but they have also shifted attention away from another factor that directly affects long-term reliability. Corrosion rarely creates immediate problems during construction, making it easy to overlook until equipment is commissioned or placed into service.
Related:
Meeting AI Demand: Alternate Power, Design, and Site Strategy
Corrosion is still widely treated as a maintenance issue. In reality, it often begins months before a facility becomes operational as equipment moves through manufacturing, transportation, storage, and construction. For facilities expected to operate continuously while supporting billions of dollars in computing infrastructure, preservation decisions made during these early phases can have lasting consequences for reliability and asset life.
A Growing Challenge for Next-Generation Data Centers
Industry studies estimate that the cost of corrosion is approximately 3.4% of global GDP each year, much of it preventable through established corrosion management and preservation practices. While data centers have historically faced relatively limited exposure to corrosion, the rapid adoption of liquid cooling is changing that equation.
High-density AI infrastructure introduces extensive liquid-cooled equipment, cooling distribution systems, heat exchangers, pumps, valves, and piping networks that combine multiple metals and increasingly complex
water chemistry
. As a result, corrosion can reduce cooling efficiency, delay commissioning, shorten equipment life, and affect the reliability of mission-critical computing infrastructure.
Corrosion Is Often a Governance Issue, Not a Technology Issue
Most large construction projects include well-defined governance processes for quality assurance, commissioning, safety, and risk management. Preservation, however, is often absent from those same governance frameworks. As equipment moves through manufacturing, transportation, storage, installation, and commissioning, responsibility shifts between manufacturers, logistics providers, contractors, and owners.
Related:
OpenAI’s Proposed IPO: A Trifecta of Opportunities, But Don’t Lock In Yet
As schedules shift and equipment remains idle longer than originally planned, preservation activities may become inconsistent or overlooked altogether. Without clearly defined ownership as equipment moves between manufacturers, logistics providers, contractors, and owners, corrosion can begin long before it becomes visible. By the time it is discovered, the opportunity to prevent it has often passed.
Other Asset-Intensive Industries Recognized This Challenge Decades Ago
Oil and gas, petrochemical, power generation, marine, and heavy industrial manufacturers routinely establish preservation requirements before purchasing equipment. Preservation activities are documented throughout construction, verified during commissioning, and incorporated into project quality programs because maintaining equipment condition is recognized as part of protecting the overall capital investment.
AI infrastructure is reaching a similar level of complexity and capital intensity, making many of these established practices increasingly relevant.
Related:
How Changing AI Workloads Are Redefining Data Center Design
Preservation Begins During Design
The most effective preservation strategy starts long before construction begins.
During project planning, designers can evaluate material compatibility, identify potential risks of galvanic corrosion, specify coolant chemistry, minimize stagnant flow areas, and establish preservation requirements for equipment that may remain in storage for extended periods.
Early planning also allows preservation requirements to be incorporated into procurement documents and construction specifications. When preservation expectations are documented from the outset, contractors, suppliers, and commissioning teams have a common standard to follow rather than making decisions independently as project schedules evolve.
Organizations may choose to develop internal preservation standards, incorporate requirements into engineering specifications, or engage independent specialists to help establish procedures and verify asset condition throughout construction. Regardless of the approach, clearly defined responsibilities and documented inspection points improve consistency while reducing project risk.
Preservation Across the Project Lifecycle
Preservation should extend across manufacturing, transportation, storage, commissioning, and operations. Equipment often spends months moving between suppliers, ports, laydown yards, warehouses, and partially completed facilities before entering service, creating repeated opportunities for corrosion. Whether protecting cooling systems, electrical infrastructure, computing equipment, or spare assets, the objective remains the same: maintaining equipment condition until reliable operation begins.
(Image: ZERUST Integrity Solutions)
Looking Beyond Maintenance
As AI data centers continue to
scale up in power density
and capital investment, preservation should be viewed as part of overall asset management rather than simply another maintenance activity.
The question is no longer whether corrosion will occur but whether preservation has been considered early enough to prevent it. Organizations that incorporate preservation planning into design, procurement, construction, and commissioning will be better positioned to protect capital investments and support the long-term reliability expected from modern AI infrastructure.

title: AES Andes begins testing 340 MW/1,360 MWh BESS in Chile - Energy Storage
content: AES Andes has begun testing the battery energy storage system (BESS) at its Cristales project in Chile’s Antofagasta region. The BESS has a power output of 340 MW and four hours of duration, equivalent to 1,360 MWh of storage capacity. The company is using the testing phase to verify the performance of the equipment, control systems and safety devices. AES Andes said it will also begin commissioning the solar plant at the complex soon. In its latest corporate information, the company puts Cristales’ solar capacity at 287 MW to 288 MW, while Chile’s Ministry of Energy lists the project as having 400 MW of PV capacity in testing. The ministry’s latest Energy Sector Construction and Investment Projects Report, published in July, already listed the Cristales BESS among systems undergoing testing. At 340 MW/1,360 MWh, it was the second-largest system in the portfolio by power output, behind Grenergy’s 430 MW/3,010 MWh Elena Phase I BESS. The project has undergone several configuration changes since it was originally proposed. When submitted for environmental assessment in 2023, it comprised 379 MW of PV and a BESS of up to 542 MW with five hours of duration. Cristales received environmental approval in April 2024. The approved configuration included up to 340 MW of solar and 542 MW of storage with five hours of duration, as well as the Cristales substation and a 220 kV transmission line. The planned investment was then $710 million. In August 2025, AES Andes announced the start of construction of Cristales and the Pampas project. For Cristales, the company then reported a configuration of 288 MW of solar and 340 MW of storage. The two projects represented a combined investment of more than $1.1 billion. title: EDF brings €160 million, 600 MWh Navagne BESS online in Belgium - Energy Storage
content: EDF subsidiary Luminus and infrastructure fund I4B have officially commissioned a 150 MW / 600 MWh battery energy storage system in Lixhe, Belgium. Backed by a €160 million capital investment, the Navagne facility directly connects to transmission system operator Elia’s high-voltage network, establishing itself as the largest operational battery asset in the region. Sited adjacent to the existing Lixhe hydroelectric power plant, the project leverages established generation hubs and preexisting grid infrastructure to bypass interconnection bottlenecks. It reached financial close in June 2025 and was scheduled to be commissioned by October 2026. Newelec, a Luminus subsidiary, executed the medium-voltage (33 kV) distribution network build-out and retains ongoing supervision of the electrical installations.  Re-Power said on Linkedin that it performed the hot and cold commissioning. The exact battery energy storage integrator wasn’t announced, but is understood to be a Sungrow model, with 132 storage containers installed. With 600 MWh of capacity, the system’s four-hour dispatch is part of a growing trend across the Benelux region and wider. As shallow but high-value ancillary service markets come closer to saturation, developers are pivoting away from one-hour frequency response systems toward deeper energy shifting, wholesale arbitrage, and capacity provision. At €160 million for a 600 MWh system, the project-level capital expenditure lands at roughly €266.7 per kilowatt-hour. The project was realized in tandem with I4B, The Belgian Infrastructure Fund and the delivered project is its first completed investment. A video on YouTube shows more of the site . What they said: Grégoire Dallemagne, CEO of Luminus, subsidiary of EDF power solutions: “With the inauguration of this 150 MW battery storage facility, the largest in Wallonia, we are taking another important step in the energy transition. This project demonstrates how we can accelerate the development of renewable energies while strengthening grid stability. Flexibility lies at the core of our #Electrify2030 strategy. It allows us to fully embrace our role as an integrator, bridging our generation assets, storage solutions, and customer services to help users consume energy when it makes the most sense.” Mathieu Bihet, Federal Minister for Energy: “A year ago, I was here to lay the foundation stone for this project. Today, I am pleased to see this ambition has become reality. With 150 MW of power and 600 MWh of storage capacity, this battery storage facility brings new flexibility capacity to our electricity system. This is essential to strengthen the integration of renewable energies, better balance the grid, and ensure the security of our supply. I therefore welcome Luminus’s investment, which concretely contributes to building a more flexible and resilient Belgian energy system.” The post EDF brings €160 million, 600 MWh Navagne BESS online in Belgium appeared first on Energy Storage .

title: Furo and Luox Energy launch pilot for 15-minute optimization of commercial batteries - Energy Storage
content: Furo and Luox Energy will offer a combined solution for market access and optimization of commercial and industrial battery energy storage systems (BESS). The companies said they are combining Furo’s platform for battery planning, optimization and control with Luox’s time-variable electricity products. These include Luox’s “Dynamisch RLM” and “Direktvermarktung” tariffs. The aim is to optimize battery operation in every 15-minute interval. Commercial and industrial battery storage systems can perform different functions, including peak shaving, increasing self-consumption, shifting electricity consumption and feed-in, or providing marketable flexibility. The most appropriate operating strategy depends on the individual site, load profile, generation assets and battery configuration. The companies also need to determine which application should take priority. Furo’s platform covers the entire battery storage lifecycle, from system design through to forecast-based operation. For the latter, Furo forecasts peak loads, generation and electricity prices and operates the battery accordingly, either through its own energy management system or on top of an existing energy management system. Luox Energy will provide market access under the cooperation. “LUOX Dynamisch RLM” links electricity procurement for commercial and industrial customers to 15-minute wholesale electricity prices, the companies said. This allows periods of low electricity prices to be used for battery charging. The “LUOX Direktvermarktung” tariff covers electricity fed into the grid. Electricity fed into the grid is also marketed based on 15-minute wholesale prices. For suitable systems, this means that electricity procurement, as well as the marketing and timing of electricity feed-in, can be incorporated into the economic assessment. Furo’s optimization determines when electricity is fed into the grid based on forecasts for prices, generation and load. The cooperation will begin with selected pilot projects. The companies will test how the battery systems operate under Furo’s optimization in real-world conditions. They will assess how operating schedules can be adapted to the 15-minute prices of Luox’s products, including how peak shaving, self-consumption and market optimization can be balanced in day-to-day operation and what revenue the marketing of available capacity can generate. The companies said the findings will be incorporated into the development of additional battery storage projects. They also plan to launch joint sales, communications and information initiatives. Christian Chudoba, managing director of Lumenaza, said commercial battery storage should be planned and operated by considering on-site energy management, grid electricity procurement and electricity feed-in together. He said the partnership with Furo would allow operators to factor market access into project planning from an early stage and improve the economics of solar-plus-storage systems. title: Horizonte Group, Metelligent and Einklang target battery storage for C&I customers - Energy Storage
content: Lucerne, Switzerland-based Horizonte Group AG is developing a joint battery storage service with its subsidiaries Horizonte-Group Technik (HGT), based in Cologne, and Metelligent, a joint venture with German energy supplier EAM. Cologne-based energy supplier Einklang NE Solutions, also known as Einklang Energy, is the third partner. The companies aim to provide a joint implementation service for manufacturing companies, logistics operators and retailers with annual electricity consumption of around 250 MWh or more that want to optimize battery storage under Germany’s planned Market Integration of Storage and Charging Points (MiSpeL) rules. HGT will handle installation, project planning and registration of metering concepts, while Metelligent will install meters for registered power metering (RLM). Einklang will be responsible for operating, optimizing and marketing the battery systems. The partners are targeting 50 joint projects in the first year. A competitive metering point operator will be responsible for metering point operations in each project. Germany’s Federal Network Agency (Bundesnetzagentur) published an updated working version of its MiSpeL rules in early August. The rules are scheduled to take effect on Oct. 1, subject to transitional periods. The partnership is targeting a market expected to emerge from a provision known as the separation option. It would allow battery storage systems to charge from both photovoltaic installations and the grid without affecting the PV system’s eligibility for support. The companies said this configuration must be implemented from the outset. “Anyone who only adds the metering concept later is giving up the benefits of the separation option,” said Marko Dreskrüger, managing director of HGT. The main bottleneck for such projects is the metering concept, which requires electricity volumes to be allocated at 15-minute intervals according to specified calculation formulas. This requires RLM meters at different metering points and must be incorporated into project planning from the beginning. The partners expect their joint approach to reduce project timelines by improving coordination between different trades. MiSpeL is also expected to significantly change the economics of battery storage projects. “A battery that only cuts peak loads uses a fraction of its potential,” said Lucas Jonas, CEO of Einklang. “From October, it can trade, and that means operations management will determine what a project ultimately earns.” The companies said similar projects have often stalled because of regulatory uncertainty. They now expect demand to increase significantly, with the first joint projects already in preparation. title: Norvento expands into utility-scale energy storage in Latin America - Energy Storage
content: Spanish renewable energy company Norvento Enerxía is expanding its focus in Latin America’s growing energy storage market, with Brazil, Chile, Argentina, Mexico and Guatemala among its priority markets. The company plans to supply its new nXL power conversion technology to utility-scale storage projects while building on existing experience in microgrids and industrial self-consumption. Norvento Enerxía, a renewable energy company based in Lugo, Galicia, Spain, wants to expand its presence in Latin America as energy storage deployment accelerates across the region. Founded as an engineering company and later expanding into wind and hydropower project development, Norvento added an industrial division in 2009 focused on manufacturing proprietary technology, mainly wind turbines and power electronics equipment. Lucas López Piñeiro, Norvento’s business development manager, told pv magazine that the company already has experience in Latin America, although its activity to date has focused mainly on microgrids, industrial self-consumption and smaller-scale energy storage systems. In Argentina, Norvento has worked with local partners for several years and has supplied equipment for commercial and industrial projects, López Piñeiro said. The company has also participated in projects in the Caribbean, particularly in the Dominican Republic, where he sees opportunities linked to energy security and the increasing deployment of solar power. Many of these projects have used Norvento’s nGM converter family, with power ratings of between 50 kW and 200 kW. The equipment is designed for energy storage and microgrid applications, including off-grid systems combining PV, small wind turbines, conventional generation and batteries. López Piñeiro said Norvento’s strength in the commercial and industrial segment is providing solutions for such microgrids. Strategy for Latin America Norvento’s new strategy in Latin America has a different scale. A key objective of its recent participation in Intersolar South America was to present the nXL family, designed for large-scale energy storage and solar generation projects. López Piñeiro said Norvento does not necessarily intend to act as a full BESS integrator in the utility-scale segment. Instead, it will primarily supply power electronics to system integrators, battery manufacturers and developers capable of integrating complete systems. This approach reflects the economics of energy storage projects, he said. Batteries account for around 70% to 75% of total system costs, while power electronics represent a substantially smaller share. As a result, full BESS integration and system-wide warranties are generally handled by the integrator or battery supplier. nXL converters The new nXL reaches up to 9 MVA per unit and is designed for large-scale energy storage installations. Norvento highlights its modular architecture, efficiency of close to 99% and advanced grid-support capabilities. These include grid-forming and grid-following functions, voltage and frequency regulation, black start, STATCOM and active filtering. López Piñeiro expects these capabilities to become increasingly important as Latin American power systems integrate larger volumes of solar and wind generation. Norvento also sees potential advantages in the equipment’s thermal design for several markets in the region. The nXL has a fully sealed IP65 enclosure and combines liquid cooling with HVAC. According to López Piñeiro, this configuration allows the equipment to maintain its rated power at temperatures of up to 40 C while reducing maintenance requirements associated with air filters. The company believes these characteristics could be particularly suitable for arid locations and areas exposed to high levels of dust, humidity or demanding temperatures, including parts of Chile, Argentina and Brazil. Norvento’s international expansion in power technology is also coinciding with the development of a new factory in Lugo. The company is finalizing neFO, Norvento Enerxía Factory Zero, a facility of approximately 23,000 square meters dedicated to manufacturing power electronics equipment. The project received €27.5 million ($32 million) from the European Commission’s Innovation Fund. López Piñeiro said the facility will have potential manufacturing capacity of up to 16 GW and will support Norvento’s industrialization process and the launch of its nXL product range. Countries in focus Norvento is not concentrating its Latin American strategy on a single country. López Piñeiro identified Brazil, Chile and Argentina, along with Mexico and Guatemala, as the company’s current focus markets. Peru and Colombia are also on its radar, although they are not currently among its priority markets. He considers Chile one of the clearest examples of how the region’s storage market could evolve. Strong growth in solar and wind generation, combined with transmission constraints and curtailment, has accelerated the deployment of energy storage. López Piñeiro said similar dynamics are beginning to emerge in other countries. He argued that having generation capacity alone is not enough, as power must also be available when it is needed. He sees Argentina, Mexico and Guatemala incorporating storage into new procurement mechanisms in an effort to avoid some of the problems encountered by markets after deploying large volumes of renewable generation. Brazil could play a particularly important role in this development. Norvento is monitoring the evolution of capacity procurement mechanisms and potential local-content requirements. López Piñeiro said the company is assessing how it could adapt if such requirements eventually affect the participation of foreign suppliers. For now, however, Norvento has not announced plans for an industrial presence in Brazil. Beyond the regulatory differences between individual markets, López Piñeiro identified a common factor across much of the region: growing solar and wind capacity is increasing the need for resources that can provide flexibility and firm power to electricity systems. He said energy storage is the key tool available to renewable generation for providing this firmness. In his view, growth in Brazil could also have a knock-on effect across Latin America by attracting integrators, manufacturers and developers to the region. Norvento wants to be present wherever integrators and developers capable of integrating storage are building projects, López Piñeiro said. The company sees Chile as evidence of the potential for the market and expects Brazil to help accelerate the development of energy storage across Latin America. title: Alliance for Automotive Innovation begs Congress to stop automotive innovation
content:
The entire US auto industry is back at it again, lobbying Congress to stifle competition and ensure that Americans remain stuck with overpriced, second-rate, highly-polluting vehicles.
The auto industry is rapidly moving towards electrification, and everyone knows it. This has been the case for more than a decade now, and smart countries and companies have worked to get themselves prepared for the future.
China is in this category, having prepared its auto industry for this moment by securing raw materials partnerships, supply agreements, production capacity, and a thriving EV startup culture – and contrary to the common story we’re told in the US, much of this preparation was bottom-up, rather than top-down. As a result, Chinese automakers are making some of the best, most affordable cars in the world right now, and the world is taking notice.
Then, there are the companies that seem desperate to lose, to sit on their laurels in a shrinking market and pretend that nothing is changing, and to beg for government to coddle them into feeling better about their poor decisions.
The US auto industry fits into the latter category, and John Bozzella, head of the main US auto lobby group the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (formerly known as Global Automakers), is king of the babies.
Chinese cars are already blocked, we need to block them again?
He pleaded with Congress on Thursday to pass multiple proposed bills banning Chinese vehicles from operating in the United States, despite that Chinese vehicles are already functionally banned from the US, in two different ways.
Not only is there a “connected car rule” (which Polestar just fell victim to), but there’s also a 100%+ tariff on Chinese EVs, making them simply uneconomical to sell in the US.
So as of yet, there has been little attempt to bring Chinese EVs to the US. Besides, why bother when the rest of the world wants them so badly, leading China to rapidly become the world’s #1 auto exporter, leapfrogging the US and 4 other nations that had held the top 5 for decades until the 2020s.
But that’s not enough protectionism for the free market capitalists in America, they must beg for government to coddle them further.
So Bozzella has now targeted the cowardly new effort in Congress that wouldn’t just ban the sale of Chinese EVs, it would ban Chinese EVs from even driving on American roads at all (e.g. if driven in from Canada or Mexico, two countries whose citizens are allowed to purchase these affordable, advanced vehicles).
In current form, it could also apply to companies with partial Chinese ownership, which would mean that Mercedes and Volvo would both be disallowed from operating in the US, though those and other provisions of the bills are subject to change.
Weren’t we told freedom and competition conquered all?
It’s an interesting strategy in a country whose mythos has always suggested that restrictive authoritarian regimes can be defeated by displays of “freedom.”
A common story in America goes that Soviets attempted to show American films to their people to highlight the depravity of American culture, but that the people instead saw the abundance of American life and were made jealous. The story is meant to show that freedom and cultural exchange can beat propaganda, and will lead to better outcomes for a populace.
Apocryphal or not, America is now on the other side of that story. At this very moment, Chinese cities are the most advanced in the world. Due to the abundance of cheap, clean electric transportation options, their air is clean and their streets are quiet. And their people have been the least negatively affected by the world’s oil-conflict-du-jour.
This lobbying only harms Americans’ health and pocketbooks
But John Bozzella and basically the entire US auto industry simply can’t have that. They’ve had it too good for too long, shoving gas-guzzling, child-killing SUVs down the throats of Americans, saddling everyone with more auto debt than ever, and ensuring skyrocketing war profits for their partner industry, oil.
All along, the auto industry has lobbied for more pollution. It does this even when it knows its a bad idea. It simply can’t help itself, it must try to harm the planet and even its own business prospects, as long as it will result in more gas being burned in America in the short term.
It’s a strange message coming from the “Alliance for Automotive Innovation,” where Bozzella has never found an opportunity to fight against innovation that he didn’t jump at.
The companies providing innovation in EVs, at this moment, are mostly focused in China. Automakers outside of China are stumbling all over themselves to cancel EV projects and push back targets, while China is just getting on with improving transportation.
They said Americans didn’t want EVs, now Americans want EVs too much?
After spending years pretending that Americans don’t want EVs and that government needs to roll back EV targets, and even losing themselves $70 billion seemingly for no other reason than to spite their face, Bozzella and the auto lobby are changing their tune.
Now they’re telling government that, no, Americans probably want EVs too much, well, at least Chinese EVs, and it’s totally not fair that China’s actually trying to make good EVs and we’re not and can you please ban them so we don’t have to try very hard pretty please?
Even the EVs that the US auto industry does make are overly large, overly expensive, and generally retrofit onto gas-vehicle designs that don’t properly leverage the advantages of EV powertrain packaging.
This is why the only EVs that sell well in America are those that were designed from the ground up to be electric, by a company that isn’t saddled with a century of combustible baggage.
Incidentally, these are the type of EVs coming out of China right now – clean sheet designs from startups that develop cars quickly and don’t have a parts bin of full of pistons and spark plugs they need to justify the existence of.
US automakers feel the need to stop Americans from even knowing that these cars exist. The entire rest of the world gets access to the best EVs out there, saving them money and saving their lungs, but you can’t have them.
We’ve been through this before. It didn’t work.
But protectionism hasn’t worked before, and it won’t work now. In the 1970s, the US saw an ascendant Japanese auto industry, with better processes and higher quality material inputs, and tried to stop it with tariffs. It failed to do so, but at least it bought itself some time to sit on its laurels and let Japan continue to improve, cementing them as a top auto exporter for the next half century.
The same story is playing out now, with China in the place of Japan. American Luddites like Bozzella are desperately trying to dig their heels into the ground and force a nation of 350 million people, who all have access to the internet, to close their eyes and stick their fingers in their ears and refuse to see what the rest of the world has access to.
Top comment by Noise
What happened to protectionism being bad for our economy and free trade being good? What happened to 'the wisdom of the marketplace' deciding what product people want? This Congress doesn't care about the people of America it only cares about the few rich people that own our corporations - including the auto manufacturers. North American auto manufacturers can make products people want. It's only a question of whether or not they want to make those products. November is a chance for the American people to send a message about what they want. Personally I want to buy an electric vehicle and I believe we need to sunset ICE vehicles.
The US will not compete, and will not win, by refusing to act. It will lose, more miserably than any other national auto industry (except, perhaps, Japan), if it does not immediately shape up and knock it off with this idiotic rent-seeking behavior, begging to be declared the winner by government without even putting in an effort.
And as long as John “I can’t do math” Bozzella is making a plea to Congress, you might as well too.
Find your members of Congress and give them a ring, and let them know whether you think the defenders of capitalism and innovation in the auto industry should have to compete with the world’s state of the art vehicles, or whether you prefer to have the overpriced, second-rate crap they keep shoveling down your throat. You can guess where I stand on the topic.

title: Defender's smaller off-road EV spotted testing ahead of its debut
content:
Jaguar Land Rover
Range Rover
Peter Johnson
| Sep 4 2026 - 7:22 am PT
Defender is preparing to launch its first fully electric SUV, a compact off-roader that’s expected to debut by the end of the year.
When will Defender launch the Sport EV?
After the
Range Rover Electric
finally went on sale earlier this week, JLR is preparing to introduce its first EV under the Defender brand.
The electric SUV is expected to arrive in 2027, likely as the Defender Sport EV, and could make its official debut by the end of the year.
While the Range Rover Electric is fairly expensive, starting at £154,070 in the UK and about $140,000 in the US, the Defender “Sport” EV is expected to be positioned below the standard entry-level Defender SUV.
JLR has been talking about a “mini Defender” for years now, but it’s finally coming together. Ahead of its debut, expected later this year, a prototype was spotted testing around the Nürburgring.
Although it’s still disguised, the new spy images from
@Wilcoblok
reveal the Defender Sport EV will retain its signature boxy, rugged design in electric form.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by ᴡɪʟᴄᴏ ʙʟᴏᴋ (@wilcoblok)
It will also be just as capable, if not even more so with electric propulsion. Defender’s electric SUV will be the first to use JLR’s EMA platform, which will also underpin the upcoming Range Rover Velar EV.
The platform is expected to support battery packs ranging from 70 to 90 kWh, which should provide a range of at least 300 to 320 miles.
JLR’s EMA platform supports 800V fast charging and, although it was initially expected to be a dedicated EV platform, it will also support hybrid powertrains.
(Source: JLR)
Although it will be the brand’s smallest SUV and first EV, Mark Cameron, global managing director of Defender, told
earlier this year that the electric SUV will still feature the “epic, built-to-last, go anywhere capability” that Defender is known for.
As such, it’s expected to have a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain and JLR’s Terrain Response system.
Inside, it will feature a setup similar to the full-size Defender, but with larger display screens and a new user interface.
Defender 110 Trophy Edition (Source: Land Rover)
The Defender Sport EV, as it will likely be called, is expected to make its official debut by the end of 2026.
The sighting comes after Jaguar Land Rover’s CEO, PB Balaji, confirmed
during an investor update
in June that the company will focus on the Defender brand to drive growth in the US.
“Our aspiration, in the coming years, is to grow our US business to the size of the entire JLR business as it exists today,” Balaji explained.
JLR also recently announced a partnership with Jeep maker, Stellantis, to potentially develop and produce vehicles for the US. We should learn more soon. Check back for updates.

title: Macfox X1S e-bike review: More mini-moto than bicycle, yet still street legal
content:
Micah Toll
| Sep 4 2026 - 8:37 am PT
There’s a fairly wide spectrum of moped-style electric bikes these days. Some are essentially conventional e-bikes wearing motorcycle-inspired designs, while others lean so heavily into the mini-moto experience that the pedals start to feel like little more than a legal technicality.
The Macfox X1S definitely falls closer to that second group.
After spending some time riding the bike, I don’t think this is the model I’d recommend to someone who actually enjoys pedaling. But if you want a fun little urban runabout with a motorcycle-inspired design, fat tires, and a right-hand throttle for cruising around at compliant 20 mph (32 km/h), and is street legal, then the X1S starts to make a lot more sense.
At $1,399
, the Macfox X1S is built around a 500W rear hub motor rated for 750W of peak power. Those specs are key, because along with the throttle on the handlebars, they help it fit just inside the Class 2 electric bicycle regulations used by most areas in the US. That keeps the bike street legal, even if it looks and feels more like a moped-style bike than anything else.
The Macfox X1S gets a 500Wh (48V 10.4Ah) removable battery, 20 x 4-inch fat tires, front suspension, hydraulic disc brakes, and a long bench-style saddle.
Macfox rates the single-battery model for up to 28 miles (45 km) of range, though there’s a dual battery version that gets twice the range.
That’s a pretty straightforward setup for this style of e-bike, with the exception that the battery is smaller than most you’d find on this style of bike.
But again, there’s that dual battery version, so if you’ve got an extra $299 burning a hole in your pocket, you can double up for twice the run time.
Going beyond the base specs, there are a couple of interesting details that help the X1S stand out.
First, as I mentioned, it’s a true Class 2 e-bike with a 20 mph (32 km/h) top speed. There are plenty of moped-style e-bikes out there that arrive capable of 30, 35, or even 40+ mph, putting them
well outside the legal e-bike classification
in most of the US.
The X1S doesn’t play that game. Macfox specifically markets it as Class 2 street legal, and the 500W motor is plenty for having fun around town without turning this into an e-motorcycle pretending to be an e-bike.
It may not crush hills the same way other models with twice the power can, but the smaller motor keeps the price lower and keeps the battery drain in check.
In my experience, cruising the urban jungle is really where the bike shines.
The X1S is just fun to zip around on. It has that little urban assault bike feeling where you can hop on, hit the throttle, and squirt around town like you’re on a miniature motorcycle. Sure, 20 mph isn’t going to rip your arms off, but on a small moped-style bike like this, it’s enough to put a smile on your face. Of course, “small” is relative. It’s a compact moped-style bike, but it still weighs a hefty 65 lb (29.5 kg).
And Macfox gets bonus points from me for putting the throttle on the right side – especially at a time when so many e-bike companies seem to be going insane and installing left-side throttles. Technically, the throttle is adjustable and removable, so theoretically you can reposition it, but having a right-hand throttle just feels more natural to me as someone who rides a lot of motorcycles and scooters.
It’s just the way the good lord intended two-wheelers to be. If they were supposed to have left-side throttles, they would have been born that way. (That’s a bit of sarcasm, before you blow up my comment section. But I still firmly believe in the virtues of right-side throttles, even if I support your right to choose. Get it? More sarcasm. I’ll be here all week, folks!)
Pedaling, on the other hand, isn’t exactly the X1S’s strong suit.
The bike has three pedal-assist levels and uses a cadence-based pedal assist system. Levels 1 and 2 aren’t overly jumpy, and I found them reasonably manageable. Kick it up into level 3, though, and the power comes on much more abruptly. At that point, there’s no mistaking this for a torque-sensor bike. You turn the pedals and the motor responds with a fairly binary-feeling shove. That’s a basic cadence sensor, through and through.
More importantly, the riding position simply isn’t conducive to effective pedaling. The long fixed-height bench seat and moped-style geometry leave the X1S borderline unpedalable in the traditional sense.
That isn’t universally true of this category. I’ve tested plenty of moped-style e-bikes that are surprisingly decent to pedal. The X1S just isn’t one of them.
So I quickly found myself treating those pedals more as auxiliary equipment and riding the X1S the way it seems to want to be ridden: with the throttle.
The component quality also generally matches the bike’s position in the market. You get front suspension rather than full suspension, and while it helps take the edge off rougher roads, don’t expect a particularly refined suspension setup.
The same goes for the hydraulic disc brakes. They work, and I’m glad to see hydraulic brakes here, but they didn’t have as much bite as I expected. It’s another reminder that simply reading “hydraulic disc brakes” on a spec sheet doesn’t tell you everything you need to know. Not all hydraulic brakes are created equal.
Fortunately, we’re dealing with a 20 mph e-bike here, not something that will be repeatedly hauling itself down from highway speeds. And over time the brakes did wear in a bit better, but still never got to where I’d prefer them, or where I get them to on higher end models.
There’s also some welcome news on the battery-safety front. Macfox says the X1S’s electrical system is UL 2849 certified, while the single battery is UL 2271 certified. Macfox notes that the dual-battery configuration falls outside the standard UL scope, an important distinction if you’re specifically shopping based on certification.
If you’re shopping for an e-bike because you love cycling and want something that enhances your pedaling, I’d look elsewhere. The X1S’s cadence sensor, geometry, and fixed bench seat simply aren’t designed around that experience.
If what you really want is a fun little 20 mph electric mini-moto that still fits neatly into the Class 2 e-bike framework, though, the Macfox X1S makes a much stronger case for itself. It’s simple, it looks cool, it’s fun to rip around on, and you can double the battery capacity if you want to spend more time cruising between charges.
Just think of the pedals as more of a supporting cast member than the star of the show.

title: Tesla Cybercab is already under NHTSA investigation after launch
content:
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Sep 4 2026 - 5:46 am PT
Tesla’s Cybercab is already under federal investigation. NHTSA opened an audit into how Tesla certified the vehicle the same day the company started putting passengers in it in Austin.
The probe targets the exact thing that makes the Cybercab unusual: it has no steering wheel, no pedals, and no mirrors, and Tesla certified it as road-legal anyway.
Tesla launched the Cybercab commercially in Austin yesterday, and the event turned out to be the nothing-burger we
expected
. There was no livestreamed reveal, no stage presentation, and no public remarks from Elon Musk.
Instead, Tesla invited a small group of shareholders and friendly influencers to ride in the two-seater, with guests reportedly required to sign NDAs, before rides opened up more broadly through the Robotaxi app.
What NHTSA is investigating
The investigation is an Open Audit Query, numbered AQ26002, from NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation. It was “prompted by public information,” according to the filing, opened September 3, and it covers an estimated 1,000 Cybercab vehicles.
NHTSA says it’s examining “the process and technical data on which Tesla relied when certifying the Cybercab and related issues.”
Tesla told the agency it certified the vehicles as compliant with all applicable Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards, and that it plans to gradually expand deployment to more vehicles and more locations.
The question is how Tesla got there. NHTSA says it will consider “the extent to which Tesla’s certification depended on determinations that certain FMVSS are inapplicable to the Cybercab.”
A car with no controls, self-certified
In the US, automakers don’t get their vehicles pre-approved by a regulator. They self-certify that a vehicle meets the federal safety standards, and NHTSA can investigate after the fact.
That system runs into a problem with the Cybercab. Many of the FMVSS were written around a human driver. They assume there’s a steering wheel, a brake pedal, side mirrors, and controls the driver can reach. The Cybercab has none of those.
Tesla’s answer was to decide that some of those standards simply don’t apply to a car with no human controls. Now NHTSA wants to see the work behind that decision.
This isn’t happening in a vacuum. Tesla’s driverless ambitions are already under a stack of federal scrutiny. NHTSA has an open probe into “Full Self-Driving” covering 3.2 million vehicles after a series of
visibility-related crashes
, and it collected crash data showing a
Tesla remote operator crashed a Robotaxi
earlier this year. The Cybercab runs on a very similar FSD software.
Electrek’s Take
Of course, this is an NHTSA investigation of Tesla, so like the Cybertruck launch, it’s more likely than not going to be another nothingburger.
Anyway, as we previously reported, Tesla is only going to deploy Cybercab in its limited geo-fenced robotaxi service. They won’t be sold to the public anytime soon.
In fact, Tesla is trying to pull another FSD and have fleet owners buy the Cybercab to deploy their own robotaxi services – shifting the burden to them. It’s going to be a mess.

title: Tesla Full Self-Driving can now take over manual driving to avoid a collision
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Sep 4 2026 - 6:56 am PT
Tesla is rolling out a new version of its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software that can take control of your car to avoid a crash, even when you’re driving manually.
The automaker announced the feature, part of FSD Supervised v14.3.9, in a post from its AI team early Friday.
FSD steps in even when you’re not using it
Tesla said v14.3.9 is “starting to roll out shortly” and includes what it calls “a new active safety feature set.” FSD Supervised “can now activate on your behalf when an imminent collision is detected and Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) may not be enough,” according to the company.
FSD Supervised v14.3.9 starting to roll out shortly
This release includes a new active safety feature set: FSD Supervised can now activate on your behalf when an imminent collision is detected and Automatic Emergency Braking (AEB) may not be enough.
It may also engage if we…
Standard AEB brakes. This lets FSD take directional control and steer to avoid an obstacle when braking alone won’t cut it.
Tesla added that the system “may also engage if we detect you’re heavily distracted or have accidentally disengaged FSD.” So it can kick in two ways: an imminent collision that braking can’t solve, and moments when the driver looks checked out or FSD was switched off by accident.
A background safety net during manual driving
Until now, FSD only ran when you turned it on. A slice of the same
v14 software stack Tesla has been rolling out since April
now sits in the background while you drive manually, ready to intervene.
Tesla hasn’t said whether the feature can be turned off, or how it decides that steering is safer than braking. Those are big questions given the software’s record. We’ve documented v14
swerving toward a ditch for no reason
and Tesla’s long-running
phantom braking problem
in Autopilot. A false positive that brakes is jarring. A false positive that steers is a different level of risk.
Electrek’s Take
Automatic collision avoidance is a good idea in principle. AEB has prevented countless crashes, and letting the car steer around something it can’t brake for is a logical next step. Tesla isn’t alone here either; several automakers have been building evasive-maneuver systems for years.
But I hope it’s optional. AEB kicking in makes sense, and I want it – even though I use the most forgiving settings in my car because I think Tesla’s system is too aggressive. What I don’t want is FSD’s directional control taking over my steering when I’m in manual mode and have chosen to drive the car myself. Braking to save me is one thing. Deciding to grab the wheel and steer is another. If I’ve accidentally disengaged FSD, sure, catch me. I just want to know I can switch this off.
The bigger issue is trust. This is the same v14 that we’ve watched swerve for no reason and brake at phantoms, and now it’s cleared to act during manual driving. If Tesla gets the false-positive rate wrong, the feature could cause the exact crashes it’s meant to prevent.

title: 三晶电气、宁德时代等6企海外储能订单新动态
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期全球储能市场海外项目加速落地。富储科能、三晶电气、三一锂能、中国能建、宁德时代、三星SDI等6企相继披露相关海外订单动态，涉及储能项目投运、签约项目、达成战略合作等。
富储科能泰国储能项目投运
9月2日，富储科能宣布，近日其AIO 261液冷储能柜在泰国某工厂顺利完成安装调试并投入试运行。
据悉，在泰国持续高温下，AIO 261液冷储能柜依然展现出高安全、高能效、高可靠、长寿命的品质，液冷温控精准控温，电池簇温差维持在合理水平，电芯压差控制优异，消防与液冷子系统全程无故障告警，整套系统运行稳定。
三晶电气罗马尼亚光伏储能项目投运
9月1日，三晶电气宣布，罗马尼亚5.22MWh VPP项目投运。
据介绍，三晶电气携手本地合作伙伴，在罗马尼亚打造2.5MW光伏+储能标杆项目，部署20台CM2一体化储能系统，总容量达5.22MWh。该项目既是罗马尼亚首个采用CM2的规模化工业光储项目，也是欧洲同级别在建的三晶电气工商业储能项目中规模最大的一个。
三一锂能供货欧洲175MWh项目
8月31日，三一集团表示，旗下三一锂能将为欧洲罗马尼亚客户175MWh储能系统提供先进交直流整体设备方案，包含储能直流仓、逆变升压一体仓全套核心装备。
此前，三一微电网罗马尼亚多布雷什蒂光储一体化项目顺利开工，成为集团在欧洲首个大型光储并网示范项目。此次罗马尼亚175MWh储能项目落地，代表着三一储能装备在欧洲市场实现从项目示范到百兆瓦级批量供货的跨越。
中国能建签约非洲单体最大光储项目
据能建国际集团消息，8月27日，中国能建国际集团、西南院和建筑集团以联营体形式，签署摩洛哥米德尔特一期光储项目EPC合同。
项目位于摩洛哥米德尔特地区，主要建设约630MW的光伏电站及1300MWh电化学储能系统，工程范围涵盖勘察设计、设备供货、建设安装、调试及相关服务等。建成后，将成为非洲单体规模最大的光储项目。
宁德时代签巴西储能战略合作
8月29日，宁德时代宣布，在2026年南美智慧能源展开幕当天（8月25日），与南美最大电池企业Moura达成战略合作，双方将联手参与巴西矿产能源部主导的储能容量储备拍卖（LRCAP 2026），共同开拓南美巴西储能市场。
根据合作协议，宁德时代将为其提供储能解决方案，Moura则提供本地制造经验与渠道网络。宁德时代表示，当前宁德时代已在巴西储能市场占据45%的份额，标杆项目Registro是巴西输电领域首个公用事业级电池储能系统。
三星SDI将向某储能系统集成商供应电池
近日，据外媒报道，三星SDI将向一家全球知名储能系统集成商供应磷酸铁锂电芯，交易金额预计达数万亿韩元。双方计划于第四季度敲定一份为期三年的主合同，每年供应量为数GWh。
报道还称，该客户为全球最大储能企业，自身不生产电芯，外购电芯组装储能产品，三星SDI将向其供应电芯而非整套系统，两家公司曾于2014年在中国设立合资企业共同开展储能业务，该客户储能产品此前以方形磷酸铁锂电芯为主，货源多来自宁德时代、中创新航、亿纬锂能等电池企业。

title: 天合储能12GWh储能电池项目环评公示
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，8月27日，江苏省盐城市大丰生态环境局发布公示，受理天合储能科技（盐城大丰）有限公司年产12GWh储能电池项目重新报批的环评文件。
文件显示，本次公示并非建设新项目，而是调整既有在建项目。该项目建设实施阶段废气治理工艺、原辅料消耗等发生变动，按法规要求开展环评重新报批手续，项目主体建设进度维持原有节奏不变。
该项目位于盐城市大丰区大丰港经济开发区，项目用地面积约330亩，新增建筑面积约12万平方米，主要构筑物包括电芯化成分容厂房、PACK模组厂房、储能系统集成生产厂房、应急事故池、NMP罐区等。
据悉，该电池项目产品为磷酸铁锂储能电芯，一期规划4GWh电芯产线，整体规划总产能12GWh。项目实施主体为天合储能科技（盐城大丰）有限公司，是天合储能的全资子公司。
此外，在产能分配上，规划12GWh电芯产能中，6GWh电芯直接对外销售，剩余6GWh电芯内部自用，用于PACK模组与储能系统集成出货。
资料显示，大丰基地是天合储能国内三大制造基地之一，其余两大基地布局常州、滁州。该基地项目2025年9月已实现投产，叠加滁州生产基地，天合储能电芯规划总产能将达到25GWh。

公司经营范围包含：新兴能源技术研发；节能管理服务；储能技术服务；余热发电关键技术研发；风力发电技术服务等。

title: 瑞浦兰钧斩获国家级专利优秀奖
content:

title: 鹏程无限/希倍动力等4企加快储能电芯及钠电项目布局
content:
集邦光储观察获悉，近期，多家企业推进储能电芯及钠离子电池等项目建设，其中，鹏程无限48亿元储能电芯项目进入设备安装调试阶段，希倍动力、超钠新能源分别推进钠电项目落地，焕文科技储能集装箱项目落地永仁。
鹏程无限宜宾储能电芯项目进入设备安装调试阶段
9月3日，随着装载6套新能源容量化成工艺设备的工程车驶入厂区，鹏程无限新能源科技有限公司宜宾储能产业园电芯制造基地由项目施工阶段转入设备安装调试阶段。
据介绍，下一步项目将开展设备开箱验收、就位安装、单机调试及整线联动调试，并同步推进技术人员培训、质量体系搭建及供应链配套等工作。
鹏程无限宜宾储能电芯项目总投资48亿元，总产能54GWh，分期建设。其中，一期项目预计于2026年底正式投产，投产后将批量生产587Ah储能电芯。
1.5亿元储能集装箱项目签约落地永仁
9月2日，贵州焕文科技有限公司与永仁县签署储能集装箱项目招商引资协议，项目计划投资1.5亿元。
据介绍，双方将围绕储能集装箱项目开展合作，并进一步推进储能装备制造、新能源项目开发等相关业务。
希倍动力2.5亿元钠电项目落户自贡
8月30日，北京希倍动力科技有限公司与四川自贡高新区签署高性能钠离子电池生产基地项目合作协议，项目正式落户自贡高新区。
该项目计划总投资约2.5亿元，建成达产后预计形成年产0.5GWh高性能钠离子电池产能。
以此项目基础上，希倍动力将根据市场发展节奏稳步推进产能扩张，远期规划产能规模达10GWh。
超钠新能源6GWh钠电项目签约绵竹
据四川绵竹市人民政府官网消息，8月28日，绵竹高新区管委会与湖州超钠新能源科技有限公司签订年产6GWh钠离子电池生产线项目投资协议。
此前，2024年1月28日，超钠新能源计划总投资30亿元，在绵竹建设8万吨级钠离子电池正极材料的生产基地。此次6GWh钠离子电池生产线项目签约，将进一步延伸超钠新能源在绵竹的钠电产业布局，推动业务从正极材料向电芯制造环节拓展。

title: BYD’s Electric Kei Car Was Driven In Japan. It Fits Right In
content:
This early English-language of BYD's kei EV reveals a roomy, comfy and thoughtfully engineered EV that feels right at home in Japan
Photo by:
Everything Electric APAC
6:59am ET
An early drive finds the $13,000 BYD Racco roomy, comfortable and remarkably well suited to Japanese roads.
It’s the first ground-up, mainstream kei passenger car developed by an overseas automaker.
It matches the Nissan Sakura’s power, but with less torque, yet offers up to 199 miles of range, versus the Nissan’s 112 miles.
Chinese automakers typically enter foreign markets trying to overwhelm rivals with their cars’ power, tech, and range. But BYD couldn’t use that playbook with
the Racco
because Japan’s kei-car rules tightly restrict dimensions and power output, forcing BYD to try to win through packaging, practicality, and attention to local tastes.
One of the first English-language drives of the Racco suggests BYD may have just pulled it off.
Everything Electric APAC
presenter Elliot Richards went to Himeji, Japan, where BYD lent him a Racco for the day.
This wasn’t a conventional press launch, and Elliot says he paid for the trip himself, so the fact that he calls the Racco an “absolute banger” holds more weight than if it had been the result of a fully paid (and often highly curated) official media drive.
What seemed to impress him most was how thoroughly BYD embraced the kei-car brief. The Racco’s tall, boxy body and power-sliding rear doors make it exceptionally easy to enter, while its high seating position gives great all-around visibility. Despite its tiny footprint, the host found the rear legroom better than in many much larger SUVs and described the back seats as “supremely comfortable.”
The Racco has a highly modular interior with seats that can also be folded, reclined, or flipped forward to accommodate unusually tall cargo. With them folded, the Racco becomes a tiny electric van with a long, nearly flat floor and a useful, square cargo area.
As with any kei car, the cabin is pretty basic, but Elliot says it is one of BYD’s best interiors precisely because the company resisted the urge to fill it with gimmicks. Front seat comfort is rated excellent, and the vehicle is easy to operate thanks to physical climate controls and a small touchscreen with Apple CarPlay.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
On the road, it feels remarkably similar to its main rival,
the Nissan Sakura
. The steering is reasonably direct but slightly soft, while the brakes were sharper than Elliot says he would have liked. Acceleration is merely adequate, but with low urban speed limits and narrow streets, he concluded that it has all the performance it needs.
BYD’s effort with the Racco compares well with the Sakura, Japan’s best-selling EV for four consecutive years through 2025. Both have exactly the same footprint and power output dictated by kei car regulations. However, the Racco stands 5.7 inches (145 mm) taller than the Nissan.
More BYD Stories
The Sakura features a 20-kilowatt-hour battery with 112 miles (180 km) of WLTC range. The Racco offers either a 22.4-kWh pack with 130 miles (210 km) of range, or a much larger 35.8-kWh battery capable of 199 miles (320 km). The Nissan counters with 144 lb-ft (195 Nm) of torque, compared with the BYD’s 118 lb-ft (160 Nm), which should make it feel noticeably nippier to drive.
The Racco starts at around $13,000 before Japan’s almost $1,000 clean car incentive has been factored in, although the Sakura can become slightly cheaper after Japan’s more generous subsidy for domestic models is applied.

title: Can Xiaomi Take On Porsche On Its Home Turf? It’s About To Try
content:
Eight dealership groups have signed on as part of Xiaomi's entry into Europe, which starts next year.
Photo by:
2:19pm ET
Xiaomi is officially headed to Europe, including Germany, in 2027, the company announced on Thursday.
Eight dealership networks have now signed on.
German luxury brands have been feeling the heat in China. Now that's coming to their backyard.
Xiaomi has spent the last two years proving that a company that builds cell phones can also build your favorite car. The Apple of the East makes EVs that are fast, desirable, and chock-full of tech that makes most American cars feel archaic.
It's passed the test in its home
market, having sold over 700,000 vehicles there to date. Now it's setting its sights on Europe.
On Thursday, the company announced plans to enter European markets, including Germany, in 2027. After bringing the heat to Porsche, BMW, Mercedes-Benz, and Volkswagen within China, the country's automakers are increasingly exporting the fight to European turf. Xiaomi is just the latest disruptor. Based on its popularity in China and
high praise abroad
, it could be a formidable competitor.
Photo by: MIIT
After years of raking in healthy profits in China, European luxury brands have been
struggling to keep up with the country's fast-moving homegrown automakers
. Their sales have dwindled as a result. Only
125 vehicles
were imported into China in July, a figure that's down 99% from its 2023 peak. One example: Porsche's China sales fell 26% last year and have been more than cut in half since 2021. Now the same tech that is winning over Chinese consumers is headed straight for the Germans' backyard.
Xiaomi SU7 Ultra sedan has already been doing battle with Porsche on the Nurburgring
, even dethroning the Taycan Turbo GT. Then there's the
, a curvy crossover with 990 horsepower, which is about 300 more than you get in the highest-performance Porsche Macan EV. Xiaomi hasn't said which model (or models) it plans to sell in Europe.
If pure speed isn't your thing, Xiaomi is also catering to tech-hungry buyers with its "Human x Car x Home" ecosystem, which integrates more than 1,000 different Xiaomi devices with the car. Xiaomi's cars are also aggressively priced in its home market and have a number of premium features baked in that make a pretty convincing value proposition over many of the offerings on the market today wearing a badge from a German luxury brand.
How well Xiaomi manages to do in Germany, and Europe more broadly, may ultimately come down to price and positioning. The SU7 and YU7 could launch as Porsche and BMW rivals for a much better value. But if the brand prices its vehicles too close to cars from already well-respected brands, that could be a tougher sell.
Stay informed with our newsletter every weekday
Xiaomi is just
one of the Chinese brands
making its way to Europe.
Chinese-imported cars made up 14.2% of all EVs sold across the region
during the first half of 2026, meaning that Western automakers across the board are already feeling the pressure.
Some have even
resorted to importing their own made-in-China vehicles
into Europe
as a way to stay competitive
. But as up-market models from Xiaomi and others gain more traction, it could prove to be a tough road ahead for even Germany's most prestigious brands.

title: Electric Cars Were The UK's Best-Selling Powertrain Last Month
content:
Electric Cars Were The UK's Best-Selling Powertrain Last Month
At 30% of the entire UK market, the country is buying more EVs than any other vehicle type.
- EVs now make up 30% of all UK sales, beating combustion, plug-in hybrid, and hybrid models.
- Tesla is the top-selling EV brand, capturing 8.8% of the UK market so far this year. Kia and BYD are in second and third place, respectively.
- Government policies, plus rising oil prices, are driving the sales growth.
While tariffs and the destruction of plug-in vehicle subsidies have gutted the market for electric vehicles in the U.S., elsewhere in the world the numbers continue to surge.
In the UK in August, sales of battery-electric cars surged 30% year over year, according to data from New Automotive, a research firm. As a result, EV market share hit 30% of new car sales, beating gas vehicles, hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and diesel models. Notably, non-hybrid combustion models only made up 27% of the UK market, so even if they’re not buying a full EV, buyers are opting for something that is electrified in some fashion.
UK EV sales have been on the upswing this year. Data from New Automotive, shows that in July, the country's EV registrations jumped 50% compared to the year before, bringing their market share to 27%.
Jaecoo E5
It’s a no-brainer as to why the UK is EV crazy. For starters, there’s a zero-emission vehicle mandate that aims to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035. This goal is tiered, with EVs to account for 33% of new car sales in 2026, 80% in 2030, and 100% by 2035. Manufacturers that sell enough EVs to hit the ZEV target get credits, while those who don’t meet it must pay penalties. This incentivizes automakers to develop and sell EV models. The UK also has direct subsidies for buyers of EVs.
The UK also has a lot of Clean Air Zones that disincentivize cars that pollute too much, making drivers who wish to drive into certain areas pay a fee. Cars that are clean-air compliant, such as an EV, don’t need to pay any clean-air fees.
Those incentives seem to be working. Rising fuel prices due to the Iran war have been boosting EV sales across Europe too.
Tesla remains the UK’s most popular EV maker, with 8.8% of the EV market so far this year. Kia is in second place, with 45% of its new car sales being fully electric last month. The UK has also become an important market for Chinese brands. BYD is in third place with about 6.3% of the UK EV market, according to New AutoMotive. Its registrations are up about 60% so far this year. Cars like the BYD Dolphin Surf, Atto 2, and Jaecoo E5 no doubt help with these numbers.
Some of the UK’s own brands aren’t actually helping much. Tata, which encompasses Jaguar and Land Rover, has sold 43,000 units this year, but none of them have been EVs. Perhaps this figure will change when cars like the new Range Rover Electric and Jaguar Type 01 go on sale.
