title: New helium system moves KRONOS microreactor closer to prototype stage
content: A critical cooling component for a new nuclear microreactor has moved into detailed design, marking another engineering step toward building a prototype. The helium circulator is being developed for the KRONOS MMR Energy System, a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor under development by NANO Nuclear Energy.The circulator will move helium through the reactor core to carry heat away from the fuel and maintain the reactor’s thermal performance. Its design will therefore influence how efficiently the reactor transfers heat and how reliably the system operates over time.NANO Nuclear is developing the component with Howden, a Baker Hughes business with experience in helium turbomachinery and high-temperature gas-cooled reactor systems. Howden is leading the engineering work while working with NANO Nuclear’s reactor team.The collaboration has now progressed beyond preliminary engineering. Howden has completed engineering evaluations, created three-dimensional design models, carried out supporting analyses and held formal design reviews with NANO Nuclear.Reactor cooling takes shapeThe move to detailed design gives the team a more defined engineering basis for testing, qualification and eventual manufacturing. The companies will continue work on materials and performance testing, component qualification, design optimization and manufacturing planning.The helium circulator is particularly important in a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor because helium serves as the coolant that transports heat generated inside the core. Unlike water-cooled reactors, the system relies on a gas coolant operating at high temperatures.For KRONOS, the goal is to integrate the circulator into a compact reactor system while meeting requirements for thermal performance, manufacturability, and long-term operation.“Progressing the primary helium circulator into detailed design represents another important milestone in the continued development of the KRONOS MMR™ Energy System. Advancement of the circulator design strengthens the technical foundation of the overall reactor program and demonstrates the disciplined engineering execution essential for successful commercialization. We continue to make steady progress across both engineering and regulatory activities as we advance the KRONOS program toward prototype construction, regulatory licensing and future deployment,” said James Walker, chief executive officer of NANO Nuclear Energy.The company is also working on other parts of the reactor architecture. Its collaboration with Fortil covers the fuel handling and storage system, which will support the handling, storage and management of nuclear fuel during reactor operations.More systems move toward testingNANO Nuclear says the parallel development of these subsystems is intended to build a standardized engineering foundation for future reactor deployments.The company is also engaged in pre-application activities with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission for the KRONOS reactor and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. The reactor is intended to be a stationary high-temperature gas-cooled microreactor.The helium circulator’s detailed design will now need to progress through additional qualification and testing before the component can move toward manufacturing. That work will help determine whether the design can meet the performance requirements established for the reactor.“NANO Nuclear’s strategy is built upon developing advanced reactor technology through disciplined engineering execution and strategic collaborations with world-class supply chain partners. Our continued work with Howden reflects that commitment, bringing together complementary expertise to advance a critical reactor subsystem. Each engineering milestone strengthens the industrial ecosystem supporting KRONOS while further positioning the program for future first-of-a-kind deployment and long-term commercial success,” said Jay Yu, founder and chairman of NANO Nuclear Energy.The company says the broader KRONOS program is progressing toward prototype construction, regulatory licensing and eventual deployment, although the latest announcement represents an engineering milestone rather than authorization to build or operate the reactor.

title: New ship-mounted system uses shotguns to shoot down attacking drones
content: German company Mehler Protection is set to unveil a new ship-mounted counter-drone system at SMM 2026, designed to protect naval vessels from threats that penetrate conventional air defenses.Called SCILT NAVAL, the system targets FPV drones, loitering munitions and other unmanned aircraft operating close to ships. It is intended to provide a last line of defense when crews have little time to respond, particularly near ports, around marine infrastructure and in confined waters.Closing a gap in naval defensesThe growing use of inexpensive drones has created a significant challenge for naval forces. Even well-equipped vessels can be threatened by multiple unmanned aircraft approaching simultaneously, especially when the drones fly close to the surface or attack from short distances.Long-range air defense systems can engage aircraft and missiles before they reach a vessel. However, their effectiveness may be limited when targets appear at close range or operate in environments where reaction time and maneuvering space are restricted.SCILT NAVAL was developed to address this gap. It can be deployed during operations near ports, aboard vessels navigating narrow waterways, around floating infrastructure, and during missions involving amphibious forces.The system is also designed for use on different types of vessels, including smaller craft that may not carry extensive air defense equipment. According to Mehler Protection, it can engage individual targets as well as multiple drones during coordinated attacks.Three-stage response to drone attacksSCILT NAVAL combines its detection equipment and effectors in one onboard system. Its sensors identify approaching aircraft and provide information that helps operators assess and respond to potential threats.The system divides its response into three stages: detection, warning, and engagement. It uses commercially available shotgun calibers to strike drones at close range, with different ammunition types available for different operational requirements.Possible options include ammunition designed for varied levels of impact, including armor-piercing configurations. Compared with earlier versions of the technology, the naval system offers greater range and an automatic reloading capability.Human operators will remain responsible for engagement decisions in the initial configuration. Mehler Protection said greater automation could be introduced as relevant regulations, certifications and operational procedures develop.SCILT NAVAL can also be connected to a ship’s existing command-and-control infrastructure. If integration is not possible, it can operate independently using its own sensors and response components.Control units can be installed at several locations aboard a vessel, allowing crew members to monitor threats and access the system without relying on a single operating station.System undergoes 48 maritime testsMehler Protection developed the naval defense system over 18 months and subjected it to 48 tests before its planned unveiling.The testing program assessed factors including information transmission, ammunition behavior, and the system’s ability to withstand operational conditions at sea. Engineers also examined its performance when exposed to saltwater, vibrations, and other stresses encountered aboard naval vessels.Further trials evaluated the effectors and helped establish the appropriate engagement range for different targets. The findings were then used to refine the system’s configuration. SCILT NAVAL expands Mehler Protection’s portfolio of protective systems for land, air, and maritime applications.

title: Nuclear reactor simulations advance with new quantum transport method
content: Physicists modeling nuclear systems have long faced a basic computing problem: particles do not move through neat, uniform blocks of matter. In a nuclear reactor or radiation shield, neutrons and photons travel across jagged edges, dense metals, fluids, and empty voids. Tracking these paths requires tracking every shift in material, and on standard computers, the calculations quickly become overwhelming.Quantum X Labs has designed a new way to solve this problem on quantum computers. The company’s Nuclear Quantum division built an algorithm that directly translates complicated physical shapes into quantum data. Instead of chopping an object into billions of tiny digital cubes, the system mathematically embeds the boundaries and material densities into quantum states.“Efficient geometric encoding is fundamental to making quantum transport algorithms relevant to realistic physical systems,” said David Shnaiderov, Head of Nuclear Quantum in Quantum X Labs.“This milestone demonstrates our progress in addressing one of the key computational bottlenecks in the field and establishes an important foundation for the next generation of quantum transport methods.”Solving the state preparation bottleneckThe breakthrough matters because physical shape is one of the hardest things to program into a quantum processor. Before a quantum machine can simulate a physical event, researchers must first load the environment into quantum bits. In scientific computing, this initial step is called state preparation. If an engineer wants to model an irregular structure, such as fuel rods sitting inside metal cladding, the digital instructions needed just to describe that shape can grow too long. Quantum hardware easily accumulates errors during lengthy operations, which can ruin the simulation before it even starts.The new technique cuts down that operational overhead. It compresses how the boundaries are defined, which shortens the sequence of basic quantum operations needed to load the model. Once the geometry is loaded, the quantum computer can track how particles fly through different zones. It calculates when a particle should bounce off a wall, pass through a barrier, or get absorbed by a heavy metal.Spatial layout requires fewer instructionsBecause the spatial layout requires fewer instructions, the quantum processor has enough operating capacity left over to run the actual physics calculations. David Shnaiderov, who directs the Nuclear Quantum division at Quantum X Labs, pointed out that simulating particle transport is useless without a practical way to represent real physical shapes. He noted that removing the computing traffic jam at the boundary level provides a workable base for running future transport programs.The project is part of a wider effort by Quantum X Labs to apply quantum computing to core nuclear problems. Particle movement depends on several moving parts at once, including energy levels, speed, spatial coordinates, and angles of travel. By clearing the technical barrier of spatial geometry first, the team plans to combine this encoding layer with other quantum equations to calculate three-dimensional nuclear systems that standard supercomputers still struggle to solve.

title: Nuclear-powered USS Abraham Lincoln ends record 286-day deployment
content: The USS Abraham Lincoln reached Laem Chabang Port in Thailand on Wednesday, after 286 days at sea during a deployment that stretched far beyond its original schedule. The 1,092-foot nuclear-powered carrier brought around 5,000 U.S. sailors and Marines ashore for a four-day rest stop after months of operations in the Middle East.This is the carrier’s first full stop since it left San Diego in November 2025. The long deployment has raised concerns about the crew’s well-being, supplies, and the ship’s condition.Record time at seaThe Lincoln went 264 days in a row without a full port visit. By early July, it had broken the modern U.S. Navy record of 206 straight days at sea, set by the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower during the COVID-19 pandemic.Aircraft carriers normally enter port every 30 to 45 days for resupply, maintenance, and crew recovery. The Lincoln’s extended absence meant sailors faced a much longer period without the usual break from shipboard operations.Families and crew members had reported concerns about food and water shortages, disrupted mail, laundry problems and declining morale. Mental health also became a major concern, with relatives raising fears about self-harm during Navy town hall meetings in August.Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao said no meals had been missed and explained that calls home had sometimes been restricted because of operational threats. He also acknowledged that personnel were “pushed to their limits”.Months of combat operationsThe Lincoln left San Diego on November 21, 2025, for what was initially described as routine operations. Its deployment was later extended as the carrier remained in the Middle East to support U.S. military operations against Iran.The strike group spent nearly seven months in the U.S. Central Command area. By August 14, the carrier had spent 200 days in a combat zone, while its aircraft had flown more than 10,000 sorties and dropped about 1.5 million pounds of ordnance.The USS George Washington later arrived in the Arabian Sea to relieve the Lincoln, allowing the carrier to begin its journey east toward San Diego.Rust shows deployment strainPhotographs taken after the Lincoln reached Thailand showed large areas of apparent rust along its hull, especially above the waterline and around the flight deck. The carrier’s commanding officer, Captain Dan Keeler, said the appearance was expected after such a long period at sea.“It is normal for a long deployment, and we’re not going to make further comments,” Keeler added.Defense expert Euan Graham described the appearance as evidence of a ship that had remained continuously at sea for 286 days. Former U.S. Navy captain Carl Schuster said treating waterline corrosion requires the ship to remain stationary, making extensive work difficult during combat operations.Crew gets first major breakThe Thailand stop gives sailors and Marines time to rest in nearby Pattaya before the carrier resumes its trip home. Each service member is expected to receive three liberty days and one day of duty aboard the ship.Keeler said the carrier will make additional stops to replenish supplies before reaching San Diego.“There’s no big delay about when we are going home,” he said. “They move us around where they need us to be.”

title: Quantum-proof platform aces US Army exercise, achieves TRL-7
content: The US Army has tested a quantum-resistant cybersecurity platform under live battlefield conditions, demonstrating its ability to protect tactical communications from emerging quantum threats.QuSecure’s QuProtect R3 was deployed during Project Convergence Capstone 6 (PCC6), an annual Army experiment held at the National Training Center in Fort Irwin, California. Operated by soldiers during the exercise, the system provided secure communications, cryptographic agility, and an inventory of cryptographic assets used across tactical mission systems.Quantum security tested on tactical networksPCC6 brought together thousands of soldiers, military systems, and emerging technologies to test future concepts and formations for the US Army, joint forces, and multinational partners.The exercise evaluates technologies under realistic operational conditions rather than controlled laboratory environments. Its broader objective is to improve the military’s lethality, agility, and survivability while strengthening its ability to deter and respond to potential adversaries.During the event, QuProtect R3 helped identify cryptographic assets and enabled quantum-resistant protection across Army tactical networks. Its successful use by soldiers earned the platform Technology Readiness Level 7, or TRL-7.That rating indicates a system prototype has been demonstrated in an operational environment. It also gives QuProtect the highest score in the “Technical Readiness” category outlined by the Post-Quantum Cryptography Coalition’s assessment guidelines.Two years of development with US ArmyQuProtect’s appearance at PCC6 follows nearly two years of development work between QuSecure and the US Army’s Command, Control, Communications, Computers, Cyber, Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Center, commonly known as C5ISR.The platform began as part of a Small Business Innovation Research program and has since developed into a system positioned for wider military adoption.“Participation in PCC6 caps off almost two years of close, iterative development work with C5ISR to adapt the product and add new capabilities for tactical networks,” said Joey Lupo, Product Manager at QuSecure. “C5ISR has been instrumental in helping QuProtect mature into the product it is today. This event also marks a critical milestone for the Army,” he added. “Besides demonstrating that tactical networks can be hardened against the quantum threat before a possible 2029 Q-day, we demonstrated improvements to the network today in terms of automation, cryptographic agility, and zero trust that will improve resilience against advanced cyber adversaries for years to come,” Lupo added. Preparing agencies for quantum threatsQuantum computers could eventually undermine widely used encryption methods, exposing sensitive government and military information.This has prompted US agencies to begin replacing vulnerable cryptography before sufficiently capable quantum systems emerge.The demonstration comes as federal agencies work toward post-quantum cryptography migration deadlines set for 2030–2031 under Executive Order 14412.“Executive Order 14412 and the Department of War’s PQC Strategy have set binding deadlines every federal agency now has to meet,” said Brian Cunningham, executive vice president of growth and strategy at QuSecure.“TRL-7 at PCC6 means the Army is not waiting. They have a proven, deployable platform operating in live-force tactical conditions right now, years ahead of the 2030-2031 compliance window,” he added.

title: Scientists solve ‘mystery-signal’ hidden in quantum material
content: Researchers at the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS) and the Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) have solved the years-long mystery about the origins of the ‘beating’ signal in the topological insulator (TI) nanowires. The discovery paves the way for better interpretation of signals from topological quantum devices and attaining their desired electronic states. Emerging quantum technologies like quantum computing and sensing hold the promise of a new era of devices with capabilities that are hard to believe could be real. Quantum computers could beat the fastest supercomputers of the day in just a few seconds, while advanced sensors can measure changes in electric or magnetic fields even at nanoscales. For all their advantages, quantum technologies are extremely sensitive, and these devices can be thrown out of gear by the slightest changes in temperature or environmental noise. Topological devices leverage mathematical properties of topology to protect quantum information and ensure that data remains coherent for longer and resilient to external noise. Beating signal in TITopological insulators (TI) are materials that are insulating in their interiors but can conduct electrons on their edges or outer surfaces via special electronic states. Scientists use this materials to make nanowires where electrons travel along the perimeter. When a magnetic field is applied to these wires, electron waves passing through different paths interfere, producing Aharonov-Bohm (AB) oscillations. Here, the conductance of the material changes at regular intervals depending on the intensity of the magnetic field. When a TI is doped, it can create a thin layer beneath the surface where the electrons can flow. However, whether this layer participates in the AB oscillations was not well known. When working with antimony (Sb)-doped bismuth selenide (Bi₂Se₃) nanowires, researchers found a ‘beating’ signal where oscillations of slightly different periods and signal intensities were observed, confirming the presence of another oscillation. What causes the beating signal?The researchers analyzed electrical conductance data from previous years of research working with TI and confirmed that this beating signal had been present all along. The team attributed this to the oscillations emerging from the ‘Topological Surface State’ (TSS), the electronic state on the surface of the TI, and the ‘Two-Dimensional Electron Gas’ (2DEG), where electrons gather and move under the surface. Electrons passing through the two paths pass through the conduction states and through slightly different cross-sectional areas of the nanowire, causing their oscillations at different periods, thereby producing the beating pattern. While this seems straightforward, it was difficult to distinguish these oscillation components using conventional frequency analysis. So, the research team, with help from Song Taegeun, a professor at the Kongju National University and used machine learning to differentiate oscillation components, even when beating patterns changed with the gate voltage. “This achievement shows that electrons can undergo quantum interference by moving through not only topological states but also ordinary electronic states,” said Bae Myung-Ho, Principal Research Scientist in the Quantum Device Group at KRISS in a press release. “To make use of only the desired topological state, it is important to precisely control doping and the gate so that the ordinary conduction state does not intervene.”“The principle of understanding and controlling the interference between different electronic states could also be applied to the design of topological quantum devices in the future,” concluded Choi Sang-Jun, a professor at the Department of Physics and Photon Science at the GIST in the press release.The research findings were published in the journal Nano Letters.

title: Tesla's new Cybercabs hit Austin roads without steering wheel controls
content: Elon Musk’s Tesla has deployed dozens of its purpose-built Cybercabs on public roads in Austin, Texas, marking a new phase in the company’s push toward fully autonomous ride-hailing.The gold-colored vehicles have no steering wheels or brake pedals, meaning passengers cannot take control if something goes wrong. Tesla is using the rollout to test both the technology and whether riders are willing to trust a vehicle that offers no manual driving option.The push beyond supervised robotaxisTesla has operated a self-driving robotaxi service in Austin since June 2025, but those vehicles still came with conventional controls and initially carried safety drivers who could intervene if necessary.The new Cybercabs go further. They are designed from the outset as autonomous taxis, without a steering wheel or pedals.Musk also revealed the Cybercab uses no rare earth metals. The Cybercab motor uses no rare earth metals, but maintains the same range! This was extremely hard to achieve. https://t.co/2SrdikvrUM— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) September 4, 2026An invitation-only launch event was also expected to be held later Thursday as Tesla prepares to expand the service to additional cities.The company already operates more than 200 unsupervised robotaxis across cities in Texas and Florida, according to RobotaxiTracker. However, Tesla still trails Waymo, which has more than 4,000 driverless vehicles operating across 14 cities.The major safety testFor Tesla, the challenge is not only scaling the fleet but proving that its autonomous driving approach can operate safely without human intervention.Tesla relies heavily on cameras and artificial intelligence for its self-driving system. Rivals including Waymo and Amazon-owned Zoox use cameras alongside radar and lidar, which use radio waves and lasers to help vehicles understand their surroundings.That difference makes the Austin rollout an important test of whether Tesla’s camera-based system can consistently identify pedestrians, vehicles, road markings and unexpected hazards in real-world traffic.The company’s partial self-driving software has faced multiple safety investigations in the United States, while approvals remain limited across much of Europe.Musk ultimately wants to make full self-driving software available to hundreds of thousands of Tesla vehicles through software updates. His broader vision would allow owners to place their cars into Tesla’s robotaxi network when they are not using them.Public trust could be the bigger hurdleEven if Tesla can demonstrate that the Cybercab works reliably, convincing passengers to climb into a vehicle without any manual controls may prove difficult.A Pew Research Center survey conducted in February found that seven in 10 U.S. adults were either “not too” or “not at all” comfortable with the idea of riding in a driverless car.Only 16 percent said they would be “somewhat” comfortable, while 7 percent said they would be “extremely” or “very” comfortable.Separate Gallup polling from 2025 also found growing skepticism about autonomous vehicle safety compared with earlier surveys.Tesla is making the Cybercab push while its core vehicle business faces pressure. The company recorded a second consecutive annual decline in vehicle sales last year, profits fell, and China’s BYD overtook Tesla as the world’s largest electric vehicle seller.That puts added importance on Musk’s robotaxi bet. Tesla now needs to show that Cybercabs can operate safely, scale quickly, and convince riders to give up control entirely.

title: The Unblinking Eye
content:
The future of military aviation is becoming increasingly complex. As defense forces seek better intelligence, more flexible missions, and safer conditions for personnel, General Atomics Aeronautical is developing the next generation of uncrewed aircraft.
With more than 30 years of experience, GA-ASI is launching platforms that can scale rapidly and operate in tough environments to support critical surveillance and combat missions.
They’re built to operate where conventional aircraft cannot
Modern military missions often need aircraft to launch from locations far from standard air bases. GA-ASI’s Mojave Short Takeoff and Landing (STOL) uncrewed aircraft system was created for this challenge. It can take off from aircraft carriers, dirt airstrips, and other non-traditional sites without needing long paved runways.
This flexibility allows military units to deploy air support much closer to the battlefield. Mojave STOL can quickly provide armed reconnaissance to ground forces, then land at remote spots to refuel or reload before heading back to the fight. Its ability to operate from temporary landing zones gives commanders more choices when there is little or no infrastructure.
Advanced surveillance stays in the air longer
A major advantage of uncrewed aircraft is that they can keep watch for extended periods — up to 40 continuous hours or more — depending on the configuration. These long-endurance aircraft can fly over a target area to help commanders track movement, watch for threats, and get a real-time view of changing situations. When aircraft are relieving each other in shifts for nonstop surveillance, nothing can happen on the surface without them seeing.GA-ASI’s unmanned aircraft systems were made for these tough intelligence missions.
New aircraft are taking on the air superiority mission, too. The Gambit 1 collaborative combat model can fly ahead of both crewed and uncrewed strike groups, using advanced sensors to spot, identify, and track possible airborne threats before they get close to friendly aircraft.Engineers built a common core for this aircraft that can go into other Gambit Series platforms with different wings, tails, or onboard systems. Gambit Series aircraft can provide reconnaissance, armed escort, air-to-ground strike, and more depending on their configurations.
Human operators remain at the center of every mission
Although these aircraft can be tasked to perform missions independently through autonomy software, human operators continue to play a critical role in its operation. Semi-autonomous systems such as the Gambit Series of aircraft can take off, navigate, and detect threats without the need for a human operator manually controlling them, watching every move.
But these aircraft aren’t telling themselves what to do. Human operators task them, review the intelligence they gather, monitor aircraft performance, and issue commands whenever mission requirements change. The U.S. Air Force calls them “semi-autonomous” aircraft. This combination of onboard automation and human oversight creates an effective partnership that improves operational awareness while preserving direct human control over critical decisions.It also reduces the workload on aircrews without removing them from the decision-making process.
Supporting modern military operations worldwide
GA-ASI has spent decades developing technologies that support U.S. and allied forces, engineering systems that can execute critical mission support while keeping aircrews out of harm’s way.

title: Top EVs retain over 90% battery health after 93,000 miles, study finds
content: A new analysis of more than 500,000 independent electric vehicle battery tests has revealed which EVs retain the most battery capacity as they rack up mileage, and the results show that some batteries age considerably better than others.The study, conducted by Austrian battery diagnostics company AVILOO, examined 20 popular EV models using real-world battery health measurements collected between 2022 and 2026. The data comes from AVILOO’s global database of more than 1 million independent tests across North and South America, Europe, Australia, and Asia.Mercedes EQA leads after 150,000 kmThe study measures State of Health (SoH), which represents the percentage of a battery’s original usable capacity that remains. A battery at 95% SoH, for example, retains roughly 95% of its original range per charge.At 150,000 km (93,000 miles), the Mercedes-Benz EQA comes out on top among the 20 models, with a median battery SoH of 94%. The Hyundai IONIQ 5 follows at 93.8%, while the BMW i4 reaches 93.6%.The Hyundai Kona EV and Volvo XC40 Recharge round out the top five, with both retaining more than 92% of their median battery health at the same mileage. The IONIQ 5 is particularly notable because it starts at the top of the dataset at lower mileage. Its median SoH is around 97% at 50,000 km, before falling to 92.8% at 150,000 km.That means an IONIQ 5 reaching 150,000 km has, on average, retained nearly 94% of the usable capacity it had when new. Other strong performers include the Ford Mustang Mach-E and Polestar 2, both at around 92.5% median SoH after 150,000 km, followed by the Cupra Born and Volkswagen ID.3 at around 92%.How do Tesla batteries compare?Two of the world’s most recognizable EVs sit noticeably lower in the rankings. The Tesla Model Y records a median SoH of 90.3% at 150,000 km, down from 94.5% at 50,000 km in AVILOO’s detailed analysis. That corresponds to an estimated real-world range of roughly 379 km at 50,000 km and about 362 km at 150,000 km.The Tesla Model 3 performs somewhat worse, with a median SoH of 88.9% at 150,000 km. That doesn’t necessarily mean either Tesla has a poor battery. Both still retain the majority of their original capacity after roughly 93,000 miles. Rather, they illustrate how battery degradation can vary substantially between models.The Nissan Leaf ZE1 sits at the other end of the study, with a median SoH of 86.3% at 150,000 km. AVILOO highlights its relatively small 40-kWh battery as an important factor. Covering the same distance requires more charging cycles than it would with a much larger battery. The Leaf isn’t alone at the bottom. The MINI Cooper SE and Renault Zoe also record median SoH figures below 88% at 150,000 km.The biggest surprise isn’t the rankingsThe most important finding may be that two identical EVs can have very different battery health. AVILOO found that the gap between individual vehicles of the same model can reach 13.5 percentage points of SoH. The variation generally becomes wider as mileage increases.For the Tesla Model Y, for example, individual vehicles at 150,000 km can differ by up to around 11% in SoH. For the IONIQ 5, the spread exceeds 12%. In the Nissan Leaf, it reaches 13.5%.Those differences are more meaningful than they might sound. A 10% difference in battery health can translate into tens of kilometers of real-world range, potentially determining whether a used EV completes a journey comfortably or needs another charging stop. That means mileage alone isn’t a particularly good indicator of the condition of a used EV’s most expensive component.Why batteries degrade differentlyMileage is only one part of the equation. AVILOO points to factors including battery chemistry, climate, charging behavior, and how long a vehicle remains at a high state of charge.Temperature can affect both battery degradation and charging behavior, which is one reason the study’s global dataset is useful. Its tests span multiple continents and a wide range of driving and climate conditions.The study also uses independent measurements rather than simply taking the battery-health figure displayed by the vehicle. AVILOO’s three-minute FLASH Test connects through the vehicle’s OBD port and uses a statistical model trained on hundreds of thousands of real used vehicles, incorporating factors such as mileage, age, cycles, cell-voltage spread, and energy measurements.Overall, the results are reassuring for EV owners. Even the lower-ranked models retain substantial battery capacity after 150,000 km, while the strongest performers remain above 93%. But for someone buying a used EV, the bigger lesson is more nuanced. The battery health of the specific car matters more than the average health of its model. Two EVs with the same badge and mileage can have very different amounts of usable life left in their batteries.

title: Transparent chips made on 300-mm wafers bend thousands of times
content: Silicon-photonics chips can move data using light instead of electrical signals, but conventional versions are rigid and opaque. MIT researchers have now developed a way to make these chips both flexible and transparent, while using semiconductor manufacturing methods that can work across large wafers.The new process could make silicon photonics useful in applications where rigid chips do not fit. Potential uses include health monitors that conform to the body and augmented-reality displays built into curved surfaces such as aircraft pilot visors.The researchers developed the process with engineers at NY Creates’ Albany NanoTech Complex. Instead of producing individual flexible or transparent devices in the laboratory, their approach creates 300-millimeter wafers containing the optical structures needed for silicon photonics.The resulting chips are only a few microns thick. Tests showed that a chip could be bent thousands of times around cylinders of different sizes, including one roughly as wide as a small screw, without losing performance.Chips built for bendingThe manufacturing process starts much like that used for conventional silicon wafers. Researchers deposit and pattern optical waveguides, which act as tiny pathways for light, on a silicon substrate.A temporary silicon wafer is then bonded to the structure before the original silicon substrate is removed. This leaves behind the oxide and waveguiding layers. The researchers attach a thin, transparent polyester film to the remaining structure before removing the temporary support. The result is a thin wafer that can bend while allowing light to pass through it.“Because we are using stable 300-millimeter foundry fabrication tools, we can design systems with a very large number of devices and feel confident that they are going to perform up to specifications, which is extremely important,” lead author Tal Sneh says.Getting to that point required careful control of stress during fabrication. Removing most of the silicon from a large wafer can cause it to bow or develop ripples, potentially damaging the ultrathin layers.The team kept fabrication temperatures at or below 500 degrees Celsius to manage this stress. It also combined industrial silicon-thinning methods with a more selective chemical etching process for the final material removal.Transparent enough for displaysThe researchers then tested whether the new platform could maintain its optical performance while being flexible and transparent.In bending experiments, the chip showed no performance degradation after thousands of bends around small cylinders. It only began to degrade when bent around a toothpick several times.The team also tested transparency using a bionic-eye setup. The chip produced minimal haze and did not noticeably distort images viewed through it, suggesting that the material could work in optical systems placed directly in front of the eye.That could enable curved augmented-reality displays integrated into windshields or pilot visors. Such systems could potentially replace some of the bulky optical components currently used to provide pilots with real-time information.The researchers also see possibilities for discreet wearable devices that need to follow the contours of the human body.“We’ve now developed a wafer-scale process that produces wafers that are mechanically flexible and optically transparent, enabling novel applications that weren’t previously possible with silicon photonics. We hope that, by working closely with our colleagues at NY Creates and using the foundry at the Albany NanoTech Complex, there’s the potential for us to make the platform accessible to other groups within our research community and open these new application areas to the field of silicon photonics as a whole,” says Jelena Notaros, senior author of the study.The researchers plan to add more complex components, improve waveguide efficiency, and further increase transparency as they develop the platform.The study is published in the journal Optica.

title: Turkish firm's deep-strike munition penetrates two-storey concrete structure
content:
Successful release of the weapons
The significance of the demonstration lies not simply in the successful release of the
, but in the different effects that the three TOLUN variants are designed to deliver.
TOLUN I is configured with an impact fuze and fragmentation warhead. During the trial, it scored a direct hit on a container, demonstrating its ability to deliver a fragmentation effect immediately upon impact.
TOLUN F takes a different approach. It was employed against an armoured personnel carrier using a proximity sensor and fragmentation warhead. Its selectable impact angle and software designed to resist GPS spoofing are intended to provide greater
flexibility
against personnel and other targets in the vicinity of the engagement point.
TOLUN P penetrated a two-storey concrete structure
The most specialized demonstration involved TOLUN P. This variant penetrated a two-storey concrete structure before neutralizing designated elements at the selected level. It combines a penetrating warhead with a programmable time-delay fuze and ASELSAN’s ASAF-Hard Target Fuze, giving it a role against reinforced and hardened
structures
The three configurations illustrate a broader trend in modern precision weapons: the ability to tailor the weapon effect to the target rather than relying on a single warhead design.
Within the TOLUN family, operators can select between fragmentation, proximity-effect and penetrating capabilities. This potentially allows the same aircraft platform to undertake different types of strike missions while carrying weapons configured for different target characteristics.
Such flexibility is particularly relevant in complex battlefield environments, where targets may range from exposed personnel and lightly protected vehicles to armoured platforms and reinforced buildings.
The integration of TOLUN with the Bayraktar AKINCI further highlights the evolution of unmanned aircraft from surveillance platforms into sophisticated strike systems.
The AKINCI can carry multiple precision weapons, allowing an operator to engage more than one target during a sortie. ASELSAN’s SADAK-4T Multiple Ejector Rack is designed to carry several TOLUN munitions simultaneously, increasing the number of weapons that can be deployed during a single mission.
This combination of an unmanned aircraft, precision guidance and specialised warheads offers a potentially scalable approach to deep-strike operations. Instead of employing different aircraft for different target classes, a single platform can potentially carry a mixture of weapons suited to the mission.
Precision Strike in a More Contested Environment
Another notable element of the demonstration is the emphasis on operating in difficult electronic and environmental conditions.
ASELSAN states that the TOLUN family is designed for day-and-night operations and varying weather conditions. The TOLUN F demonstration also highlighted resistance to GPS spoofing, an increasingly important consideration as electronic warfare becomes a central component of modern military operations.
TOLUN I provides an impact-triggered fragmentation capability, TOLUN F adds proximity-based effects against targets such as armoured personnel carriers, while TOLUN P is designed to defeat reinforced structures through penetration and delayed detonation.
Combined with the Bayraktar AKINCI and the SADAK-4T multiple-ejector system, the family points toward a flexible strike architecture in which one unmanned aircraft can potentially carry several types of precision weapons and attack different targets during the same mission.
The recent demonstration at Konya Karapınar therefore represents more than another weapons test. It highlights the growing sophistication of Turkey’s indigenous precision-strike ecosystem—and the increasing role of unmanned platforms in delivering specialised effects against targets ranging from vehicles to hardened structures.

title: US startup tests cargo drone with 500-lb payload, 450-mile range
content: US drone startup Elroy Air has completed the first autonomous, uncrewed flights authorized under the government’s eVTOL Integration Pilot Program (eIPP). The company conducted the flights using its Chaparral hybrid-electric vertical takeoff and landing aircraft in Louisiana. The week-long demonstrations were carried out with partners and focused on transporting different types of cargo, including medical supplies, food, and industrial equipment.“These test flights demonstrate how these new aircraft can expand cargo delivery options to communities nationwide and improve our logistics infrastructure,” said Bryan Bedford, Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator, in a statement.Chaparral flies autonomouslyElroy Air completed a new series of autonomous, uncrewed flight tests of its Chaparral cargo aircraft under the US Department of Transportation and FAA’s eIPP project. The project aims to safely integrate Advanced Air Mobility aircraft into US airspace, using operational data to shape aviation policy and support wider commercialization.Conducted in Houma, Louisiana, the week-long tests marked the first autonomous and uncrewed flights authorized through the federal program, bringing the aircraft closer to commercial operations. Chaparral flew without a pilot onboard while operating under Air Traffic Control oversight, demonstrating its ability to conduct cargo missions within the National Airspace System. The tests included transporting packages, medical supplies, food, water, and industrial equipment, providing a practical demonstration of the aircraft’s autonomous cargo capabilities. Elroy Air conducted the flights with LIFTOFF Louisiana and Bristow Group, using the tests to evaluate Chaparral in an operational environment relevant to potential commercial deployment across the Gulf Coast. The hybrid-electric VTOL aircraft is designed to carry more than 500 pounds (227 kilograms) of cargo and travel up to 450 miles (724 kilometers). Elroy Air said the latest flights will help inform the company’s efforts to deploy autonomous heavy-cargo aircraft safely and at scale. The tests also generate operational data for the eIPP as regulators and industry partners work toward integrating advanced air mobility aircraft into US airspace.Chaparral features interchangeable cargo pods, enabling operators to adapt the aircraft for different missions without altering its core platform. Its VTOL capability also eliminates the need for runways, fixed delivery infrastructure, or personnel at the destination, expanding its potential use in disaster relief, maritime missions, and remote areas.Chaparral boosts logisticsRecently, Elroy Air expanded the capabilities of its autonomous Chaparral cargo aircraft with three unattended delivery modes developed for the US Army. The new system allows the drone to release supplies while hovering, drop payloads during forward flight, or land and unload cargo autonomously, eliminating the need for personnel or dedicated equipment at the receiving site.The company demonstrated the capabilities during a July 15 flight test at its headquarters in Byron, California. During the test, Chaparral autonomously released a 68-pound (30 kilograms) payload while hovering over a designated target before dropping a second 70-pound (31 kilograms) payload from forward flight at an altitude of 65 feet. Both deliveries used preloaded coordinates and were completed without intervention during the release sequence, demonstrating the system’s ability to operate in communications-denied environments.A separate test demonstrated the aircraft’s autonomous ground delivery capability. After landing, Chaparral released its cargo before taking off again, allowing supplies to be delivered without ground crews or specialized unloading infrastructure.The US Army requested the capabilities under an existing development contract. The new delivery modes are intended to support resupply missions in contested, remote, or infrastructure-limited environments. The same technology could also be applied to commercial logistics operations where conventional delivery infrastructure is unavailable.

title: US stratospheric craft flies 9,300 miles to Japan to beam cell data
content: A U.S.-built high-altitude platform has completed a 9,300 miles journey from New Mexico to Japan. The flight marks Sceye’s first mission in Asia and puts its stratospheric communications system through a major real-world test.Sceye’s Service Test 1 mission launched from New Mexico on Aug. 9. The HAPS spent 13 days crossing the Pacific before entering Japanese airspace, where it worked with SoftBank Corp. on connectivity trials.The mission tested whether a platform flying about 10.3 miles above Earth could provide services normally handled by ground infrastructure. It also examined how the aircraft could support drones and process data in the stratosphere.U.S. platform crosses PacificThe aircraft traveled more than 9,300 miles before reaching its operating area over Japan. It then remained within Japanese-managed airspace for more than seven days.Sceye reported a station-seeking radius as low as 3.1 miles during the mission. That capability matters because HAPS platforms must maintain a tight operating area to provide reliable coverage.The aircraft carried SceyeCELL, the company’s stratospheric telecommunications payload. The system connects directly with standard mobile devices without requiring modified handsets.SoftBank used its core network to test that connection over Japan. Engineers demonstrated text messaging, voice calls, internet access, and video streaming from the stratospheric platform.The tests also included emergency communications. Sceye and SoftBank used an emergency alert system designed for large-scale disasters.Computing moves into stratosphereThe mission also pushed processing beyond the conventional ground-based network. Engineers installed a mobile core network and web server directly aboard the HAPS. Data could therefore move from a smartphone to the platform, undergo processing, and return without relying entirely on an internet cloud service.That setup produced an average round-trip processing time of 68 milliseconds. Sceye said the result cut latency by more than 40% compared with internet-based cloud processing.The aircraft also communicated with drones during the mission. That experiment could help connect aircraft operating at different altitudes through a single communications layer.Sceye CEO Mikkel Vestergaard Frandsen called the flight a defining moment for the company. He said the New Mexico-to-Japan route demonstrated the performance needed to make the stratosphere a viable infrastructure layer.HAPS targets wider coverageSceye sees HAPS as a middle layer between terrestrial networks and satellites. The aircraft can operate far above commercial aviation while staying much closer to Earth than orbital spacecraft.A full-scale Sceye platform could cover an area equivalent to roughly 500 terrestrial towers, according to the company. That could make the technology useful across regions where conventional infrastructure faces coverage or deployment limits.The partnership also reflects SoftBank’s interest in combining ground, aerial, and space-based communications. The Japanese operator invested in Sceye in 2025 to support development of its stratospheric infrastructure.The ST1 aircraft remains in flight and was heading back toward the United States over the Pacific when Sceye announced the results. The mission follows an earlier Sceye endurance flight that traveled more than 6,214 miles from New Mexico toward Brazil.

title: US: 100,000 GPUs to power Figure’s next-generation humanoid robots
content: U.S. robotics firm Figure has signed a strategic partnership with UK-based Nscale to secure large-scale computing capacity for training its next generation of humanoid robot AI models.Under the agreement, Nscale will deploy up to 100,000 GPUs based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform for Figure’s AI development. The partnership aims to address the growing data and compute demands of training models for general-purpose robotics. Figure says the collaboration will provide the computing infrastructure needed to scale its physical intelligence efforts and advance the capabilities of its humanoid robots.Figure expands AIThe new partnership aims to secure large-scale computing infrastructure for training the artificial intelligence systems that power its humanoid robots. The partnership will support deployment of up to 100,000 GPUs based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin platform, with initial deployment targeted for the second half of 2027 in Barstow, Texas.The agreement represents an initial $3.5 billion commitment for computing capacity, with plans to expand the investment to more than $6 billion. Nscale will also make a strategic investment in Figure, while both companies will explore using humanoid robots to support and scale Nscale’s supply chain operations.The computing infrastructure is being developed to address the growing demands of training Helix, Figure’s AI system for humanoid robots. As the company expands its training datasets, the growing volume of physical-world data requires substantially more computational capacity to process and train increasingly capable models.The partnership is designed to create a complete infrastructure pipeline for physical AI, combining large-scale model training with simulation and deployment. It will use NVIDIA’s computing hardware and robotics simulation technologies to train, test, and deploy AI models on humanoid robots, providing the computational foundation needed to advance general-purpose robotic systems.“Nscale and Figure have activated the robotics flywheel: training Figure’s models on NVIDIA Vera Rubin through Nscale’s AI cloud, validating them in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, and deploying them on NVIDIA GPUs in Figure’s robots. This is the physical AI flywheel that will accelerate the path from models to robots in the world,” said Brett Adcock, Founder and CEO, Figure, in a statement.Figure scales IndexRecently, Figure announced that it is scaling Index – a large, continuously expanding dataset of real-world human activity. The platform has surpassed 264,000 downloads across 108 countries and has more than 44,000 weekly active users, with contributors uploading enough video to generate 30 minutes of data every second.According to Figure, Index is designed to capture the diversity and complexity of physical tasks needed to train general-purpose robotic intelligence. Its dataset spans household and workplace activities, covering hundreds of tasks, thousands of objects, and numerous environments, allowing AI models to learn from varied human behavior rather than highly controlled demonstrations.Figure has built its own data pipeline after conventional data suppliers failed to meet the required scale, diversity, and quality. The system automatically filters incoming videos for technical, visual, and semantic quality before human reviewers check samples for fraud and other issues. Videos are also processed for similarity, with duplicate or highly repetitive data removed to preserve dataset diversity.The remaining data is rebalanced according to task requirements and behavioral variation before hierarchical text descriptions are generated for training. The resulting data is intended to improve Helix, Figure’s AI system, by giving it broader exposure to real-world interactions and long-tail physical tasks.Figure has paid $15 million to contributors so far and plans to scale data and compute spending substantially. The broader goal is to create the training infrastructure needed to move humanoid robots from controlled demonstrations toward reliable, general-purpose physical work.

title: Watch: YouTuber tests 50,000-volt system to pull drinking water from Namibia’s fog
content: A 50,000-volt machine designed to extract water from desert fog delivered promising results in garage tests but struggled against salt, wind, and unreliable weather during a real-world trial in Namibia. Jay Bowles, owner of popular Youtube channel called Plasma Channel, transported the experimental device 14,000 kilometers to test it near the Namibian coast with support from University of Namibia researchers in Swakopmund. The goal was to determine whether electrostatic precipitation could offer a practical way to harvest water in one of the world’s driest regions. The machine uses a high-voltage wire to ionize microscopic water droplets suspended in fog. The charged droplets are then drawn toward grounded mesh or metal rods, where they condense and drip into a collector. Garage tests deliver promising results The project began with a smaller two-stake prototype operating at a lower voltage and consuming 39 watts. It was later expanded into a three-stake, double-stacked system that was four times wider than the original version. The upgraded machine also featured solar charging, 3D-printed resin joints that made it easier to transport, and a timer. It was programmed to operate for two minutes before switching off for three minutes between 6 a.m. and 8 a.m. Tests conducted in heavy artificial fog demonstrated how quickly the technology could remove suspended water droplets from the air. Once activated, the machine cleared the surrounding fog almost instantly. A tap was then opened to release the collected water and demonstrate that the system was working. One enlarged version consumed 120 watts while producing 42 milliliters of water per minute. Under those controlled conditions, the device generated approximately 21 milliliters per watt-hour. Producing one liter required about 48 watt-hours of electricity. However, the result represented an ideal laboratory scenario rather than guaranteed field performance. Namibia conditions expose weaknesses Researchers from the University of Namibia provided access to a coastal campus site and shared local knowledge for the experiment. The prototype was assembled on location, installed outdoors, and left in place over several nights while its solar system charged the batteries. However, weather forecasts predicting eight hours of dense fog repeatedly failed to match the conditions at the site. Fog often disappeared after sunset. When it returned, droplets formed on the machine’s rods, but not in sufficient quantities to make the system practical. Salt spray from the Atlantic Ocean also reached the test location despite it being about a kilometer inland. Moisture entered the high-voltage electronics and transformer, causing electrical arcing and equipment failures. Wind placed additional strain on the prototype. Some stakes eventually snapped under the weight of the changing components, further reducing the effectiveness of the collection mesh. Passive nets retain practical advantage Passive fog nets have operated in the same desert for years without using electricity. Although they capture only a portion of airborne droplets, they require little maintenance and can continue functioning in salty coastal conditions. The electrostatic system could potentially capture a larger share of the moisture. However, its energy consumption, exposure to corrosion, and use of dangerous voltage limit its current practicality. Under field conditions, even a fully charged laptop battery might not produce one liter of water. Further development will focus on protecting the electronics from salt, improving wind resistance, and simplifying assembly.

title: Why crypto liquidity is a distributed systems engineering challenge
content: Crypto liquidity looks simple from the outside: tight spreads, visible depth, and prices that stay aligned across venues. Producing that experience consistently is a sophisticated engineering achievement. Behind the order book sits a distributed system that has to synchronize data, manage risk, and coordinate capital across markets operating independently and around the clock.Professional market making is best understood as a distributed, real-time control system operating across exchanges that were never designed as one coherent network. Every venue has its own matching engine, message format, rate limits, clock behavior, and failure modes. Prices move continuously, inventory changes with every fill, and quoting decisions have to be made while the system’s view of the market is already aging.The difficult question is therefore not simply how fast an algorithm can place an order. It is whether dozens of independent systems can maintain a sufficiently accurate shared state, allocate risk and recover from bad data quickly enough to keep the market tradable.State consistency is the foundationTo quote safely, a market maker needs a local representation of each venue’s order book. That sounds simple until a feed drops a message, delivers updates out of order, reconnects after a network interruption, or publishes an incremental update before the client has finished rebuilding its snapshot.This is not an edge case. Exchange documentation explicitly tells clients to monitor sequence gaps and reconstruct books carefully when messages are missing or reordered. A market maker that fails to do this may not merely be “slower.” It may be pricing from a market state that no longer exists.That distinction matters. Imagine the best ask on one exchange disappears, but the cancel message is missed. The local system still believes that liquidity exists and may calculate its fair value, hedge route, or quote width using a phantom price level. If the mistake persists for even a short period, the system can post quotes that sophisticated takers immediately recognize as stale.The engineering challenge is therefore closer to maintaining a fault-tolerant distributed database than reading a price ticker. Book reconstruction, sequence validation, heartbeat monitoring, and resynchronization logic are part of the trading stack because accurate state is what allows accurate pricing.Latency is a budget, not a single numberLow latency matters, but talking about “the latency” of a market-making system is misleading. There is a chain of delays between an event occurring somewhere in the market and a new quote becoming actionable.At the basic level, algorithmic trading systems depend on live market data, network connectivity, and integrated order execution. Professional market making adds a harder requirement: the feed has to reach the trading system, be parsed and normalized, update fair value and risk, pass controls, and reach the venue fast enough for the resulting quote to remain relevant.That means the relevant engineering question is not whether one component is written in a fast language. It is where the latency budget is being spent and how variable that delay becomes during load spikes.A system that is consistently 8 milliseconds behind may be easier to model than one that is usually 2 milliseconds behind but occasionally stalls for 40. Tail latency matters because the worst delays often arrive during the exact periods when market data volume, cancellations, and volatility are all surging together.Recent work on centralized crypto markets found that higher public-feed delay was associated with wider quoted spreads and thinner displayed depth. That makes feed delay more than a back-end performance statistic; it can become an observable signal of liquidity quality.This is also why infrastructure placement can matter. Some institutional platforms recommend deploying systems in the same cloud region as their infrastructure for lower latency. But geographic proximity alone does not solve the problem. A fast network path is wasted if the application pauses on garbage collection, blocks on logging, waits on a shared database, or serializes risk checks behind a congested queue.The order book is not the marketAnother subtle engineering problem is that each exchange only exposes a local view.A token may look liquid on Venue A and thin on Venue B. A move may begin on a derivatives venue, propagate into spot markets, and then be reflected in correlated pairs. A market maker therefore has to estimate a cross-venue fair value from partially asynchronous information.This is where normalization becomes more than converting JSON into a common schema. Different venues can use different tick sizes, contract specifications, fee schedules, funding mechanisms, and definitions of order state. Even timestamps are not always directly comparable because exchange clocks and local clocks can drift.A robust system has to decide which venue is leading price discovery at a given moment, how much confidence to assign to each feed, and whether an apparent arbitrage still exists after fees, executable size, and latency are included.That makes fair value an inference problem. The market maker is not reading “the” crypto price from anywhere. It is continuously estimating one from a set of noisy, asynchronous observations.For exchanges and token projects, this is where a professional crypto liquidity provider becomes part of the market infrastructure rather than simply an external trading counterparty. A strong service combines cross-venue pricing, continuous two-sided liquidity, inventory management, and execution infrastructure so that users see tighter, deeper, and more consistent markets across changing conditions.Inventory turns market making into a control problemQuoting both sides of the market creates inventory. If a market maker is repeatedly hit on its bid, it accumulates the asset. If traders keep lifting its ask, inventory moves the other way.That means the quoting system has two objectives that can conflict. It wants to provide competitive prices, but it also wants to prevent inventory from drifting into an unwanted directional position.One way to think about this is as feedback control. Inventory is the state variable. Quote skew, displayed size, and hedging are control inputs. Volatility, toxic flow, and cross-venue price movement are disturbances.The system may respond to a long inventory position by making its ask more attractive, its bid less aggressive, or by hedging elsewhere. But every response has a cost. Hedging aggressively can cross spreads and pay fees. Widening quotes protects the market maker but reduces liquidity quality. Pulling too much size can make a token’s book look fragile precisely when traders need depth most.Recent live-trading research on crypto market making illustrates why strategy design and risk parameters have to be tested against real order flow rather than judged only from static backtests. The point is not that one model “wins” universally. It is that live performance depends on how quoting logic, signals, and inventory controls interact with actual market microstructure.Capital is another distributed resourceCrypto adds a constraint that traditional systems engineers would immediately recognize: the system may know where capital is needed but still be unable to move it there instantly.Balances are fragmented across venues. Transfers can be slowed by blockchain confirmation times, exchange withdrawal controls, banking rails, or internal risk limits. A market maker can therefore be globally well capitalized and still become locally constrained on one venue.This creates a capital-allocation problem alongside the latency problem. If too much inventory accumulates on one exchange, the provider may have to reduce quoting there even when its total balance sheet is healthy.The strongest systems therefore treat capital almost like capacity in a distributed compute cluster: it has to be forecast, reserved, and rebalanced before local scarcity becomes a bottleneck. Venue-level balances, expected fills, hedge demand and transfer times all feed into the question of how much liquidity the system can safely promise at each location.Resilience and recovery are part of liquidity qualityCalm markets show how a system performs under normal conditions, but resilience becomes most visible when activity accelerates.The engineering test becomes more demanding when a WebSocket feed pauses, a venue starts rejecting orders, an API changes behavior, a price feed diverges, or message volume jumps several times above normal.At that point, a well-designed system can adapt safely. It may switch to a backup feed, widen quotes, reduce size, isolate one venue, or trigger a kill switch. What matters is not simply uptime, but whether the architecture can preserve accurate pricing and controlled risk as conditions change.This is one reason book recovery logic deserves as much attention as quote generation. A disconnected venue is obvious. A venue that remains connected while the local book is silently wrong is more dangerous.The useful metrics are therefore operational: stale-quote rate, spread uptime, depth retention during volatility, rejected-order frequency, hedge completion time, recovery time after a feed gap, and the percentage of time each local book is verified as synchronized.Those measurements reveal more about real liquidity infrastructure than a screenshot of a tight spread taken during a quiet hour.How to evaluate the engineering behind liquidityBoth token projects and exchanges have reasons to evaluate the engineering behind liquidity, although they approach it from different positions. A token project may assess whether a provider can maintain consistent liquidity for its asset across venues. At the same time, an exchange may evaluate whether the infrastructure can support reliable pricing and depth across the markets it operates in. In both cases, the useful starting point is to look beyond a single spread snapshot or exchange count. Tight pricing and broad venue coverage matter, but the more revealing question is how consistently the service maintains depth, pricing quality, and operational continuity as market conditions change. Strong providers can explain the architecture behind that consistency and support it with meaningful performance data.Liquidity is an engineering outcomeThe deepest misconception about market making is that liquidity is created simply by posting more orders. In practice, the order book is only the visible interface.Behind it sits a system that has to keep market data synchronized, infer fair value from fragmented venues, price inventory risk in real time, allocate capital, and recover cleanly from disruptions while preserving quote quality.That is why two firms can connect to the same exchanges and trade the same assets yet produce very different execution quality. The difference is not just the quoting model. It is how effectively the entire system maintains synchronization, allocates capital, and adapts when market conditions change.As crypto markets get faster and more institutionally competitive, these demands become a clearer measure of infrastructure quality. The strongest systems are not only fast, but consistently accurate, resilient, and capital-efficient across a full range of market environments.

title: FAW Hongqi's perovskite solar sunroof prototype targets 80 km of added EV range
content:
FAW Hongqi's perovskite solar sunroof prototype targets 80 km of added EV range
FAW's Hongqi brand has built what it calls the industry's first perovskite photovoltaic sunroof prototype, integrating the material directly onto curved automotive safety glass rather than using conventional crystalline silicon. Fitted to the Hongqi EHS7 electric SUV, marketed in China as the Hongqi Tiangong 08, the sunroof can generate up to 300 W of power under strong sunlight and around 400 kWh over a year. The technology remains at the prototype stage, with no mass-production timeline disclosed.
Hongqi EHS7, which is marketed in China with the name Tiangong 08. Photo: CarNewsChina
The EHS7/Tiangong 08 is a five-passenger SUV measuring 4,925 mm long, 1,950 mm wide, and 1,680 mm tall, with 253 kW (339 hp) of peak power and a WLTP-rated range of 475 km. Hongqi said it passed over crystalline silicon for the sunroof because the material is fragile and offers lower efficiency for the application, choosing perovskite instead for its light weight, thinness, flexibility, high light-to-electricity conversion efficiency, tunable coloring, and lower cost. Integration wasn't without difficulty: perovskite's known vulnerability to water, oxygen, and ultraviolet exposure, combined with the curved geometry of the sunroof glass, reportedly posed challenges for the development team.
For now, the roughly 400 kWh the sunroof generates annually is intended to power low-voltage functions such as air conditioning, refrigeration, and sentry mode rather than propulsion. Hongqi's roadmap calls for extending perovskite photovoltaic elements to other body panels, including the hood; if that expanded panel area is realized, the company projects up to 10 kWh of generation per day, enough to add roughly 80 km of range daily. Hongqi cites its own data showing that distance would cover more than 85% of Chinese drivers' daily travel needs, though the 80 km figure remains a development target rather than a confirmed production spec.
The sunroof prototype is one piece of a broader push by Hongqi in the battery-electric vehicle market: the brand's next-generation models are set to adopt BYD's fast-charging technology, said to take a battery from 10% to 97% charge in nine minutes, and Hongqi has also begun testing a solid-state battery prototype with an energy density of 380 Wh/kg.
The sunroof is a separate effort from
a flexible perovskite photovoltaic roof program FAW has pursued with module supplier Mellow Energy
, which uses flexible, module-based construction validated at up to 21.79% efficiency rather than Hongqi's rigid, glass-integrated design. Between the two, FAW has now disclosed two distinct automotive perovskite PV efforts within the same week.

title: 'Do not wait until you feel completely ready' - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
This week, Women in Solar+ Europe gives voice to Angelica Almi, Head of Legal at Kataclima and co-founder of Italia Rinnovabile. Her message is clear: approach every professional relationship with curiosity, respect and authenticity, turn challenges into strengths, and embrace unexpected opportunities with courage and enthusiasm.
Women in Solar+ Europe
04 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Angelica Almi
I never imagined that I would work in renewable energy. Then I realised how difficult it is to imagine a future without energy: it is part of who we are, how we live, produce and build our communities. The real challenge is not whether we will need energy, but how we choose to produce it, share it and manage its impact.
Working in the legal department of a company operating in the energy sector has taught me that the transition is never simply about technology, infrastructure or regulation. Every project has a tangible impact on people and territories and belongs to an ecosystem where technical, legal, economic and social expertise must learn to interact. I entered this world as a legal professional and quickly discovered that staying comfortably within legal boundaries was not really an option. That is probably what continues to fascinate me.
Being a young woman in a still predominantly male industry has sometimes meant earning credibility before having the opportunity to fully demonstrate my abilities. Overall, however, my experiences have been overwhelmingly positive. I have always preferred results to introductions and, I admit, being underestimated does not bother me too much; it makes the result more satisfying. I have also learned that expertise does not mean knowing everything. It means recognising what we do not know, remaining curious enough to learn and gradually turning our limitations into new skills.
Trust has been fundamental throughout this journey. I have been fortunate to work with a CEO who valued what I could already bring, encouraged me to develop new skills and, above all, gave me the space and time to build my own professional identity rather than expecting me to become a reflection of someone else. As a legal professional, I place enormous value on the intuitus personae that grows through competence, reliability and the quality of professional relationships. Today, I believe it is equally important to give others the trust and space that were given to me.
One of my most important proving grounds has been Italia Rinnovabile, which I co-founded and helped build from a legal perspective, from its foundations through its continuing evolution. I am also particularly proud of supporting Renewable Energy Communities in Verona and Forlì-Cesena, from start-up through to management. Every experience brings new perspectives. In my work, one size rarely fits all, and when it does, I tend to be suspicious. Every project has its own identity, needs and challenges: the real task is to build the legal solution that best fits its reality.
The same applies to people. I work predominantly with men, but I have never seen my work as an interaction between men and women. I meet people and professionals I can learn from and to whom I can contribute something in return. We do not always agree, and that is often where the interesting part begins. Respect, however, remains non-negotiable, even when firmly defending our positions. Ultimately, we are working towards the same goal: the better the quality of our dialogue, the better the outcome we can build together.
To a young woman entering this industry today, I would say: stay curious, do not wait until you feel completely ready, and, above all, do not be discouraged by difficulties; turn them into your strength. Study, work and listen, but never lose your own identity. And have fun. Taking your work seriously does not mean taking yourself too seriously. Enthusiasm and enjoyment fuel curiosity, creativity and courage. Sometimes, the most interesting opportunities arise precisely in places where we never imagined we would find ourselves.
Angelica Almi is an in-house legal professional, qualified to practise law in Italy, and Head of Legal at Kataclima S.r.l. Società Benefit, where she focuses on energy and renewable energy law, corporate contracts, company law, regulatory compliance and relations with public authorities and institutional stakeholders. She is also Co-Founder of Italia Rinnovabile Società Cooperativa Benefit, contributing to the legal and regulatory development of Renewable Energy Communities and their organisational and financing models. She holds a Law degree and a postgraduate Master’s degree in Cooperative Enterprise: Economics, Law and Management. Her work combines legal expertise, a business-oriented perspective and a strong focus on the impact of the energy transition on territories and communities.
